div.head: LEGAL FIRST AID.
div.p: LEGAL FIRST AID.
ANCIENT LIGHTS.

What ar,) called rights of light, or ancient lights, form a frequent bone ,of contention between neighbours. These rights come in question in this kind of 'way: 'lour back win- dows open on your neighbour's land, mid he, in erecting a wall or "other building, darkens your • dwelling by intercepting the light which would otherwise come to your back windows. How far can you object to this? It may be said at once that you have no natural right to light for your house. You can only gam ,such .a right by agreement with or pur- chase from your neighbour, or by the lapse of time, in the same way that you can claim support for your buildings from your neigh. bour's land.
A. RIGHT OF LIGHT.

In deciding how far you can 'object to this darkening of your lights, you should first ask this question : Did the owner of my house ever have granted to him, by the owner of the adjoining land, a right of light? When your landlord built that house he knew, or ought to have known, that the back windows were in such a position that they were liable at any time to be darkened by the erection of a high wall or other structure on the adja- cent plot. He ought, as a prudent man, to have gone to the owner of that adjacent plot and made a bargain like this: "I will give you so much if you will agree not to build so as to diminish the light of • the house I pro- pose to build." If the neighbouring land- owner agreed, their he would have signed, sealed, and delivered to your landlord a deed by which he gave- a right of light for, say, six windows in such and such positions'. When you find your windows darkened, or about to be darkened by your neighbour, the first thing to do is to consult your landlord and ask him if any such 'right of light was ever given. If "Yes," then your position is the strongest possible. You can insist on your neighbour stopping his building' operations, and if he 'fetuses to stop you can apply to the Chancery Court for an injunction to compel him to desist.

div.head: QUESTION OF TIME.
div.p: A QUESTION OF TIME.

Suppos3 there was no such agreement be, tween the two landowners, such as I have described, the next question to be asked is: How long have those windows been there? If they have been there without being darkened for twenty years, you have an absolute right to the light, and crin prevent your neighbour from obscuring it. But if there was no expres .grant of a right of light, and less than twenty veors have expired since the windoWN were put there, you are quite helpless to pre- vent your light from being cut off.

div.head: AN ABANDONED RIGHT,
div.p: AN ABANDONED RIGHT,

If you have a right, of light for a par- ticular window, you can only dose that right by abandoning it, even if for a hundred years the window is built up, or the house is pulled down. You may abandon Your right if you like, and the Courts will Often infer that you intend to abandon it from the mere fact that for a long time you have not used it. For instance, you have a iiglit of light, twenty years old; for a window in your second-floor back bedroom. Then, to suit your owa convenience, you board the window up. This does not give your neighbour a right to obstruct the light where the window used to be. But if you keep the window boarded up for years, and allow your neigh- bour to erect a building close up on that. side without giving him any notice of your claim, you will be presumed to have abandoned the right of light for that window. Most Londoners have seen boards, bearing the legend "Ancient Lights," hung upon the outer walls of houses in the City. ,This announcement, mysterious to many, 'simply means that in the place where the board now I s there used to be a window, in respect of which the owner had a right of light; and the . board is placed there with that inscrip- tion upon it to warn all and sundry neigh- bours not to build So as to obstruct the light which falls upon that space, ' because the owner may want to insert a window there again at some future time.

div.head: DEATH OF M. C. H. BINDLOSS.
div.p: DEATH OF M. C. H. BINDLOSS.

The many friends of Air. Charles Henry Bindloss, Ellesmere-road Stockton Heath, were shocked to hear of his death which took place at the Warrington Infirmary on Saturday. evening last after a short illness. It appears that deceased was taken ill last Friday week and was admitted to the Infirmary on Friday following when an operation was performed upon him for appendicitis. Peritonitis ensued and he died on Saturday evening at 5.45. Mr. Bindloss who was 25 years of age was the son of Mr. Edwin William Bindloss of Liverpool (formerly Of Warrington) and brother of Mr. Harold Bindloss the well-known novelist He. was educated: at.. the University Colleue, Liverpool and had been on the staff of Nlessrs. Pearson and Knowles f.,r 9 years. He was fond of sport and as captain of the Warring- ton Royal Hockey Club led his side to victory on many occasions. Mr. Bindloss was a member of the Samuel Wakefield Lodge' of the R.A.0.8. Fourteen months ago he married liss K. Graham of Wigton N. 8., and niece of Mr. W. :McClure of -Latchforch Much sympathy is fit with her in her sudden bereavement.

div.head: £5 AND COSTS FOR "RECEIVING."
div.p: £5 AND COSTS FOR "RECEIVING."

At the Borough Police Court on Thursdey. Alice Ann Fitzgerald of Guardiar-strret, was charged with receiv-. ing 10 men's shirts and two pairs of men pants value .£1 45., from Ernest Grayson, the prooerty of the London and North-Western Railway, Company, well knowing them to have been stolen, en November 28th. She pleaded "sot guilty."—Mr. Tait, of Euston, prose- cuted on behalf of the railway company and said defendant was the wife of Robert-Fitzgerald, who was a cripple,, hut was employed in Warrington. The defendant kept a small shop in Guardian-street. On Saturday, November 27th, 48 men's shirts and 24 rairs of men's pants were stolen from a skip in Bank Quay siding. Seven men were before the Court last Thurs- day, charged with stealing them, among whom• was Ernest Grayson who pleaded guilty. He said be sold 10 shirts and two pails of pants to defendant on Sun- day, November 2ith, for its. , In consequence of intormation received Detective's Itsddington and Clarke and Sergeant Meacock went to .the house of the defendant at 2 o'clock on the morning of Deem' er sth. They saw defendant and told her, they had come for some shirts that Grayson had sold to her. In reply she pointed to bbundle and said that there were only six shirts. She then denied having received any more. The officers left, but in consequence of further information they again visited the defendant. She again denied having received more than six hut after telling her that they would have to search the house end pointed out the seriousness of her position if any more were found she admitted that she had received four more shirts and two pairs of pants. The officer then asked her why rbe did not admit it at first, and she replied " I was frightened of the disgrace." She had failed to make the proper inquiries as to where the shirts had come from, as the same and address of the owner was stitched on the collar. She also paid a ridicuously small price for them. It was people like defendant who encouraged stealing, as they were always ready to receive property without maikng inquiries as to where it bad come from. The Company had suffered considerable from that kind of thing in Warlington.—Detective Reddington bore out Mr. Tait's statements.—Defendant sled she had no idea that Gras son had come by the goods dishonestly. She had known him for a long time,,and thought he was an honest man.—The Chairman (Mr. C. White) said they were sorry to see a woman of defendant's position where she was. She would be finedl's and costa or two months' imprisonment.

div.head: liVarrington Boraugh Court.
div.p: liVarrington Boraugh Court.
SATURDAV.—Before Megns. J. W. Hayward (in the ehair), R. T. Fairclough, A. J. Jolley, and T. Pemberton.

NEGITCT AND CONTEMPT.—Ricburd Weaver, of 51, Eldon-street. was charged with neglecting his children in a manner likely to cause them unnecessary suff4ring end injury to health.—He pleaded guilty.—Mr. A. Browne prosecuted on behalf of the- INT.S.P.C.C.. and said that prisoner was at the present time occupied in going out with a cart, gathering revs and bones. Pre- viously he was employed by Mr. Toole in Allen-street as a carter at 18s. a week, but left for a very trivial cause. He had been doing occasional work, earning anything from Bs. 6d. to 14s. a week. The charge arainst him was that he was always eoing away. Every Saturday be would leave his wife absolutely starving, and go to his sister's house, and stay there until Sunday night or ATonday moraine. Only the previous Saturday his wife found him there. He was drunk and lying asleep on the conch. 'lnstead of going to walk he wont off drinkine, and left his wife and children to the mercies of the neighbours. Irspector Wainwright had warned him time 'after time.—Prisoner was sentenced to two months hard lahour.—On going down the steps from the dock be shouted to his wife who was in Court "1 will he hung for you when I come ont."—The Clerk : He deserves an increase of sentence for that.— The Chairman (to theofficer) : Bring him tip again.— On prisoner being brought un again, the Chairman said tha% after his conduct in Court that morning, the magis- trates would make the sentence six months instead of two months.

ARREARS ON iIiAIIiTENANCE.—John Kirby of Chester- road, was brought up on a warrant for maintenance, due to his wife to the amount of Li 2s. 6d.—Mr. A. Browne appeared for prisoner's wife and said the case arose out of a case of desertion heard at the last Dares- bury Sessions and an order was made allowine corn ,onant Gs. a week until prisoner go: work, and then be (Mr. Bro-ane) was to apply to the magistrates for more. She now wanted her money and defendant had not paid a halfpenny.—The Case NVMS adjourned for four weeks to give prisoner a chance to pay the money. —Henry Miller, St. Ansten's-lane, was also charged with a similar offence. He was ordered to pay the money at once or go to gaol for two months.

TUESDAY.—I3.fnre Councillor H. Roberts (in the chair) Alderman Bolton, Conncillor Jackson Holmes. Messrs. J. Rymer Young, V. Richardson, and Dr. Markel. FALSE ATTESTATICN.—WiIIiam Bentley, was charged with making a false answer when enlisting in King's Liverpool Regiment.—He was sentenced to 14 days' impriscnment.

" RAN " CHILD r.Fs WITH A KN I FE.—Chnrles Shaw, Edward-street, wits charged with having been drunk and disorderly the previous day.—P.C. Skelton said he saw prisoner running a lot of children with a butcher's knife. On catching him prisoner became very violent. He was fined 10s. and costs or 14 days.
FRinAy.—Before tha Mayor (in the chair) and other
migistrates.

PR I SONE R'S STRANGE BEHAVIOUR. - George Postlethwaite, a youth. was rernaneed for 7 days on the charge of stealing 28 lbs. of scrap iron.—The Chief Constable said that priscner was seen by P.C. Clarke in liuttermarket-street, the previous day with a quantity of scrap iron in his posse‘sion.—The officer was not satisfied with his explanation and took him into custody. Whilst at the Police Station he behaved in a manner which led them to think that he was rot in his right mind. He tore up his clothes and attempted to strangle himself with his braces.—On being removed from the dock after the case was remanled prisoner attempted *e throw himself down the steps lending to the cells but was fortunately prevented by an officer standing by.

ASSAULT ON IS FATBEII.—For assanll ing his father by striking a 1-1 him, and for being drunk and disorderly, William Bramhall, 48, Marsh House-lane was sent to prison for three months. MAINTENANCE REDUCED.—An application for reduc- tion of maintenance order was made by Robert Connellr Brookes 12. Bewsey-road.—Mr. Steel, uho appeared on behalf of the applicaut, said that the maintenance order was made in May last 'for him to contribute 15s. weekly towards the support of his wife. Since the order had been made defendant had not beon earning the same wages. Mrs. Brooks had been ,earning some money ea managerers at one of her brother's shops in Noriliwich.—The magistrates reduced the order to 12s. weekly.
WARRINGTON COUNTY PETTY SESSIONS. WILDNESDAY.—Before Messrs. Charles White (chairman), W. P. Rylands, C. E. Parker and Councillor H. Roberts.

A NIONTII FOR TJIEFT is 100G.—Thotras Lawrence wss charged with stealing on August 4th, 1006, a gold watch curb, value £4, the property of Louisa Jane Crompton, Heald House Farm. Earlestown.—Arthur Crompton, farm bailiff and hrother of the prosecutor said that the curb was left in a drawer in a bedroom. Whilst they were out and when they returned they found it had gone. The bedroom window was open. Prisoner, lived next door to them.—Mary Jane Trigg, • 27, Grafton-street, Earleatown, sister of the prisoner said that prisoner took the curb to her about three years ago and asked her to sell it for him. She asked where he got it from and he said he found it amongst some cinders. She sold it to Mr. Hatrison for 15s. and her brother gave her 2s. Thomas Harrison,insorance agent 399, Bolton-road, Ashton-in-Makerfield, said that be bought it for 159. and handed it over to the police last, Sunday.—P.C. Litmie said that he received informa- tion about the robbery on December 12th, and went to Mr. Harrison and recovered the curb. From further inquiries made be arrested prisoner.—The Chairman asl4ed how it was that it had been recovered and he was told thatathe police kept their eyes open about it and no information could be ascertteated,sooner.—Prisoner said that, he only received is. td. for it. was sentenced to one month's imprisonment.

div.head: NOTES BY " OVALIST."
div.p: NOTES BY " OVALIST."
How to see Warrington thrasb Barrow and hear Churchill mince up the Lords, is a problem which has taxed many great minds during the week without much result. A solution is still needed.

The £25 fine has been paid, and Stuntz and the C tub are at liberty to take it out in points. Barrow come at rather an unfortunate time for themselves and need expect little mercy at Wilderspool. War- rington's score ought to be somewhere up in the thirties, if not higher. Having been out to grass for a fortnight the men are more than a trifle keen.

The other matebes to-day are as follow :-- 8 3 Rochdale Hornets v. Batley. 30 3 Bradford v. York. 41 7 Hull v. Bramlef. 19 8 Wigan v. Broughtoa Rangers. 5 5 Dewsbury v. Huddersfield. Widnes v. Ebbw Vale. 14 3 Halifax v. Lef ds.
22 8 Humlet v. Hull Kingston Rovers. 35 3 Witkefleld Trinity v. Keighley. 8 0 Swinton v. Leigh. 0-10 Treherbert v. Merthyr Tydvil. 13 —0 Oldhami v. St. Helens. 7-18 Salford v. Runcorn.

There have been some interesting results since our last issue, and one wquel is that Warrington are now second in the league, thanks to the defeat of Salford at St. Helens. The Saints have had a good week-end, as they followed up Saturday's performance with a fine win at Swinton on Monday. The one big blot on their record is that 37-5 beating from Oldham. They go to Watersheddings to-day, and I should 1 ke toblay very long odds that they are not beaten by anything like such a margin again.

Another club which has had the temerity to startle the football world is Ebbw Vale, described as the Welsh champiGns. They have been quietly strengthen- ing their t' am, and the way they took in and did for Hunslet on Saturday and Leigh on Miinday should give warning to other teams who have yet to invade the Welsh fastnesses. Leigh seem to have struck a bad patch just lately, and I feel more and more con- timed that they will ga down before Warrington next Saturday.

Wigan also are showing erratic trm, and they were lucky even to draw at Widnes on Wednesday. The locals ran them all over the field and were leading five minutes from the dose, ,when I.2.ytham charged a weak kick by a home defender and got a soft try. The result practically puts Wigan out of court so far, as the South West Lancashire competition is concerned.

WIDNES OUTPLAYED AF BATLEY.

Batley's victory over Widnes at Mount Pleasant was not unexpected, Litt it was runt%) complete than the Lancastrians had barga'ned for-12 points to nil. Widnes played the team that beat Runcorn last week, whilst Batley %Are without Will Davies, Settle, and Fozzard. From the start the ball was controlled by the home forwards who got wassession in nearly every scrummage, and the visitors hal little or no chance of distinguishing themselves. Jack Joncs played a fine game' tut Haigh (from the second tam), who was given a trial of " flying " half mulled pass after pass, and the home passing machinery lacks down. Jones soon scored a try, and ‘Vattie Davies dropped two goals before the interval. _

On rEsurning Davies, tits) made a try for Ward, and then kicked a goal. Widnes had a few openings in the second half, but they allowed them to go a-begging, and Batley ran out et sy %inners by 3 goals 2 tries to nil.
GREAT GAME AT ST. HELENS.-SALFORD LOSE.

This home fixture of St. Helens, which attracted a great crowd, was productive of a fast and exciting game, the issue hanging in the balance till the call of time. The openingostages were of an even character, until St. Helens took up an attacking position, and for an informality against Salford C. Creevey succeeded in landing a flue goal. The ground, which was in a sodden condition was responsible for several break. downs as the results of-toad combination, the leather being d fticult to - hold. St. Helens were penalised twice in quick succession, but Alesley and Lomas failed to pilot the ball. Preston broke away at the centre, with Lomas in attendance, and, being unopposed, he scored a grand try at the corner. Lomas's kick at goal went wide. Half-time score :—Salford 1 try (3 points), St. Helens 1 gool (2 points). After the usual breather Salford at once got dangerous, Cook and Lomas being accounted for close in. " Mitt" Creevey ran off-side in his own half, but Lomas again failed to put the ball over the bar. St. Helens invaded the Salford quarters, and from a penalty Turtillgaue his side the lead with a neat place-kick In the closing stages St. Helens rallied, and from passing between Flanagan, Creevey, and Kelly, the latter grounded the ball over the line. C, Creevey failed to improve from an easy position. Result 1 try (3 points).
PEARSON & KNOWLES v. WIDNES WHITE STAR.
Pe3rson and Knowles visited Widnes on Saturday last and were defeated by It points to 3, Ashton scoring' for the visitors.
To-day (December 18th) Pearson and Knowles engage in a friendly match with the St Helens Ca,-)le Co., and on Christmas Day they will meet Rylands Bros.' Recreation Club at Widnes.

div.head: FOOTBALL GOSSIP.
div.p: FOOTBALL GOSSIP.
BY B. BENNISON.
ILLUSTRATED BY JACK DODWORTH.

I doubt whether any other footballer has made so much money out of the sport as Jack Sharp, of Everton. And everybody who kpows him Will agree that he is worthy of all the good fortune that has come his V;ay. Sharp has. a great natu- ral gift for playing games, but in a fascinating way, it has been dogged that does it with the clean-limbed young man who upholds the best traditions of Lancash;re County cricket in the summer, and who plays such a distinguished game in the winter- months for Everton. Sharp. is the typo of man who maps out his career in early youth, and does not deviate one bit from the line along which ho proposes ‘4:o travel until he has got "right there." When Sharp left his home in Hereford, .where he played for the Thistle in company with his brother Bert, he went to Aston Villa. If I mistake not, Bert was regarded more favourably by the Birmingham officials; it is at least true that in and around Hereford Bert was thought to be the better footballer; but we know that he did not fulfil

expectations. Jack went one better than most people iniagined, and if ever the Villa regretted parting company with a player it must surely have been when Sharp took himself to Everton. The Man for a Crisis. But it is not as a footballer alone that Sharp has made his mark. Always playing cricket well, like his brother, he set out to perfect him- eelf at John Stanuing's nursery at Leyland, and

when he appeared fa the Lancashire team, somewhat raw and inexperienced, it may be, one knew because of the very stamp of the man that he would win renown, not quickly but in the end, by his patience and insatiable desiro to work and become indispensable to his adopted county. Sharp as a cricketer first took hold of one as a fhtlter—a man for a crisis. He began by finding -his way readily to the wickets; then he generally made runs when they were wanted, and by patient toil demanded a place in the English team last season. He has already had his benefit at Evcrton, which brought him seve- ral hundred pounds; next cricket season the Lancashire and Yorkshire match will be set apart as his reward, and if the weather be bud 11,- will increase his balance at the bankers by £2,000 at the least. I have written thus about Sharp with the idea of demonstrating to the younger school of footballers that, despite tte ridiculous limit- wage, they have every opportunity, barring accident, of course, of becoming men of sub- stance. Sharp has never relied upon football for his sole income; and I see no reason why all footballers should not devote their 'time and attention to some other business besides cbasing the big ball—that is, of course, if they have the opportunity. The greater part of a pro- fessional's life is profitlessly spent, and I shall al- ways hold that he puts too much time in at the ground, training, so it is said, but in most case's surfeited with football and all that hangs upon it. And in this way he has his imagination killed. David and Uoliath. The draw for the first round of the English Cup has given rise to a. discussion "which, I sup- pose, was inevitable about some of our preten- tious teams having to make long journeys, with little prospect of reaping any profit, in order to meet some little club whose average takings are not more than £5O a week, perhaps less, and who may be writ down as being only third-class. Some people have enlarged upon the absurdity of the thing; for instance, the question has been
A little known club who have got into the first round of the Cup resent the idea that they will be beaten by the Go!laths they are to meet.

asked, How can it be possible for Accrington Stanley to expect to escape a terrible hiding when they meet Blackburn Rovers? The match is counted as being as good as over; and Man- chester City are sympathised with because they are 'asked to go as far as Workington, while West Ham are supposed to be able-to walk over against Carlisle. Now, why should there not be these ties, though the difference in the strength of the teams is great, and if there were such a thing as "form," a runaway for the better known and more expensive teams? If ‘,Blackburn Rovers, who are sticking to the leadership of the First League in a way that is most com- mendable, do not cause Accrington to make a hurried exit from the competition it will be an astounding thing; but the extraordinary has happened and will happen again, so long as the English Cup competition lasts. The Rovers may reasonably assume that they are certain to enter the second round; but I would like to know whether Manchester City, improved wonderfully though they be, relish the idea of going to Workington? And as for West Him, they may be unpleasantly surprised at Carlisle. Good luck to the little clubs, say I. If they are clever enough to creep into the competition propei, then the fact that they are linked up with a team with a great reputation gives piquancy to the competition; it is its raison d'être; the big clubs must*take the rough with the smooth; they cannot pick and choose their opponents, and this is why I dislike the selling of territorial privileges to the highest bidder. The Poor Deutcher. •

- - The English amateur is supreme/in games with Continental sides, and I do not suppose that the general football public for this very reason troubles very much about him or his football be- yond looking at the result of the match in which

he engages. Holland came to Chelcea, .and, as everybody knows, were beaten by nine 'goals to one. Now this result is apt to create quite a wrong idea; it is supposed, I do not doubt, that the Englishmen had nothing to beat. This, in a way, is true, for the Dutehman, though he is in deadly earnest, and draws upon his strength to the last ounce, has no reat cleverness; but to those who are disposed to believe that dribbling and good, hard, first -line shooting are a lost art, the play of our amateurs, granted that they had no formidable team to contend with, was quite refreshing, inasmuch as it proved beyond question that there is nothing like individuality. The man who can run with the ball at his toes, controlling it completely, is the man after my own neart. wooaward ana tserry, to mention only two of the English forwards, flabbergasted the Dutchmen, who must now know that even the good, hard tackle and the big:_kick can be circumvented by the footballv 7.1D0 C 1 $I SIATOUgh on Itils OWn,

div.head: ARTS AND CRAFTS SOCIETY.
div.p: ARTS AND CRAFTS SOCIETY.
Exhibition Opened by MN. A. H.
Crosfield.

The admirable work which the Warrington Arts and Crafts Society is doing in promoting and develop- ing artistie taste and culture is well illustrated at the annual exhibitiov. which was opened in Trinity Chambers, Market Gate, on Tuesday afternoon and will continue until; nine o'clock this (Saturday)evening Lovers of art will find much to interest them and it is due to the Society to say that, generally speaking, the work reaches a high standard worthy of the traditions of the town. The exhibits number 163 and most of the pictures are by local artists. Our towns- man Mr. Oswarld Garside, who is making for him- self a great reputation in the artistic 'world, sends some choice and well varied pro- ducts of his undoubted genius, and all are charactPrised by delicacy of treatment and Subtle colour effects. "Twilight on the Loggia "is one of the most beautiful of his studies. Mrs. Houghton exhibits some charming work, a pastel sketh of the little fishing village of Ruswick fully realising the quaint setting and peaceful atmosphere of the place. Another of Mrs. Houghton's most striking efforts is "Blackberries." It is a pretty picture of happy child-life, and the colouring is iu the best of taste. Mrs. Houghton has another really fine sketch of a chubby, smiling infant, which is full Of freshness and life--a speaking study. Mr. C.'‘Mawson, A:R:0 A., has a clever illustration of still life, the tone being remarkably good. Miss G. W. Ridgway contributes an excellent piece of portraiture—" An old gardeners after the day's work" and a number of pleasing sketche : Miss Jessie M. King's exquisite drawing "The dance" has attracted much admiration. Miss Helen Fairclough, to whom much of the credit for the formation of the society is due, shows some highly creditable work: Mrs. Henry Kimber has s me delightful landscape studies, marked by refreshing vigour and rich colour- ing. Mrs. Gertrude Pidduck, A.R.C.A., sends a most attinctive series of paintings and etchings, conspicuous being a charming study of " Evening.' Mr. Ikarold K. Gornall's sketch of" Winter: Toronto" is original and „full of suggestion. Miss M. P. Sefton's picture of " Bardsea " is notable for the lovely sunshine effects and agreeable tone. Mr. A. Hayward, secretary of the society, shows several sea studies, the colouring of which is delicate and charming. He also executed the very artistic poster announcing the exhibition. Miss Constance H. Broadbent, Miss Waring and Miss B. Lees also exhibit good work in the paintings section, Mr. Frederick J. Barnish is to be complimented upon his skilful designs for cottages and mantels and Mr. D. C. Leigh has some capital architectural drawings. ncluding a fragment of " Disappearing 'Warrington" which we reproduced in our columns. ia short time ago. In the section devoted to craftsmanship, Mrs. Kate Garnett exhibits a number of exquisite silver worked necklaces, brooches, rings &c., and Mr. Hugh Wallis sends some very fine art metal , work. Mrs. Reginald Frampton has some rich specimens of embroidery. Taken as a whole ths exhibition is distinctly creditable to Warrington and those of our readers who have not already inspected it should take the opportunity of doing so to-day.

div.head: OPENING BY MRS. CROSFIELD.
div.p: OPENING BY MRS. CROSFIELD.

The exhibition was opened on Tuesday afternoon by Mn'. A. H. Cresfleld, who was accompanied by Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P. There was a good attendance, chiefly of ladies. Mrs. CROSFIELD, who was received with applause, said: I feel greatly honoured at having been asked to open your exhibition this afternoon. To my mind though there are many important things in life At is at the very forefront of them. There are some who con- sider that art is simply a pleasant way of spending the time But you know better. You know that art not only completes our education but also completes our lives. Without it we are mere machines, revolving end- lessly and monotonously in an everlasting circle. That is why I think we ought all to fel greatly indebted to the Warrington Arts and Crafts Society for its inititative. (Applause). And though the artistic side of life is already considerably developed in Warrington I feel certain that this society will develop it still further by stimulating ambi- tion by \ fostering the spirit of emulation, and by bringing forth many talents that are now latent (Applause.) Furthermore we who have forsaken the beauties of nature to live under the sombre sky of industrialism are doubly in need of an, artistic environ- ment, are doubly in need of influences to counteract the monotony of our lives and to refresh and re-inspire our thoughts dulled by our daily routine. You may have noticed how different is the effect produced upon us by different surroundings. We enter a room which reveals the touch of the craftsman and of the artist, and at once the atmosphere unconsciously elevates the whole tenor of our thoughts and impulses. We may have been feeling jangled and out of tune, but the quiet harmony of this spot attunes our spirits once more to sympathy and good fellowship. And do not think that our feelings influence us alone ; we are constantly sending forth waves of thought which purity or vitiate the atmosphere which surrounds us and react accord- irgly on all those with whom we come into contact. Thus I believe that each of you when you are engaged on these useful and charming works of art of which I see so many beautiful examples around me,are not only fashion- ing things of beauty but are also setting in motion those powers that help to develop the onward movement of societ y.lt is,therefore &double pleasure to me to welcome your society and to open your exhibition, which will not only help to create an artistic atmosphere, but will elevate the moral and mental atmosphere Of our town. (Applause). Miss BROADBENT, in proposing a vote of thanks to Mrs. Crosfield, said that lady had not been connected with Warrington very long, but she had won her way into their hearts and they found her quite irresistible (Hear, hear.) She (Miss Broadbent) was glai Mrs. Crosfleld had time not only to encourage thPir philan- thropic aspirations, but their artistic ones wh;ch should not be lost sight, of in the hurry and press of modern life. They had great names connected with Warrington —Warrington Wood, Harry Woods,Luke Fildes,and that brilliant and erratic genius that Mr. Crosfield had such a great admiration for—George Shefffeld—but everyone bad not heard of Selin Rothwell, who was educated at the Schoolof Art and who died very roung. She bad two of his drawings—given by an artistic friend, Mr. Charles Cborley—in her room, and they were the most charming works of the kind she had ever seen. (Applause). Mr. H. N. HOUGHTON seconded, and the motion was heartily agreed to. Mr. CnosnELo,lll.P., responded on behalf of his wife who, he said, greatly appreciated the kind vote of thanks which had been proposed in such a charming way by Miss Broadbent. He thought that one speech from the same family was quite enough for an after- noon—(laughter)--and he did not know that he was a fitting persgn to say anything in an artistic gathering like that. They would perhaps look upon him as a sort of crafty politician or an artful dodger—(laughter)— and the less he said the better as he would have s great deal to say in the weeks that were to come, perhaps more than enough. At any rate he quite agreed with what Miss Broadbent had said about the artistic talent they bad in Warrington One thing struck him as rather curious. While in this country they cut a very respectable figure w•th regard to portrait and figure painting, and might he thought certainly claim to take the lead in landscape painting, it did seem to him a strange thing that they had not produced any musician in the very fore front rank of the world's composers. It was strlnge that this branch of artistic talent should—he would not say find its way to Germany—btit find its way so largely to that and other countries on the Continent. He hoped that the Arts and Crafts Society would in so far as it led to further artistic development in their town, help the splendid onward movement in Warrington in musical circles, as Well as ip other branches of art. (Applause).

div.head: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
div.p: LOCAL PARLIAMENT.
BUDGET TO BE "REFERRED TO THE
COUNTRY."

The debate cn the tariff reform Budget in the Parliamentary Debating Society ended on Tuesday evening in the Government accepting the Opposition amendment that the Budget be referred to the country. Mr. M. JOHNSToN (Secretary for Scotland) supported the Bill and said that they heard from the Free Traders that the effect of a tariff of 10 per cent. on manufac- tured goods would be that the foreigner would not send his goods into the. conntry and therefore we should draw no revenue. On the other hand they were told that the foreigner would send his goods in and then the British worker would have to pay the increased prices. Such arguments as those could not be taken seriously. Certainly a tariff such as was proposed would keep a certain amount of goods out and as we would be able to make them ourselves it would relieve unemployment. (Applause). The Liberal Government had recently given us at least two of the most highly protectionist measures—the Merchants Shipping Act and the Patents Act. They were working well. He claimed that Tariff Reform as laid down by Mr. Balfour would go far to 'provide 'steadier and better paid work. Mr. As PERRIS (L., Central Bradford) said that be was speaking on a most momentous °cession, not only to the various parties in this House but to every man, woman and child in the realm. (Hear' hear). His mind carried him back to the time which immediately follow d the Crimean War. They were awful times and he certaiuly would do all ho could to prevent us going back to them.He would offer the most strenuous opposition to the insidious proposal of the Chancellor of the Exchequer. It required an audacious man to make such a proposal. They might be told that a 2s. registration tax per quarter on corn was only small. It seemed a small thing, hut he did not like that small, shy insinuating infant that they proposed. (Laughter). That curly locked infant would grow. We bad had experience of that prodigy. (Laughter and Opposition applause). Germany bad first bad a tax of 2s. but it had grown to 12s. or 13s. France had a tax of is. 7d. at first, now it was 13s. He also maintained that the cost of collection would fritter the revenue away and the delay of the goods at the Customs Houses would be very serious. (Applause). Mr. RIGBY, (N., Scotland Division of Liverpool) said that the Budget would not be supported by his section of the House. The demands of the nation were increasing. There was a public demand—an unfortunate demand—for the increase in armaments to enable us to keep and maintain our position as leaders in a braggart company of war lords. There was a more Christian demand to provide for the aged workers. Money was also required for Labouf Exchanges aud for pro vision for invalidity. There was a demand for the fostering and development of our natural resources and the interests and industries dependent upon the land. Protective tariffs would add to the burdens of the community. If a tax were put on manufactured goods the cost of production would be more and there- fore the output would be less. This would cause a reduction in wages and that would bring about a condi- tion worse than the present deplorable conditions (Hear, hear). The FIRST LORD OF THE ADMIRALTY (Mr. G. H. W. Steel) said that when they introducei the Budget they were thinking of those who were poor, and they were hoping to lift them more out of the mire. If Free Trade was such a great policy, how was it that Mr. Lloyd-George told the members of the Colonial Con- ference that we had more distress than they had and they were protected ? (A Voicz "We have not free land.") He maintained that Free Trade was a policy which was responsible for the ruin of agrieulture, and the decay of many once flourishing industries. That was a Budget which would cure unemployment. Mr. RATHBONE (L., Exeter) maintained that to reduce imports would be to reduce exports as we had to pay for imports by exports. Could anyone point to one sinsle csse where the Englishman paid the tax on goods enter- ing foreign countries? Mr. W. P. ITA.RTLEY (C., Skipton) while supporting the present Budget, said he would take a little bit from Mr. Lloyd-George's Budget and introdnce it into the present one; because we should do very well to raise a little more revenue than we really needed. He should include a super, tax,—(Opposition Applause) —also the unearned increment taxes (Opposition applanso, Government silence and a voice from the Opposition : "Come over to this sieke.") 11•15 thought that. those taxes did not bit anybody hard. If a man made 100 per cent. profit he could well afford to pay 20 per cent. (Opposition applause). Mr. Hartley then dealt with Tariff Reform maintaining that it would relieve unemployment. The LEADER of the Opposition (Mr. E. WYNNE- JOSISS) said be hoped that the House would reject the Budget bra very large majority. The Chancellor of the Exchequer in introducing it said that labour was the stock-in-trade of the individual and remuneration was the reward for its use. With regard to that his (the speaker's) party ,said that the reward for labour was far too low at the present tithe—(hear, hear)—and they believed that by various and just laws it would be raised. They affirmed that if the Budget were passed it would reduce the rewards of labour to a very great extent. Since the adoption of Free Trade the population of this country had grown more than 50 per cent, but the exports and imports bad grown by 500 per cent. The income of the country had increased three- fold and many great benefits had accrued. It was one of the grestest boons ever given to any nation. They would not raise the money as they propcsed by the Budget. A Finance Bill 'imposing tariffs would have to have a separate clause for each article. (" No no.") When the last German revision took place it took' from 1901 to 1906 before it came into force. The Tariff Reformers had no idea of the amount of labour that would have to be done if a Tariff Reform Budget were introduced. With regard to the question as to whether the proposals meant more or less unemployment, on one occasion they were told by gentlemen opposite "Tax the foreigner, keen him out; and we will pro- duce the goods." The -Chancellor of the Exchequer denied the assertion and said " Tax the foreigner and he will give us a revenue." He maintained that the days of miracles were not over if that could be done. (Laughter.) They could not have it both ways. (Voice: "Yes, we can." Opposi- tion laughter.) With regard to the duty to be imposed upon corn, whereby £2,000,000 could be raised, he would guarantee himself that the British people would have to pay £10,000,000 for the State to have £2,000,000. ("No, no.") He said that the con- sumer would have to pay all the taxes. (Applause.) Concluding he said that Protection was vicious in principle ; it was unequal in its terms ; it was degrad- ing in its consequences. (Hear, hear.) Wee Trade stood for brotherly relations the world over, and if,we wanted to du away with national distrust and hostility Free Trade was a necessity. (Applause.) The CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER (Councillor Fulton Smith) replying said that most of the talk on the other side had been in the P.S.A. style. (" Oh, 011.'t) He accepted the amendment that it be referred to the country. _ This was received with loud laughter, and there was no division.
The House then adjourned until the second Tuesday after the Warrington election, when a Liberal Govern- ment will take office.

WHY WE MAKE SO LITTLE BUTTER.-It is of the highest importance that the British butter-making industry should not be allowed to languish and eventu- ally to disappear altogether, Large quantities of butter are still in in this country, but, writes Professor Long, "Farm and Home," we believe that at least 90 per cent. is second or third-rate in quality, and that no more thin 10 per cent. is of the finest, most of this butter being consumed by those who pro- duce it. The reason why we make so little butter is that the demand for milk has induced the great majority of owners of dairy herds to sell it for con- sumption, and they are wise in most cases, obtaining, as they do, a higher price. But we venture to believe, notwithstanding, that where butter is made a leading article of produce, the price obtainable is such that it pays equally as well as selling milk, and is an infinitely less anxious and troublesome business.

div.head: OVERLOADING THE STOMACH
div.p: OVERLOADING THE STOMACH
CAUSES INCOMPLETE DIGgSTION, WEAKENS THE SYSTEM, AND 'BREEDS INDIGESTION.

div.p: Bewsey-road Wesley Guild.

At the Bewsey-road Wesley Gu:ld on Monday even- ing Mr. C. Wilcockson &livered a very interesting and instructive lecture entitled "1n wildest Wales." The lecture was illustrated with about 100 views, almost all of which were taken by Mr. Wilcockson. lie also made the slides himself. Mr. J. Parkinson manipulated the lantern and Mr. Upson presided over a good attendance. The lecturer was accorded a vote of thanks en the pro- position of Mr. Mitchell, seconded by Mr. Norman.

div.head: " Messiah " Service at Legh-street.
div.p: " Messiah " Service at Legh-street.

A musical service consisting of selections from "The Messiah "wee held At Legh-street Primitive Methodic Church en Sunday evening, presided over by the pastor Rev. J. B. Bugloss. Aliss Alice Griffiths soprano, gave tasteful renderings of "There were shepherds &c." and 'I know that my Redeemer liveth " Miss Linn Plieston contralto, was highly successful in "0 Thou that. tellest," " He shall feed," and "He was despised." Miss B. Bracegirdle sang "Come unto me" very swee' Iy. Mr. A. Griffiths gave a good account of himself in " Comfort ye "and " Every valley." Much disappoint- ment was felt at the unavoidable absence of Mr. E. H. Pearce who was expected to takepart but was prevented from doing so by a severe cpld. The choir conducted by Mr. A. t'pruce gave lie renderings of the following choruses "And the glory," "0 'non that tellest,' "For unto us,"" All we like sheep," "Worthy is the Lamb " and " Hallelujah." Mr. A. W. Cl itwmthy ably accompanied all the aoove itlms sad in addition playa d with good effect the overture.

div.head: Wycliffe P.S.A, Society.
div.p: Wycliffe P.S.A, Society.

There was a good meeting of this Society on Sun- day last, presided over by Mr. McEachern. Councillor Joseph Hawthorn gave the address upon "What Christianity has done, and whit Christia;iity requires of us." This country has risen from the d irk ages to [be preterit enlightened age thrcrigh the life and influence of Christianity. Noble cause: and nstitutions were the off-spring of the Christian Faith while Christianity bad increased. The individual and the home life had been n:ade better and purer. "Many and gracious eacr:flc,es Lad been made by the power of the Gospel. Christianity demanded from us a loving and sterling service, to make both ourselves and others better. Mr. W.Beswick and Mr. C. Cutton also took part in the meeting. Mr. W. H. Pa 3 ton Mus. Bic. rendered an organ solo in pleasing style. The Secre- tary asked for addresses of old membera who hid loft town so that on behalf of the brethren he could send them a Christmas greeting. One new trembir received a hearty welcome. The Secretary also referred to the service rendered to that brotherhood by the late Mr. William Hickman who was one of that early members of the brotherhood, and became a very want wor',er and speaker. A vote of sympathy was sent to to the family.

div.head: United Mission. Mr. Clarke Tells the Story of His Life.
div.p: United Mission. Mr. Clarke Tells the Story of His Life.

Last Sunday was the concluding day of the mission which has been held for three weel,s in the Parr Hall, conducted by Mr. George Clarke, of London, under the auspices of the Warrington and District Free Church Council. In the afternoon he addressed a crowded audience on "Mv life's motto —He shall live" (Psalm lxxii. 15). in the evening he delivered his last evangelistic MO:...S3ge. On Monday evening Mr. -Clarke gave a lectu r entitled "The story of my life." .Mr. C. E. Parker presided ever a large audience and amongst those on the platform were the Revs. John Yonge, Wall, T. Gladding, T. Miller, and Messrs R. lienshall and W. Carter (secretary), Mr. Jameson (local secretary of the Y.M.C.A.)

Prior to giving his lecture, Mr. CLARKE th-mked the ministers who had stood round him so well, choir, con- ductors, organists, pianists, and secretaries and stewards. He said it bad been a pleasure to come down to talk to Lancashire folks. He told his aucrence that Mrs. Savage had passed away suddenly. She had attended every meeting in connection with the mission and had even got her gloves on on Sunday evening ready to come to the service when she was taken ill and died soon afterwards. He hoped that they would stand and give an expression of their sympathy to thoss whg bad suffered a sudden loss,

This request of Mr. Clarke was omplied with. Mr. PARKER said that they bad come to the last service of that very blessed and successful mission. The last service was in special connection with the Y.M.C.A. —an organisation which had doce much good in the country—and they were very glad to see a representa- tive of that association there. (Applause.) They were very anxious to hear Mr. Clarke's lecture as he was a very distinct personality. (Applause). Mr. JAMESON hoped that as an outcome of that service they would see the re-establishment of a Y.M.C.A. in Warrington. (Applause.) Mr. CLAnKe delivered his lecture in h!s usual racy style and the anecdotes he told made the audience roar with laughter. He said that he was born during the mutiny in India, His father who stood 6ft. sin., and 521 n. round the ohost, held the pqsition of Chaplaie General in the Madras Presidency. He was in Delhi at the time of the Beige, and his father forgetting that he was a chaplain be fought like any other man for the protection of his wife and his children. When the mutiny was over he came to England and t he spe iker w is carried about on a pillow until he was three years old, owing to being such a sickly child. Atter wards he got well fled 2trollg and had been so ever sinus. When he went to schoml he had five lights on the first day and he enjoyed them. (Laughter). He thought the other fellows did too. (Laughter). lie was brcught up with plebty of luxuries. When 13 he took a scholar- ship for mathematics which was competed for by all the boys in England. In due course be went to Cambridge University to live the ordinary life of a man who owned property and was the eldest son. %Mist he was at college his father lost all his money and instead of being rich they suddenly became very poor. He—one of the 14 -children— decided to go abroad and endeavour to get enough money to buy back the old family estates. His father would not hear of it, but when he (the speaker) was determined to go his father told him he would not give him a penny. However he worked his way actress to Ainerica, first as a steward. When he was leaving home his father told him to piny the man and he determined to do so. While he was on the journey the old Celtic signalled for them, as it was in distress and he along with several men was one who rowed the little boat which attached the hawser to the Celtic, which W./S towed back to Queenstown by his steamer. When they got to Queenstown his actipn was rewarded by being promoted from cook's boy to purser and he had a fine time with the girls sitting around him in his office. (Laughter). He knew how to row because he had rowed at Cambridge. Although he had 100 letters of introduction he could not get any work. The last letter be used was that from the Y.M.C.A. The first job he had in America was that of sweeping snow. Through the influence of the he got work and then be started f' to be the man." To do this he thought that he would only have to be a [great athlete and so he set to work and when great honours in that line came to him he sent word to his father and woo surprieeii to 'receive the reply that he 77115 only a third of a mats.. Then be thought that to be a man he must cultivate his brains. SO he worked bard at his books and In the course of time be read a paper' to a literary Society in New York. He sent a news- paper cutting to his father, which spoke very highly of it and then he was staggered when he received a letter from his father to say that he was only two-thirds of a man. Ile proceeded to cultivate the spirit and went to Church each morning at 5 o'clock and thenl read tLe Bible and prayed for two solid hours. He also attended Church at noon and in the evening, but be nould not find God. He journeyed to Ceylon in search of God and tried Buddism and then he sought God in Mahomedanism but he could not find God so he returned to America and gave religion up. When his Chairman was Converted he saw that be possessed some strange power which he had not gct and determined to tey religion again. He .experienced the same process for another six months. but be could get no sat:sfaction out of it. At last he was told that a great fight was being held at night in Madison-square Gardens, New York, so he went there. It was Moody and Sankey's Mission—a fight against the devil. There he was converted, the chief men being Moody and a Wesleyan minister. Since then he had never despised Nonconformists, although ho bed been brought up to believe that they were this wrong and that wrong. When he returned to England 21 years ago he took up Mission work and bad carried it on ever since. In conclusion he asked his audience to "play the man."

On the proposition of Rev. J. YONGE, seconded by Rev. J. g, HUGHES, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Mr, Clarke for his lecture, and fqr his services during the Mission. Mr. CLARKE, in reply, intimated that he expected to be invited to come again in a few years, and this announcement was received with loud applause.

div.head: TOWN'S RIGHTEOUSNESS.
div.p: A TOWN'S RIGHTEOUSNESS.
REV. A. M. MITCHELL RETURNS TO THE ATTACK.

In the current issue of the Burtonwood Pariah Magazine, the Rev. A. M. Mitchell writes: Warrington has been roused; .we are glad. Wan ington is angry; we are sorry. Truth even when only partial, is seldom acceptable, and when put bluntly and forcibly is never palatable. Our strife is not for victory but for truth, and, ultimately, truth the day must win.

Warrington was given a bitter pill to swallow ; even gilded pills may be difficult to stomach; ”. Warrington for Christ ' was no gilded pill. A great cutcry.has been raised, a loud outburst of declamation has been heard, and • the Vicar of Burtonwood has caught it "hot "—exceeding hot. Mayor, ex-mayors, certain aldermen, councillors, magistiates, and even parsons have all gone for his reverence, taking him to task severely for his temerity. Mr. Mitchell's friends will liike to be assured of his safety ; though badly unfilled and violently rent asunder he is still alive; he has come by his parts ; voice and pen still are busy ; there is life in the fight- ing parson yet: he can bear a few more storms, a few more peltings; and—he will not be silenced. Those gentlemen, who by virtue of their civic posi- tion, have underthken the town's defence, who have entered tho lists as champions c.f Wan ington's righteousness, have left us very little to do; we could wish for a more difficult task, for something more worthy of our qui 1. _ _

Wairington's- th fenders, with their repudiations, disclaimers, justifications, arc test left to the judg-- ment of their fellcw citizens; our knowledge of them is but small; they are, however, no strangers in the grimy, brewery town; their histories, deeds, achiev- meats, as public men, must be known to all Warringtonians who, no doubt, value them at their true worth; their names, reputitions, personalities, should be familiar to all their., follow-townsmen,—to slum dki ellers and suburban residents alike. Let these speak, by these let them be judged, to their own fellow citizens they stand or fall—" by their fruits ye shall know them.'

The defence of inevitable admissions, and half admissions, must, necessarily, prove poor and feeble. When the best that can be said amounts to this,- - " We are no worse then our neighbours ; other Lancashire towns are as black as our own black selves; we're not so black, you know, but we might be blacker," nothing more ' need be said, to particularize further were labour in vain. " More guilty than not guilty" is Warrington's own irrever- sible verdict on itself. Warrington's righteousness has not been made quite plain; Warrington's unrighteousness cannot altogether be hid. Mr. Alderman Bennett's via media is the outstanding feature in this defence of a town's righteousness ; it is sane and well-balanced. Mr, Bennett's " inter- view " comments are precisely what may be expected of a public man who is an ardent citizen of cultured mind and civic ideals. He sees the evil and deplores it; he cleaves to the good and longs to increase it. Our` admiration for the cultured writer and idealist is greater than for the Alderman, qua Alderman, but when Alderman Pennett's turn has. come to fill the chair of Chief Magistrate of his native town, Burton- wood congratulations. to the man and, the town will be hearty and sincere. That day should be full of hope for Warrington, meaning as it will the sway of a cultured mind, the inauguration of a reign of new ideals. Speed the glad and joyful hour ! - Warringtonians should remember that their Town Hall is not the only chamber of civic government their town can boast of : they seem to be forgetful, or are ignorant of the existence of another chamber which, at the present time, is under the chairman- shiP of a brewer who, in virtue of his office, is entitled to sit as a Magistrate on the Bench. The personnel of the Board of Guardians includes, at least, two drink traffickers and one bookmaker.

These facts should give citizens of the better sort pause to "think furiously." In the judgment of all right-thinking men and women, the callings of these individuals, whatever their own personal worth may be, make them impossible as holders of civic office. Great good, it is said, will result from this Warrington explosion. Letters which have come to hand from far and near, from at home and 'abroad, lead to this conclusion. But after all, letters of thanks and apprecia ion are of little moment, so long as something is attempted, something is done by those who have the power to right the wrong. If, through this local outburst, attention has been seriously directed to gross social evils which Should not be tolerated, no, not for an hour in any city, town, or hamlet, if the sense of social righteousness has been quickened, if drink traffickers have been made to wince, if slum property owners and oppressors of the poor have been taken to task, if a fres,h inspiration has been-imparted to citizenship, wo are content, more will have been aebielie4 than we really -hoped for. The Ifnited Mission which suggested the article— ' Warrington-for Christ' and -led to this 'madding fray ' has, it is to be hoped, done great things, physioally, mentally, and spiritually, for hundreds, if not for thousands of Warringtonians. The promoters of it, and the Missioner himself, will Iwo evor7 redson to thank God and tahn courage if by their praiseworthy effort§ the downtrodden are imbued with hope, if the' heads of the poor are lifted up among their betters," if the drunkard is reclaimed,- iLthe temptations to drink are lessened, if Warrington is led to tread the pathway of social penitence, if the Gospel of Health—Salvation—has been fully proclaimed—the Gospel of Soul and Body. We must very reluctantly repeat our conviction, with such damning evidences of social unrighteous- ness in so many of our cities and towns, that the need of the hour is nc tso much missions to the people as the conversion to the principles of Christ of those upon whom is laid, or who have t4ice4-I:ipan themselves the responsibilitie§ of c.:ivie government, If the root is goo 4 and the tree is good the fruits of social righteousness will not be wanting. . .

-individual personal righteou-sness is altogether impossible to many under present social ocsuchtions. Angels could not preserve their purity unsullied if forced to herd together a$ the mine. Outside the Holy Book no grander words were ever spoken than these which we commend to Warring-, tonians, and citizens further afield than the old parish,—" Comfort the poor, protect and shelter the weak, and with all thy might right that, which is wrong. Then shall the Lord 14V0 thee, and God Him- self shall be thy gre4t reward."

div.p: THE RT. HON. WINSTON CHURCHILL. M.P., AND MRS. CHURCHILL. (From a photo taken at Southport on December 4th.)

illuminating history of the Nile War. The trouble in South Africa drew him to the front as correspondent, to be captured by the Boers, to escape from Pretoria, and to have a price set upon his head—a price which he complained, with some humour, was ridiculously small. From that time onward the eyes of the world were upon him. Between his campaigns Mr. Churchill made his first attempt to enter Parliament by favour of Oldham. He stood as a Conserva- tive and he was beaten by Mr. Walter R'unciman, who now sits in the Cabinet with him. He came back in the height of the war fever to test Oldham again and he won handsomely this time. His beginnings in Parliament were marked by the impetuosity and audacity of his previous career. After a maiden speech, in which he replied to Mr. Lloyd-George, he raised the banner of "peace, retrenchment and reform" before the put- raged leaden of his own party. He attacked Mr. Brodrick's now notorious army corps" scheme, and he killed it, although it was only officially abandoned a year 'later. Already he was at loggerheads with Con- servatism, and the Tories cursed the impudence of ,the clever young man from whom they had hoped so much. On the morrow of Mr. Chamberlain's declaration for Protection Mr. Churchill's fate was decided. He denounced the new departure unsparingly and on every possible occasion. The day came when the whole of his Party rose and walked out of the House when he rose to speak. No young man ever had more dramatic testimony to his power. With characteristic boldness he decided to attack the seat held by Sir W. Houldsworth in North West Manchester. What seemed a forlorn hope* was turned to a magnificent triumph. Mr. Churchill came to Westminster with a majority of 1,241. He had accepted the office of Under-Secretary for the Colonies, and through more than two years he was the spokesman of that depart- ment in the Commons. They were times of critical moment, but Mr. Churchill showed himself not less sagacious and large-minded in administration than he was formidable in debate in the House itself. His opponents learned to respect and beware of him, for whether in the complicated difficulties of reconstructing South Africa, in the gradual abolition of Chinese Labour, or in the com- plexities of the Colonial Conference, he showed himself a master of facts and of men.

Upon the reconstructiorr of the Govern- ment, Mr. Churchill succeeded Mr. Lloyd- George, his close friend, at the Board of Trade. His seat in Manchester was attacked, with extraordinary energy. The whole attention of the country concentrated upon the election, in which he just fell short of victory. At once he was offered several seats, and he chose Dundee, which involved a second three-cornered battle, ending in a splendid triumph. Now, Mr. Churchill is
Manchester Guardian

div.head: Persistent Heckling .and Cheers for the
div.p: Persistent Heckling .and Cheers for the
Budget.

Many Peers have been "on the stump" against the Government this week, and some of them have had great difficulty in obtain- ing a hearing. At a meeting at Crowland, in the Stamford Division, Lord Kesteven was on Tuesday practically refused a hearing. "Do you -want a song?" his- lordship asked, when the interruptions compelled him to resume his seat. At this there was general utsroar and shouts of " The Constitution." "If you'll only let me get a word in edge- ways—only edgeways," pleaded the noble -peer, but they wouldn't until cheers had been given for the Liberal candidate. An elector wanted to know by what right Lord Kesteven controlled" all these villages." " Because I've put my money into them," was the reply. Then, as the interruptions broke out afresh, he went on: "I love all this; it's all the joy and the fun of the fight and it's what I like." Whereupon someone shouted: "Yes, and you'll have to fight this time, too." Lord Donoughmore and the Poor Man's Budget. Lord Donoughmore was badly heckled at the East Ham Town Hall, and a large section of the audience cheered again and again for for Mr. Lloyd-George. "We have heard that it i a poor man's Budget," he proceeded, and the audience cheered lustily at this. "We are given to understand that the Budget is to tax the rich man and that the poor man is to get all the benefit and none of the inconveniences." Just here someone cried: "What price the Duke of Northumberland ? " and derisive laughter followed. So the meeting went on, with interruption and dissent almost to the nend.

div.head: Lord Newton Waxes Humorous.
div.p: Lord Newton Waxes Humorous.

At North Camberwell on Tuesday Lord Newton talked of the Peers being prepared to" knuckle under" if the people declare in favour of the Budget. Not that his lord- ship thinks they will so declare. Oh, dear, no! On the contrary, he likened the terrible Radicals to some " hectoring swashbuckler" who had made an attack on a peaceful-look- ing middle-aged citizen, and who found that he suddenly got a blow upon his own nose! The noble peer had a very mixed reception, and our old friend" the voice" had a great deal to say. What, asked Lord Newton,was •the actual 'situation? Someone promply replied, "Helping the landlords and the brewers." But the climax came when his lordship asked a remarkable question: "If a peer— myself, for instance—makes an ass of him- self, is it open to the Commons to say that the members of the House of Peers are all asses ?" The audience, laughed too heartily to reply. Lord Harris Refused a Hearing.

--- - Lord Harris, who endeavoured to speak at a Tariff Reform meeting at Sheerness, found the opposition too strong, and he ultimately left the hall. He seems to have aroused local indignation by certain comments upon the action of the district councillors in opposing a railway company's Bill seeking to impose additional tolls on the King's Ferry Bridge. Lord Denbigh Waits While Audience Cheer the Ministry. The Earl of Denbigh, at a Tory ticket meeting at Finsbury on Wednesday was interrupted by cheers for Mr. Lloyd George and other members of the Government whom he mentioned, and at length he suggested, as • he 'was out for the night, it would simplify matters if the audience cheered for the whole 'Cabinet one by one, and "got ,them off their chest." This the audience did with great heartiness. When it had subsided, Lord Denbigh made another reference to Mr. Churchill, whom he quoted as saying that the Government did not want to injure individuals through the 'land-tax, but only wanted to alter the land -system of the country. This brought forth a burst of applause and a great shout of" Tax the land not bread." There were many more interruptions of the same sort, all made in a good-natured way and accepted in the same way by the speaker. The greatest uproar was occasioned when, in answer to an interruption that " The House of Lords never rejects the measures of a Conservative Government," he retorted, "All I can say is that a Con- servative Government is more particular as to the measures it puts forward." Th 4; audacious bit of special pleading pro- voked a storm of opposition.

div.p: BEER AND THE MARQUIS.

THE MARQUIS OF LANSDOWNE 'having decided to submit the Malicious Budget introduced by Mr: Lloyd George . to the WISDOM AND JUDGMENT OF THE PEOPLE, The Pzoprietor has much pleasure in announcing that ALL BRERS ARE REDUCED TO THR POPULAR PRICES Existing before the introduction of the Finance Bill.
