div.head: STATESMAN OF 35.
div.p: THE STATESMAN OF 35.
MR. CHURCHILL'S REMARKABLE CAREER.
Biographical Sketch.
In view of Mr. Churchill's first visit to Warrington to-day, the following interesting summary of his crowded and exciting career will be read with interest.

Mr. Churchill is now thirty-five; he is in the Cabinet, already winning fresh laurels for himself by the skill and force he is bring- ing to the control of the Board of Trade. He is one of the four or five men who have the ear of the Commons and of the country upon any topic upon which they care to talk. Fate has made him, since the reconstruction of the Government, the most interesting figure in public life; nature, genius, and hard work have enabled him to fill the great stage upon which he has been moving. Three years ago Mr. Churchill was chosen as the first of a series of "Coming Men." To-day he has come, and men speak with certainty of his future. He has fought two great by-elections this year, and alike in defeat and in victory he has added to his reputation. There is no man in whom more hopes are centred, and the brilliant rapidity of his advance gives the fullest promise that those hopes will be realised.

No brief sketch can hope to touch the activities that have been crowded into the last thirteen years of Mr. Churchill's life. At twenty-five it was said of him that he had sden more of war than half the generals on the active list. At thirty he had a literary reputation that might be envied by men who had given successful lives to writing. The son of Lord Randolph Churchill and of the lady whom the world now knows as Mrs. Cornwallis-West, he joined to the dash and ability of a famous family the spirit of progress of the United States. He went from Harrow to Sandhurst and became a lieutenant in the 4th Hussars in 1895. When Spain was making its last effort to crush insurrection in Cuba, he obtained leave and hurriecl out there as correspondent of the "Daily Graphic." Then .he went to India with the 4th Hussars, took part in the fight- ing on the Malakand Frontier, wrote brilliant accounts of the doings of the British force for an English journal, and published a book after the campaign was over. Still in India, he fought through the Tirah expedition. Always on the watch for active service, he joined the 21st Lancers for the Egyptian expedition which resulted in the re-conquest of Khartoum. He was in the famous charge at Atbara, and he told the story of the fighting in a series of letters home which afterwards formed the basis for the most

settled down at the Board of Trade, learning the administration of his new Department with that extraordinary quickness of intellect which is the main secret of his success. He has already settled one great labour dispute, and he is continuing with success the policy which, under the present Chancellor of the Exchequer, made the Board of Trade a magnificent instrument of com- mercial advancement and industrial peace.

div.head: MR. CHURCHILL'S LANCASHIRE CAMPAIGN. The Speaker and His Speeches.
div.p: MR. CHURCHILL'S LANCASHIRE CAMPAIGN. The Speaker and His Speeches.

The whiteness of Mr. Churchill's face— really it seemed only a degree less white than his shirt front I gave his Manchester friends at the Reform Club on Saturday night some uneasiness (says the "Manchester Guardian"), and when they gathered round him at the end of the speechmaking they proffered earifest advice. "You are doing too much, Mr. Churchill; take a rest" was the note. Mr. Churchill thanked his friends with a very reassuring smile, and told them with obvious sincerity that he was feeling very much better in health at the end of his tour than he did at the beginning of it. As a matter of fact Mr. Churchill was not at all well when he was at the Free Trade Hall last Monday, and he felt the strain of his work on Tuesday and Wednesday so much that at one time a curtailment of his programme was seriously contemplated. But he "picked up" before the great meetings at Crewe, and proof of his continued improvement was given in the finished form of his fine after-dinner speech at the Reform Club—a speech admirably delivered without a single reference to any notes.

The most impressive audience Mr. Churchill had during the week was that which waited on his words at the Free Trade Hall, but the Liverpool audience, not much if anything smeller than that of Man- chester, had the good luck to hear a long satirical passage which, prepared in the happiest mood and delivered with admirable mock gravity, was as skilful a piece of popular platform work as Mr. Churchill has done. The audience at Bolton was, if not in point of numbers, certainly in its warm and enthusiastic spirit and its musical accom- plishment, as fine a one as any which Mr. Churchilffaced. The Bolton meeting was the only one which Mrs. Churchill did not attend. Throughout all the speeches, if Mr. Churchill's mind has ever deviated for a second from the matter .in hand, it has been when he has glanced at Mrs. Churchill to see if she has noticed how particularly well some shot has told. Always on these 'occasions Mrs. Churchill has been ready with an appreciate smile.

div.head: CHANCELLOR'S WEAL.
div.p: CHANCELLOR'S WEAL.
RIGHTS AND DUTIES OF FREE CHURCHMEN.
Government by Drink Trade or People?

Mr. D. Lloyd George, the Chancellor of the Exchequer and the author of the Budget over whose corpse the Lords have stepped to their doom, addressed a great meeting of Free Churchmen in the Queen's Hall, London on Thursday night.
" We are not free men so long as this
veto exists, and it must go."

This emphatic declaration in a letter from Dr. Clifford gave the tone to the great demonstration, where the Chancellor of the Exchequer was surrounded by and confronted with the flower of the Free Churches of England. The breath of ancient liberties inspired every man in the vast audience, and there was no one who listened to Mr. Lloyd George's striking speech who did not recognise the importance and the greatness of the enterprise upon which as Free Church- men and citizens of a free country they are engaged. POINTS FROM THE SPEECH.

Our grievance as Free Churchmen is that our case is examined by a prejudiced tribunal. The Lords are a biased court. If there is perfect freedom in this land for any man in any place of worship it is because , its doorposts and its lintels are sprinkled with the blood of the Noncon- formists. There is a great deal of talk about the sanction of the electorate, If it is possible to get a mandate for anything, it was secured for Mr. Birrell's Education Bill. What happened? The Bill was torn to little bits.

There were many great moments in the course of the evening, but none so impressive as when, towards the close of his address, the Chancellor, alluding to his recent political excursions through England, told his listeners in plain homely language of the things that had impressed him most. The country-side wase bautiful, even grand ; but it was not its grandeur or its beauty that had most deeply affected him. It was the contrast in social conditions, and something else. THE CHAPEL AND THE CASTLE.

"On one side of the road," he said, "you will see the high walls surrounding a great estate, on which there is a lordly castle. On the other side you will see " And here that delightful " Voice " which is so disconcerting to Peers and Food-Taxers, but in whose interruptions the Chancellor of the Exchequer revels, put , in—" a little tailor's shop." The Chancellor of the Exchequer, who misses nothing, retorted, "Yes, and some- thing else. You will see the great castle on one side and on the other a little red brick building—the Nonconformist chapel—and there is one thing you may be certain of, and that is that it is the only place in the village that will stand up to the castle." The audience rose at the speaker and cheered and cheered again, and it was some minutes before he was able to add to his description that these little Bethels through- out England were "the very sanctuaries and citadels of independence." Humour and pathos, passionate pleading in the name of liberty, were the characteristics of the Chancellor's speech; and through it all there ran a serene confidence in the result of the people's verdict. The Chancellor concluded with a passion- ate declaration that all that Liberals wanted was justice, and, he said, "We mean to get it."

div.head: MR. AUSTEN CHAMBERLAIN SHOUTED DOWN.
div.p: MR. AUSTEN CHAMBERLAIN SHOUTED DOWN.
Refused a Hearing in His Own Constituency.

Mr. Au.sten Chamberlain addressed a very mixed audience at Bromsgrove, in his own constituency, on Thursday night, and at times met with considerable opposition. Saying that there should now be no doubt that old-age pensions would continue, he was met with cries of "Why didn't you vote br pensions ?" He did not vote for the Old Age Pensions Bill, he said, because he did not believe it was conceived on reasonable lines.

The Unionist party asked the Government to look at what Germany had done, but they would not do it. Here a voice from the audience drowned the speech. "Let's have three cheers for Lloyd George," it cried, and aniid great enthusiasm three hearty cheers were given for the Chancellor of the Exchequer. Several times Mr. Chamberlain attempted to resume his speech but he was shouted down. For some minutes he stood looking upon such a scene as Bromsgrove had never before witnessed.
Again the audience called for "three cheers for Lloyd-George," and the demand was responded to with a loud outburst. This was followed by the singing of" For he's a jolly good fellow." _ _
- li .-Was evident there would be no further speech-making. .

Mr. Chamberlain, rising again after some minutes, shouted, "It is of course quite impossible for anyone to address you while a portion of the audience of either sex is as noisy as some of the ladies in the gallery or you men on the.floor. lam not going to try an impossible task. I can trust my fortunes in the hands of my constituents."

div.head: CHURCHMEN AND THE ELECTION. STRIKING LETTER FROM CANON HICKS.
div.p: CHURCHMEN AND THE ELECTION. STRIKING LETTER FROM CANON HICKS.

The Rev. Canon Hicks has addressed the following letter.to the Editor of the " Manchester Guardian" —Sir,—ln common with other rectors of Manchester and Salford I am receiving repeated appeals, circularg and messages from the Diocesan Office, urging me to see that my parishioners are canvassed from house to house, and every elector pregsed to vote only "for Church and schools." This means, of course, that the whole machinery of our Church and parishes is to be placed at the service of the Tory party. Why are we warned RO often not to talk politics in the pulpit, if we are told to rally Churchmen to vote "only for Church interests," which avowedly means voting only for Tory candidates?
I venture to make my solemn and public protest against this pressure, because I hold it to be mis- guided, uncharitable and mischievous.

It is a misguided policy to tell Churchmen that they must not, on peril of their Churchtnanship, consider the momentous issue of Free Trade, which means so much not only for the well-being of' Lancashite but. for the peace of the world. It is misguided to make it a test of good Churchrnanship to be blind to the question of the rights of the House of Commons, or the menacing power Of selfish wealth. or the bloated tyranny of the, liquor trade. All these questions touch morality and religion at many points. The Church can exist, aye, and thrive, though dis- established and disendowed ; but she cannot survive at all unless she remain a spiritual and moral leader in the cause of freedom and sobriety, and a champion of the poor. _ _ _

It is an unchatitahle policy; for it assumes that no man can be a good Churchman and vote for the. Government and the Budget. But I know that great numbers of loyal Churchmen, lay and clerical, dis- approve of this diocesan pressure, and intend to vote and use their influence on the other side. Why should we not be allowed in this diocese to Share the opinions of the Archbishop of York, of the Bishops Of Birmingham, Hereford and Chester? Was not Mr. W. E. Gladstone a loyal Churchman? is there to be no room in the Church,if these zealots have their way, for Liberals or for Socialists as well as for Tories? Why provoke an internecine strife? This polieF is also mischievous; it threatens the best interests of the Church herself. Hitherto the Church has alwayS allowed full play to the pro- gressive forces within her ranks, and thus has shared in the great onward march of the nation. Hitherto, thank God, we have never seen " Clericalism" dominant, and a widening gulf between the Church and the politics of the people. It has been otherwise in Italy and in France, and the divorce has worked ill for the nation and ill for the Church. The sacred cause of freedom has become associated with unbelief and irreligion; the Church has shrunk in numbers and in moral influence, until it is regarded (and with justice) as a mere interest or party, the enemy of the nation, and concerned only with manipulating politics to serve its own advantages. Absit omen ! These ecclesiastical politicians are steering straight for disaster. Their mistaken and mischievous schemes can only be frustrated and the Church saved by Churchmen of wider view, who will speak and vote quite firmly for the larger national issues.—Yours, &c.,
EDWARD LEE HICKS, Manchester, December 11th, M.

div.head: SOWING THE WIND.
div.p: SOWING THE WIND.

They came from the ends of the earth— The Lords of the fate of a nation— To show the importance of Birth, To vindicate Riches and Station. Wild men from the forests remote Swept down on the wondering city, And plutocrats scrambled to vote, And mingle their tears of self-pity. Impelled by one motive they came— The spectre of dark destitution— And, scorning superfluous shame, They started the Great Revolution. The sons ef the nobtes of old, The lords,of a later creation, Tbe masters of riches untold Must never submit to taxation! In their pride and uplifting of heart, Disdaining all thought of submission, They played a presumptuous part, And stamped on a people's ambition. Yet faint was their challenge of war, And hollow the ring of their laughter, For some of them heard from afar A menacing murmur of—AFfER ! G. H. M. (in the "Daily Chronicle.")

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD AND SHOP ASSISTANTS.
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD AND SHOP ASSISTANTS.
A Promise to Support Reforms.

A deputation from the lOcal branch of the Amalga- mated Union of Shop Assistants, Warehousemen and Clerks waited upon Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., on Wednesday, in reference to the Shops Bill (No. 2), 1909. Mr. Crosfield promised his heartiest support, and expressed his sympathy in favour of the above Bill being so amended as to provide for a universal working week of not more than sixty hours inclusive of meal times, a weekly half-holiday to commence at one o'clock in the afternoon, and a schedule contaiLing adequate provision for meal times.

div.head: NEW RADICAL MINISTRY.
div.p: A NEW RADICAL MINISTRY.

The Liberals in our local Parliament will, very fittingly, resume office when the House re-assembles after the election in January. Though " Parliament ' only dissolved this week, the new Ministry has already been formed, and the appointments are as follow : Prime Minister and First Lord of Treasury, E. Wynne-Jones. Lord President of the Council, C. E. Parker. Lord Chancellor Councillor J. T. Locker. Chancellor of the Exchequer. E. England. secretary for Home Affairs, W. H. Sherburn'. If Foreign Affairs, Councillor J. Hawthorn. War, H. Gordon Roberts. India, Peter Peacock. Scotland, G. Davey-Smith. tf Chief Secretary for Ireland, J. Howes, jun. Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, A. Perris. First Lord of the Admiralty, P. O'Brien. President of the Board of Trade, J. Jarman. Local Government Board, J. A. Morton.

71 Board of Education, Rev. C. Harvey Cook. Board of Agriculture, Chas. Healey Post Master General, Edwin Plinston. First Corn Missioner of Works, F. Garside. Attorney General, N. Cook, jun. Solicitor General, A. W. Perris; Financial Secretary to Treasury, J. Darbyshire. Patronage „ W. Mellor. Paymaster General, W. Clegg. Parliamentary Secretaries: Home Office, A. H, Rathbone• Foreign • War Colonial

India Board of. Trade, F. Morrall. Local Government Board, C. Morrall. Board of Education, T. Barnes. Junior Lords pf the Treasury, F. Monks, J. Hoyle. The vacancies in Secretaryships will be filled at an early date.

div.p: THE EXAMINER,
SATURDAY, DECEMBER 18TH, 1909.

"When in doubt, play MORE SCARE trumps," is the old TACTICS. whist motto. The Tory politician changes it into" When in difficulties, resort to a naval -scare." The fact that an attempt to raise .one of these periodical scares is being made at the present time is an indication of the -failure of the Peers to raise public enthusiasm in their cown behalfand of the Tariff Reform- ers to hold the platform successfully against :audiences who understand what it meant by ;the taxation of food. The Peers, it must be .admitted, have made a poor show. They are, for the most part, distinguished by the paucity of their ideas and the vulgarity of -their language. 'The DUKE OF NORFOLK is the premier Duke and Earl, the hereditary Earl- lilarshal, and what not, yet when he ascends .a 'platform he talks of "jolly well this" and jolly well that." Such a style of expression does not accord well with the Ducal station. Lord CURZON says that the use of the House .of Lords is to give a dignity to the Constitu- tion. Well, the platform Peers are not giving dignity to the Hnuse of Lords. Whether they think it necessary to talk (down to their audiences or whether they are using the language of their ordinary life we .are not quite sure; but a mistake has been ,made somewhere. We can assure the DUKE ,OF NORFOLK and others that the ordinary Englishman does not speak in slang phrases. if that is the style of the highest aristocracy it should be confined to drawing-rooms and •stables. _ _ _

And now mimes the naval scare, devised, as Lord Denh&m, a Liberal Peer, says, to save the House of Lords. It is assumed that the British public can always be frightened. Hence the articles, of Mr. Robert Blatchford, -Lord 'Charles Beresford's speeches, Mr. Austen Chamberlain's gibe against Mr. Asquith, and the audacious statement of , the _Navy League that Germany will' p- osseSs 'a stronger fleet than ourselves in 1912 Those," says Dr. Macnamara, "who ',tell you that the sceptre of Sea-Power is slipping from British grasp are either-ignorant of the, facts or are .seeking to retreat from a fatal ,error of party tactics under the cover of :another vamped-up Navy. scare." This is. •stating the case with strict accuracy. Therei is invincible n ignorance on the one hand, and there is deliberate dishonesty on the other. Perhaps we ought to add that there is a -third element, of sincere self-deception. These 'three forces act together, and produce, or aim .at producing, a scare about the Navy. They would do this whatever the condition of the Navy chanced to be. A Navy scare is, as a rule, entirely independent of the strength or the readiness of our fleets. It is just a scare, That is to say, and nothing ;more. Mr. BALFOUR has confessed that there was :a time during the Boer War when he could hardly sleep for thinking of the condition of helplessness to which he had been reduced by 'the great drain •of arms and ammunition made by South. Africa. We can all sleep in ,our beds now, in firm confidence .that our Navy is capable of defending us not only .against the Navy of any other Power, b,ut -against any two or three. The,Government is loosely accused of not spending money enough ,on shipbuilding. How does that accusation look in the light of what Mr. MCKENNA tells us? We are at this moment adding to the Navy, as completed ships, ready for service, -three vessels that are powerful, and that .are more effective weapons of warfare than the Dreadnought. Neptune and the Indefati- gable have been launched at Portsmouth :and at Plymouth respectively. Two other great ships are being built in private yards. Still two others are on the stocks in the dockyards, and behind these orders are ready

tto go forth for four more great fighting ships. What would the scaremongers have? How far do they think it necessary to go in order rto make ourselves reasonably secure? But it is not in the nature of scaremongers td ask themselves questions such as these.

The rival policies of the THE RIVAL two parties are now - POLICIES, before the country. On the one side we have lir. Asquith 's speech at the Albert Hall, and ~,on the other Mr. Balfour's manifesto. Never was there a greater contrast than between -these two utterances. One is all clearness and precision, and the other a vague and watery cloud which keeps changing its shape from hour to hour. No two Unionist papers can agree as to the meaning of Mr. Balfour's utterance. All he can say clearly is that he does not wish to dis- cuss Tariff Reform. That is said quite 'clearly, but everything else is vagueness. On the other hand we have Mr. Asqulth's *definite pronouncement that the aim of ;the Liberal Party in this election is to make the representative principle prevail. Then we have his final seal given to the utterances of other Cabinet Ministers confirming the ffighting policy of not taking office until the _Liberals have power to abate the veto Of the House of Lords. For the rest, the voter needs only to recollect that the Liberal policy means -really and truly "government of the people, for the people, and by the people " in place of the elaborate sham which has atleluded the democracy for too long.

No one in Warrington • CHURCHILL HERE or the surrounding dis- TO-DAY. trict needs reminding that Mr. Winston Churchill is to address two great Liberal meetings in :the town to-day. Nine-tenths •of the v'oters; and about half the population, have applied for ,tickets to give than the privilege of hearing the brilliant young Liberal leader, but, at the outside, the num- ber will necessarqy have to be limited to 5,000. The occasion• is certainly one of the greatest in Warrington's party political history, and rivals in the intense public interest and enthusiasm it has aroused, the livisit of Mr. Chamberlain—then a Radical— n 1885. One curious reflection is that Mr. Chamberlain was as soundly hated by the Tories then as he is revered now. It is a striking coincidence that the guest of to-day has also been the recipient of both the love and hate •of the Tories, and the latter testimony to his administrative talents and forceful Liberal leadership he enjoys to the full, at the present moment. , Nothing, how- ever—not even the Suffragettes—can lessen the whole-heartedness of the welcome which the democratic and freedom-loving majority of Warrington's townpeople are 'burning to extend to Mr. Churchill this afternoon. Could "he but address all the electors, we should consider the battle won. So much for the, magnetism of a great personality.

, • The tour of the wards .„ THE CAMPAIGN which Mr. A. H. IN THE WARDS. Crosfield, M.P., has been making this week has been in the nature of a triumphal pro- gress. Everywhere the Member has beer received with sWndid enthusiasm and the excellent speeches in which he has clearly defined the momentous issues of the conflict and called upon the electors to rally round the standard of Progress have called forth extremely, cordial and unanimous support. Mr. Crosfield has laid bare some of the evil deeds of the arrogant Upper House in mutt- lating and wrecking useful ,and urgently needed legislation. 'As he forcefully putit, the Peers b ave abandoned all pretence at impartial revisim and have consistently taken up anfattitu'de of unblushing partizanship. The campaign in Warrington has opened as encouragingly as the most ardent Liberal could desire—in fact a finer series of ward meetings has probably never been held in the town. The speakers have all sounded the right note in urging the people to battle for their primary rights of liberty and self. government which are now hanging in the balance. Warrington has been roused and there is every indication that on the critical day it will be found solidly on the side of the ,Government and democratic reform as against the Peers and re-action. The year 1906 .saw a glorious triumph for progress. Let the victory in January net be even more decisive, for the cause is so vital as to demand the most emphatic verdict of freedom-loving Britishers.

.The Chief Whip of the POLITICAL Conservative Party, Sir BIRDLIME. s -A. Acland-Hood, has been exposed in his own constituency in a manner that must have brought a blush to his cheek, ,if that were possible. The Central Conservative organisa- tion, of which he is the supreme chief, is sending vans through the country placarded with assurances that Tariff Reform means+ work for all. One of these vans has been going about among his own constituents, who haVe been asking him questions on the sub- ject. Standing on a platform he did not dare to say what was being said for hirn by this Perambulatory yam' He admitted that Tariff Reform does not mean work for all. It means more employment, he added, which, by the way, is no more true than the state- ment which he felt compelled to withdraw. After this contretemps will the lying state- ment on the Conservative vans be obliter- ated? We have not , the slightest expecta- tion that it will. The palpable and admitted falsehood will continue to circulate until the General Election is over.

• Visitors to Territorial Y.M.C.A. AND camps carmot have failed TERRITORIALS. to notice that poPu larand well-nigh indispensable. adjuntt—the Y:M.C.A. tent. Here it is that the citizen soldier may be seen writing his letters home or indulging in pleasant and wholesome recreation after the arduous day's work. By Territorials of all ranks the institution is regarded as a great boon ;-on wet days it is invaluable. General Bethune, C.V.0., C. 8., (commanding West Lancashire Division) and Col. Verschoyle (commanding S. Lancashire brigade) are amongst the' prominent officers who have written warmly appreciative letters bearing testimony to the value attached to the work in military circles. General Bethune says " The Y.M.C.A. not only provides all possible com- forts for its patrons in camp, but the influence for good exerted by your association is incalculable." We are glad to notice that the claims of this important branch of the Y.M.C.A.'s many-sided operations are being urged locally. The Mayor (Alderman- Forshaw) has issued an appeal to leading townsmen to support the movement by donations. He makes a point of the fact that " the Y.M.C.A. tents have pro- vided an effective counter-attraction to the. canteen and the local public-house."— a plea which will commend itself to all who have the best interests of young men at heart. Other aspects to which" the Mayor draws attention are: "The fact that the religious side of the work is not made in any way offensive and that other departments are kept in full swing whilst the meetings are in progress, has meant that thousands of young men have been reached who are not in the habit of attending religious services. The facilities provided for letter-writing, also for the purchase of 'stamps and postal orders have been much appreciated. Another factor that has helped to make the movement such a conspicuous success has been the self- sacrificing work of a big staff of voluntary helpers, more than 300 of whom spent the whole or part of their holidays, during last summer, in this work." We hope many of our readers will be prepared to express their approval of the excellent work of the Y.M.C.A. under canvass by sending donations to the Mayor or to Major Appleton at the Drill Hall. There has been some talk of resuscitating the Y.M.C.A. in Warrington and we are not without hope that there will soon be a successful branch, managed on broad and 'vigorous lines, which would certainly serve a useful purpose in our town.

div.head: AND NOTIONS.
div.p: AND NOTIONS.

Mr. Henry Greenall told the free men and voters of Stockton Heath at a Tory rnceting last week that "the Hoise, ,of Lords were their best friends." No one said audibly "'Save As from our friends," but the snigger which went round the room was eloquent of much.

Mr. A. H. Ci•osfield, M.P., i§ to appear before the Liberal Executive on Tuesday evening next "with a View to his adoption as Liberal candidate for thc Borough at the forthcoming general electbn." The ordeal should not be severe. Mr. Crosfield has already been tried and found true.

* * The Tariff Reform Budget introduced in the Local Parliament has been referred to the country. Would this bold course have been taken if the Warrington Unionist Government had had a complacent heredi- tary House of Lords behind it? We trow not. The opinion of the country would not have been asked!

* w • Mr. Balfour, in a letter to Sir Fortescue Flannery, says: "Of course, Old Age Pensions will be continued by the Unionists. No sensible man ever thought the contrary, and no truthful man ever stated it." We might add that no sensible man believes the Unionists can find the money for Old Age Pensions from Tariff Reform, and no truth- ful man on Mr. Balfour's side has staked his reputation on the party's capacity to do so. * * _

Mr. A. J. King, made a good point against the House of Lords at Grappenhall on Thursday. He said that at the last elec- tion the electors rejected the Hon. Alan Egerton as unsuited to represent them in the legislative chamber. Since then, inheritance had made Mr. Egerton a lord, and he now sat in the Upper House armed with a veto on the people's laws and taxes. Thus does the hereditary principle operate against the public interest. Knutsford Division electors can see the force of such reasoning, and there is every probability that they will abide by -the man of their own choice—honest A. J. King! •** * _ _

We fiope every Churchman will read the striking letter from Canon Hicks, dealing with the election issues, which we print on page 5. He protests vigorously against diocesan pressure" on Churchmen to give a party vote for Church and schools." There are greater issues before the people of the country, and before the Church of England also, if she be true to her sacred and guardian trust. Canon Hicks pertinently asks: "Was not Gladstone a loyal Church- man ?" and the question should remind the closest adherents to the Established Church that they have a duty to themselves and their fellows as well as to their religion. * * *

-There never was less, doubt expressed about the result of a forthcoming election than the one Warrington is preparing for in January. The only question seems to be the size of Mr. Crosfield's majority. It was the large and symmetrical figure of 1,500 four year ago, and every Liberal was more than satisfied. There are some to-day who hope and expect to beat even this record. It would be unkind to suggest as much in the hearing of a Tory, but there are whispers of wondrous things in the Liberal strongholds. ** * •

There has been a marked difference between the meetings of the two parties in Warrington so far. The Tories were first in the field, but-their meeting's were not full and questions were so plentiful that most of them were Conveniently forgotten. The Liberals have had a "crowded house" on each and every occasion since they opened the campaign, and the unanimity and enthusiasm of the audiences have been something to marvel at. There is no question that the Budget has fired the popular imagination, and that the autocratic misuse of privilege and power, by the Lords has roused the resentment of every honest toiler who realizes that the liberties of him- self and his kind are sacred and should be inviolable. There will be some wigs—with coronets on them—scattered o'er the Green before this fight is ended. " Crosfield for the Commons, and Pierpoint for the Peers," is the winning cry in Warrington. * * *

We do not wish to trespass on the province of our Hard Case Editor (says Vanity Fair ") but we cannot help remarking what an excellent Hard Case Lord Lansdownl's present predicament would make :—A, an astute and experienced political leader, has embarked on a course involving the gravest isspes. He has been so unfortunate as to arouse the enthusiasm of a number of youthful followers who announce their intention of" stumping the country" on the question. A knows quite well that these followers are chiefly valuable when silent, and that" stumping the country" will probably drown the movement in ridicule. On the other hand, they are all peers. What is Ato do? What is an amusing hypothetical case to us, is, alas ! a solemn matter of fact to Lord Lansdowne, and he has our deepest sympathy. We really can- not advise him what to do, but, judging by the specimens we have so far seen of the youthful peers' stump-speeches, we should respectfully suggest that it was something drastic with a muzzle in it. * *

The latest Balfotlrian red herring is the threat of a single Chamber. "If the Radicals have their way," he tells us, "you will be governed by a Single Chamber. No Ater civilised country is so governed." That seems a remarkably impudent utterance, for what is the present system except a Single Chamber Government? It is a Single Chamber Government when the Tories are in; a Single Chamber when the Tories are out; and there is only this difference, that when the Tories are in the Single Chamber that governs us is the House of Commons, and when the Tories are , out it is the House of Lords. * * *

Mr. Asquith's scheme would not by any means mean a Single Chamber Government. ven if it did, we should by no means be willing to say that it would not be more profitable to have a Single Chamber Govern- ment than to have the present drag upon progress that we have in the House of Lords. But for those timid souls who are still alarmed at the one Chamber bogey we would point out that the Asquith plan is very far removed from it. The absolute veto of the House of Lords would be removed. Its power over finance would be taken away. Yes, but before this year it has never had any power over finance; and it has been the boast of its own defenders that its veto has never been absolute: All that Liberals pro- pose to do is to translate these boasts into literal fact.

• What would happen under the Govern- ment plan? If the Lords throw out a Liberal bill, the only .reply now left to the Liberals is to dissolve. So that the Liberals laye to choose between powerlessness and

perpetual dissolutions. The other alterna- tive is equally bad, for either means very much the same thing. The Parliament that is always dissolving is powerless. In place of that intolerable system the Liberals pro- pose that when the Lords throw out a Liberal bill there should be a conference between ,the Houses in the same fashion that prevailed up to 1837. It was such a con- ference as that which saved England from anarchy at the time when James 11. fled from these shores and William of Orange had to be elected in his place. * * *

If agreement still failed, then that •con- ference is to be repeated at least once, if not twice, and a year's delay is to take place for consultation and discussion. Only then is the veto to give way. Thus the House of [ Lords would, under such a scheme, be left with great consultative. powers. Our only fear is that it is too moderate, and that before the end of this battle the Liberal Party will be forced to take more stringent measures, in order that the will of the Commons may prevail. For that is the essential point. Whatever the plan adopted that must be our cry, "Let' the will of the Commons prevail ! " In other words, let the Briton be master in his own house. Is it not fairly simple,?
LOCAL NEWS.

Special Notice. Our annual Sheet Altnanack —the best in the dis- trict -is given with to-day's WARRINGTON EXAMINER. Saturday next, December 25th, being Christmas Day and the 'Saturday followina being New Year's Day, the WARRINGTON EXAMINER will be published on Friday inst-tad of Saturday, at the usual hour, Women's Liberal Association. Thelmnnal business meeting of the Warrington Woulen's Liberal Association was held on Tuseday evening at the Liberal Club. Mrs. Parker priesided. and was re-elected president. Mrs. Walker (treasurer), and Mrs. Osborne (secretary) were also re-appointed. Mr. and Mrs. A. H. Crosfiela and Mr. C. E. Parker were present'at the meeting. PEAT FOR HOUSE FIRES, 3s. 9d! per 100 blocks, delivered free..—J. S. GARLAND, Kitchen Range and Stove Warehouse, 51, 53; & 55, Bridge Bt., Warrington.—Advt. Warrington Philomathic Society. A meeting of the above Society w.,as held in the Old Academy, Bridge , Foot, on Wednesday, the chair being taken by the President (Mr. Hedley Taylor) at 7.30 n.m, - The debate " Are experiments on animals justifiable ? "was opened in the affirmative by Mr. W. Rigby; and in the negative by Mr. D.. 3. Dunn.—,An interesting and instructive discussion followed, and on a vote being taken Mr. Rigby's supporters were found to be in the majority. .

Ragged School and Mission. A concert, presided over by Mr. S. Gough, and in aid of School funds was given by Miss Lawless' polar doncert party, in the Tipper schoolroom on MondaLy eveniqg the 13th inst. • The • programme whic4t consistea of action songs, flqg drills, solos, recitetrivip, choruses, and dialogues was rendered by the alistes: The audience of 350 persons shewing their.ppreciation in a very hearty manner. Miss Lawless and Mr. Moon were efficient accompanists. MILLER 6:, Co. (opposite Trinity, Church), for Whist Drive Prizea. Large Stock.—Advt. Literary and Philosophical Society. At the monthly meeting of this Socie4, held at the Masonic Hall bn Monday evening Dr. A. Hodgkinson read 'a paper entitled "Newfoundland," with lanterni illustrations. Dr. Hodgkinson gave .a short account of the early history of Newfoundland, followed by a brief description of the country as it is to-day. He said -there was little doubt that in the future New- foundland would take a more ttnportint position amongst the colonies of Great Britain than she had hitherto done. (Applause). A discussion followed and Dr. Hodgkinson was warmly thanked for his services, XMAS GIFTS of every description. See window display.—J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge st., V4'arrio gton.—Advt. Penny Popular Concert. • The Woodvilles " always prove a popular attrace tion at these concerts and a large audience assembled to greet them on Saturday evening. The" Wood- illei had bookings at Liverpool, Manchester, St. Helens, Ormskirk, Garston, Widnes, and other places, and they are an accomplished party. Their programme on Saturday night was! well varied and full of merit. Mr.l3. Ker and Mr. 'Wal Powell were eminently successful in their efforts to amuse. Mr. Harry Maynard proved a skilful zither-banjoist, and Mr. Powell and Miss Chrissie Scott were amusing in the duet" Let me take your phot,grapli." Mr. Steve Clqrke (baritone) rendered Sergeant of the line," and Miss D. Weston (soprano) gave the" De.ar, home songs," both in good style. Miss Elsie Wynn was a capable accompanist.

Walker's Brewery Band. On Wednesday evening the annual complimentary, concert in connection with Walker's well-known Brewery Band was given in the Parr Hall before a large and enthusiastic audience. The band itself under the able conductorship of Mr. W. Winatanley played a number of items including" The Bohemian Girl " overture and the Waltz " Autumn" in capital style. Mr, J. Dykes (Trombonist) took the leading part with great credit to himself in the" Death of Nelson" solo in which the band supported him with the yery stimulating accompaniments which it will be remembered form an important part of the song. There was also a trio of capable vocalists who rendered songs, duets and other concerted pieces in a most, ,pleasing manner. Then to give still greater variety to the attractions there was Professor Weber the conjuror and ventriloquist who proved a boat in himself, and, to round off the whole, Mr. John Drake (humorist) greatly amused the company with some lively impersonations. • ( Death of Mrs. Savage. A painful sensation was created on Monday by the sudden death of Mrs. Savage, 7, Springfield-street, widow of the late Captain George Savage. The deceased lady, who was 76 years of age, was apparently in her usual good health on Sunday. She had attended all the meetings in connection with Mr. George Clarke's mission at the Parr Hall and on Sunday evening she was preparing to go to the final service when she was seized with illness and died early the following morning. Mrs. Savage was born at Sankey Bridges and, with the exception of a years spent at Widnes, she had lived in Warring- ton fill her life. She was a staunch Wesleyan and had for many years been a worshipper at Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church. Her unassuming and sympathetic nature had endeared her to a large circle of friends. She leaves one son, Captain Alfred Savage, the managing director of the Zillah Shipping Company, to mourn her loss. The funeral took place on Wednesday afternoon at the Cemetery, the Rev. John Gunnell officiating. The chief mourners were as follows :—Mr.and Mrs.W.A. Savage(son and daughter- in-law), Messrs. James, Samuel, John and William Sammerfield (nephews), and Mr. arid Mrs. Andrews. Amongst others present were the Rev. E. B. Keeling, Messrs. J. Mack, James Reece, John McGwkin, I Caldwell (Liverpool) A. Caldwell (St. Helens), T. Dodd i T. Lock (Widnes); S. W. Hayward, 'lsaac Hayward, George Gough, E. Wilke, John Ashley, Arthur Ashley, and J. Bailey. The wreaths included : ---" Toni and daughter-in-law," Mr. and Mrs. Andrews, Messrs.J. Caldwell, Arthur Caldwell, J. Bailey, James Richardson, T. Dodd, T. Lock, John Hayward, Samuel Sumtherfield and James Summerfield.

A...Biowne, on behalf of Mr. William Pilkington, Fearnheadjane, Padgate, sued Mr. George Smith, brickmaker, Padgate, for breach of contract, for work done and hooks supplied aMoutring to £'3o I.ls. M.—Mr. T. S. Steel .appeared for the defendant. Mr. Browne stated that the damages amounted to £29 Its., an 4 were wages due to Mr. Smith. In April last plaintiff was working at. Sutton near St. Helens and was promised work for the summer . and winter by Mr. Rowlands. :who. said Mr. Smith had sent him. Plaintiff went to work for Mr. Smith and did so until September when he was given notice owing to slackness.-Defend%nt in his .evidence stated that he did not promise plaintiff work for the winter and. summer.— His Honour gave judgment for tho defendant with costs. . • . •

Dramatic Society. There was a large audience at the Royal Court Theatre on Saturday evening when the concluding performances of "The Idler" were given. An engagement in connection with the Federated Agri- cultural Societies of Lancashire dnd Cheshire pre- vented Sir Gilbert Greenall being present. Mr. W. Peter Rylands, chairman of the Infirmary Board of Management, was in attendance, and presented all the ladies with beautiful bouquets and numerous ether tokens of appreciation from ,admirers were also .handed across the footlights. The only regret is that the popular parts of the house have not been better patronized. A word of prailiv. is due- to Mr. .1„. W. Mien, the hon. secretary, for , the admirable arrange- ments. '

div.p: FOR WHIST DRIVE PRIZES you cannot do better than see MILLER & CO.'S seleotion.—Advt.
Local_ Delegates at Town Planning Conference.

At the To;n Planning Conference held in London on Wednesday under the auspices of the National Housing and Town Planning Council, speeches were made by two local delegates, With regard to the final stage of Town Planning—the public inquiry—it was suggested that the help of leading citizens should be enlisted. Alderman Bennett (Warrington) expressed the opinion that the ,best public feeling should be secured, for in every town the scheme would be opposed by reactionaries who, would endeavour to thwart it. He ,advocated an active educational propaganda.— An important question was raised by a Southern delegate as to the possibility of owners rushing in plans which might prevent town-planning. Councillor Pemberton (Warrington) said that he thought it might be a very serious thing if plans were passed which might stop the development of a scheme. Therefore, it was very necessary that they should adopt the Act at once. In a discussion on compensation Councillor Pemberton said that if a typical Lancashire town went in for an elaborate scheme, and afterwards discovered that the cost was going to be vastly in excess of •the estimated cost it would stagger the movement. A resolution was carried that the local authorities consider at the earliest possible moment the cost of planning a town. MILLER & CO., 10, Sankey at., Jeivellers. Xmas. Presents, great variety, from I.s.—Advt. Wesleyan Quarterly Meeting. The quarterly meeting of the Warrington Wesleyan Methodist Circuit was held at Bold-street Church, on Thursday, the Rev. E. B. Keeling presiding. The Revs. T. Miller' T. Gladding, F. W. Kernick, John Gunnell and Hawkins Pawlyn (Lymm), were also present. The Bold-street friends • were thanked for providing ,tea, on the proposition of Mr. Corbett seconded by Al r. Gill.—The numerical statement for the quarter showed a considerable increase of mom-' bership, in fact the advance was greater than had been noticed for some years. Most of the churches reported an increase. The financial statement was again most satisfactory. Mr. R. H. Meldrurn, on resigning the position of circuit steward, was thanked for the efficient servicesthe has rendered. Dr. Bennett was elected senior circuit stewardovith Mr. F. A. Harris as his colleague. Mr. J. A. Smith was appointed quarterly meeting secretary in succession t 9 Mr. F. A. Harris and Mr. Isaac E. Barlow was appointed circuit chapel secretary. Mr. W. E. Plinston was thanked and re-appointed circuit guild secretary.—A. vote of thanks was accorded to the local preachers for their services. Arrangements were made for special services to be held at Bold street Church on behalf of the West London Mission. The Rev. W. H. Walters and the Rev. J. E. Rattenbtiry are expected to preach. The next quarterly meeting will be held at. Bewsey-road on March 17th. Women's Circle Xmas Party.

At the invitation of the Rev. R. E. and Mrs. Lethereo about 250 members and friends of the Women's Circle attended the first annual Christmas gathering on Tuesday evening in the Circle Rooms, Bridge Street. The room was tastefully decorated by Mrs. Jones, Miss Gornall and others with ever- greens supplied by Mesdames Armitage, Rylands and Broadbent. Mr. A. H. Crosfield M.P. presided and in the coutte of an interesting address he thought one of the most hopeful signs in modern life was the deepening sense of social duty which was so strongly evidenced in the work of the Circle. The Rev. C. Harvey Cook, who succeeeded to the chair . when Mr. Crosfield left, also gave a short address. An interesting event of the evening was the orepntation to Mrs. Letheren by Mrs. Crosfield, on behalf of the members and friends of the Circle, of a handsome desk and chair for her indefatigable efforts in connection with the Circle. Five minutes speeches were delivered by Mrs. James _Dodds, and Miss ' Bessie Dutton. iliss Dixon rendered two solos in a pleasing manner, and Miss Corney. delighted the audience ivith two recitations. Two competitions—musical snatches and celebrities— were an enjoyable diversion.—Mr and Mrs. Letheren were accorded a vote of thanks on the proposition of Mrs. Dodds, seconded by Mr. J. B. Starkey.

div.head: MR. WINSTON CHURCHILL'S VISIT.
div.p: MR. WINSTON CHURCHILL'S VISIT.
TO-DAY'S GREAT MEETINGS.

To-day (S4turday) will be a notable day in the political history of Warrington, for we are to be honoured with a visit from that eminent young states- man, the Right Hon. Winston S. Churchill, M.P., President of the Board of Trade. Two great meetings have been arranged, and judging from the enormous demand for tickets, public interest in the occasion has reached a• height absolutely unprecedented in Warrington, as far as political engagements are concerned. .

Mr. Churchill will deliver his chief speech at a meeting to comm6nce in the Parr Hall at three o'clock. Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., will preside, and several other members of Parliament are expected to attend. Simultaneously with the principal gathering, an overflow meeting will be held at the Hippodrome, and on concluding his Parr Hall oration Mr. Churchill will proceed to the Hippodtome and deliver a second speech. Mr. C. E. Parker, president of- the Liberal Association, will preside and the speakers, in addition to Mr. Churchill, will include- Sir W. J. Crossley. Bart., M.P., Mr. Hamar Greenwood. M.P. (York), Mr, A. J'. King, M.P., Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., and Mr. J. Howes.

It is a matter for congratulation that Mr. Hamar Greenwood, M.P. has consented to speak at the over- flow meeting, for he is regarded as one of the best peakers in the House of Commons. A native of Canada, Mr. Greenwood, who is 39 years of age, took his BA. degree at Toronto University in 1805. For some time he served in the Department of Agriculture, Ontario. Military matters also claimed -much of his attention, for he was an officer in the Canadian Militia for eight years and was connected with Captain King's Colonials, I. Y., since the formation of the corps. Mr. Greenwood, who is a barrister, became Parliamentary. Private Secretary to Mr. Churchill in 1906. • •

Admission to the gallery at the Hippodrome can be obtained without ticket, but for the pit and circle tickets are necessary. Admission to the Parr Hall mebting will be by ticket only. Every, precaution will be taken against the intrusion of "suffragettes." Only a limited number of tickets have been issued to Mies, on a distinct pledge that they will not interrupt the meeting. A _portrait and biography of Mr. Churchill will be found on page 5. -

div.head: LIBERAL CLUB.
div.p: LIBERAL CLUB.
Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P. Distributes Bowling Prizes.

Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD, M.P., had a great reception at the Liberal Club on Thursday evening when he attended to distribute the• prizes gained in the recent annual bowling handicap. The proceedings took the form of a smoking concert which proved a complete success. There was a large attendance, including a good muster of the fair sex, and an excellent musical programme was appreciatively received. The room was well decorated with plants and looked bright 4nd attractive.

Mr. J. WoRRALL presided and amongst others present were :—Aldernaan Burton, Councillors W tu.ilkinson, Howard, Dickenson and Cnaington, Messrs. T. Pemberton, W. Bibby, J. Critclaky, and W. Haigh. On arriving from the Church-street meeting Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., was greeted with loud cheers. He distributed the prizes as follow :-1, case of cutlery, H. Daintith ; 2, barometer, W. Langley; 3, case of cutlery, H. Cook ; 4, salad bowl and servers, F. Dale; 5, A. Lawton; 6, barometer, G. Finch; 7, butter dish and knife, G-. Baker; 8, clock, W. Warburton; 9, match box, G. H. Shaw; 10, knives,, R. Marrow; 11, carvers, M. Tobin; 12, breakfast cruet, R. Fogg; 13, flower vases, John Wilkinson; 14. toast rack, J. Perry; 15, jam dish, H. Bailey • 16, match box, E. R. Clare. The Crosfield Cup and gold medal were pregented to Fred Dale and a gold medal for runner up to Wm. Daintith. Councillor WILKINSON proposed a vote of thanks to Mr. Crosfleld for giving such a handsome set of prizes, and attending to present them. Mr. W. HAIGH, in seconding, alluded to the coming 'election, and said that from his personal observation he believed the Liberals in Warrington had a winning chance second to none. (Applause.) The CHAIRMAN, in supporting, said he also believed that in January next they were going to repeat the memorable victory of 11106. (Applause.) He hoped every individual present would do his or her utmost to ensure Mr. Crosfleld's triumphant return. (Applause). The motion was enthusiastically carried. Mr. CROSFIRLD, in returning thanks, alluded to the successful ward meetings which had been held during the week and said he had never addressed meetings where a finer spirit had been shown. (Applause.) Having referred to the vital importance of Free Trade which they were called upon to defend, Mr. Crosfleld said an even greater issue had been forced upon them by the Lords. The issue was one that touched the self-respect, independenee and dignity of every British citizen, because he did not think it was an exaggeration to say that if they were so feeble and reckless as to allow the Lords to dominate them in th t, way they would be little better in the future than political toadies and serfs. (Applause). Much important work had yet to be done and the Government intended going on, not with revolutionary doctrines that would upset the whole country and turn it topsy-turvy, but with thorough-going measures of social reform. (Applause). He had no fear of what the country was going to do in the coming battle.(Applause). Tha people would not part with their birthright for a mess of pottage or a pint of beer. (Applause.) With regard to our own town, he hoped that if Lancashire was destined to play a great and influential part in this controversy—as it certainly would do—Warrington might play a leading part in Lancashire. (Applause.) Having touched upon the great value of games in these days of high pressure, Mr. Crostield concluded by say- ing he hoped he might have the privilege of attending gatherings of that kind at the club for many years to come, quite irrespective of what his political fortunes might be. (Applause.) During the evening songs were very creditably given by Miss Carrie Hastings, Mr. J. W. Willett, and Mr. D. Gittens. The Apollo Quartette (Messrs. R. W. Cook, J. Critchley, D. Gittens and W. Woodcock) sang "The Old Brigade" and" Robin Adair" with good effect, and Mr. Bert Hollingsworth created great merriment with his humorous sketches. Mr. W. Ford played the piano- forte accompaniments. I A vote of thanks to the Chairman concluded the I proceedings.

The prime issue was whether any choice the electors might make in future was to be worth making at all. He knew Tories who were going to vote Liberal on this occasion, although they were rather weak on Free Trade. If they believed in "government of the people by the people" their one business on this occasion was to vote for a renresentative in the House of Commons who believed in the same maxim. (Cheers). According to the forecast of the Tariff Reform Budget,publ isbed in the "Birmingham Post," the tariff reformers had already dropped the promise of compensating reductions in food taxation,of which their speakers bed made so much. Why? Because the dilemma with which they were now faced was that of finding the money and they could not afford the reductions. The preponderating proportion of the articles which the tariff reformers wanted to tax were articles of working class consumption which were wanted in the humblest homes of the poor. The people had a right to those goods and no Tory Government, had a right to come in, and by an unwarrantable infrace tion of the liberty of the subject, demand that such goods should be boycotted.
