div.head: MEETING AT SILVER-STREET.
div.p: MEETING AT SILVER-STREET.
Mr. Crosfield, M.P., on the Great Issue.

Silver-street school was filled to its utmost capacity on Tuesday evening, and the meeting was characterised by complete unanimity and enthusiasm. Mr. A. H. Crogield, M.P., attended and had a magnificent reception. Councillor Wilkinson presided, and amongst others present en the platform were :—Mr. W. Canning (Manchester), Councillors Locker. Ctinnington, Haiti - well and Dickenson, Nlessrs. C. E. Parker, J. Upson, J. Jarman, P. Peacock, and J. Howes, jun. The CHAIRMAN said that throughout the length and breadth of the land Liberals were filled with indignation at theaction of the House of Lords in throwing out tbe Finance Bill. There was no provision in the Budget to tax the food or necessities of life of any workingman. It would, however, insist on a more adequate contribu- tion from those men who had benefitted by the exertions of the community and the progress of municipalities. (Cheers.) Had the Budget been passed thirty years ago the life of the average workingman would have been a great deal better to-day. Giving a

LOCAL INSTANCE of the unearned increment which accruei to landlords, the speaker said that a short time ago the site of the 13eamont school and the newly made streets in the vicinity was all fields. It was assessed at about £4 an acre, which at twenty-five years' purchase represented a value of £lOO per acre. When the Corporation required land for a school they had to pay £B5O per acre. Under the provisions of the Budget the community would participate in the greatly enhanced value which was conferred on land by public activities and necessities. (Cheers.) Mr. J. JARMAN said the tariff reformers had issued a poster which said : "Will you tax the foreigner or pay the bill yourselves?" He did not know how they reconciled that with the statement of the chairman of the Tariff Reform League who said "he would be a knave if he stood on the platform and told them that the whole of a Protective tax was going to be borne by the foreigner." The speaker contended that the con- sumer would certainly have to pay the tax in the form of increased prices for his goods. He instanced the sugar tax imposed by the late Government and which had cost Co-operative societies millions of pounds. Alluding to the misleading poster issued by the other side with regard to the big and little loaf, Ur. Jarman quoted the frank admission of Mr. Chaplin, one of the Conservative leaders, wbo said "Of course the Radical party cannot be blamed for the recent rise in the price of bread." (Cheers). Mr. CANNING, of Manchester, dealt at some length with the fiscal question. In support of his contention that Protection increased the cost of living, he men- tioned the case of two towns, five miles apart, one of which was in Germany and the other in Holland. While Germany taxed certain articles of food Holland let them in free and the result was that hundreds of work- men employed in the German town lived in Holland, and travelled between the two towns to and from their work, because it was cheaper to live in the State where there was Free Trade. Dealing with the " dumping " of German billets into this country, Mr. Canning said the cheap supply of those billets enabled our wire manufacturers to compete in the best markets of the world, Ile was informed that to make a ton of billets about ten men were employed, but the manufacture of a ton of steel wire found work for 100 men. How much better would employment be if in order to seize the opportunity of making billets they lost trade in wire which employed ten times the number of men If they erected tariff walls they made everything dearer and instead of raising wages they lowered them, while the hours of labour were increased. Alluding to the licence duties in the Budget, the speaker made some interesting comparisons between London and New York. He said that in Loudon the average amount paid for a licence was £3B a year but in New York the average was from £205 to £245 a year. New York produced £2.175,000 by its liquor licences, but London with 1,000,000 more population produced only £200,000. Taking wholesale and retail, the total amount of licences in New York came to £2,320,000, whereas in London the total was only .C 263,000. Accord- ing to the basis of population London ought to be yielding £3,000,000 per annum from this source. (Cheers.) The Budget would redress glaring inequali- in licensing. (Cheers).

div.head: MR. CROSFIELD'S SPEECH.
div.p: MR. CROSFIELD'S SPEECH.

Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD, M.P., whose arrival was the signal for a loud outburst of cheering which was renewed when he rote to address the meeting, said they were on the eve of the greatest and gravest political struggle which bad ever beer i known in the life time of the oldest man present and probably the most serious and far reaching electoral contest, if they considered its consequences, that any man was likely to witness, however long he lived. They were face to face, as a chief issue, with the question : whether representative government as we had known it in Britain for centuries past—the right of the people to govern themselves—was to continue, whether it was to be a real fact or little better than an empty sham. (Cheers). He respectfully submitted that it was absolutely impossible to consider a graver crisis in politics than that. The issue was so tremendous that it included every other great cause which they had to fight for and carry into practical effect in the future. When they addressed themselves to such measures as reasonable but thorough-wing temperance reform, a fair and equal educational system, bona-fide social reform—not that bastard "reform" which professed to give what was urgently needed with one hand and took back a great deal mare with the other—great financial principles of graduated taxation which placed the biggest burdens on the broadest backs, the vital Free Trade controversy which concerned Lancashire perhaps more than any other part of the population—all these issues were dominated by the great Constitutional question of

WHETHER THE LORDS OR THE PEOPLE WERE TO BE TOP DOG. (Cheers). Of course, it bad been very evident during the great campaign which Mr. Churchill—(ebeers)— had conducted in Lancashire what the opinion of Lancashire men on theaa questions was, and therefore it was not surprising that their opponents were trying

o draw a red herring across the track and bamboozle he public with promises of more employment and better trade if they proceeded to tax themselves all round. It behoved Liberals to meet that .fallacious kind of argument, that absolute humbug, and nail the false coin to the counter whenever they came across it, and as far as he personally was concerned he was per- fectly willing to deal with that question every time it came up. At the same time, they must not allow the Conservatives to shirk the other great issue. (Cheers). No doubt most of his hearers had been reading the speeches,closely packed with sound argument, common-sense and logic that neither could be answered nor was it attempted to be answered by the other side—those masterly orations which Mr. Churchill had been delivering—(cheers)—and they had been imprcssed with his allusions to the position that Britain and Lancashire in particular held in many industries. They all knew that the whole commercial world, outside Britain, envied us in Lancashire the

EXTRAORDINARY PREDOMINANCE that we had in the cotton trade. Mr. Churchill bad also referred to our great engineering trade, to our ship-building trade which was another phenomenal industry, and be had pointed out that an absolutely essential factor in our world supremacy in the over- see trade was the cost of production. (Cheers). It was au astounding thing that with that fact staring us in tbe face, we shoulu be invited deliberately and with our eyes open to increase the cost of production and throw away the advantage we possessed to-day. (Cheers). From his (Mr. Crosfield's) own experience in the export trade he could give them facts to show that notwithstanding the handicap imposed by higher freights, we bad been able, thanks to our capacity to draw upon the untaxed resources of the whole world, not only to compete with our great rivals across the Atlantic, with their rich natural advantages, but even to beat them. (Cheers). Mr. Croslield laid special emphasis upon the necessity for Free Trade to the cotton industry, and contsnded that the question of employment was one of the most urgent and vital reasons for defending the Free Trade citadel. He saw from the displays on the hoardings that gifted artists and scribes who always came out of their shells at ekction times—(laughter)—were bent on making capital of the problem of unemployment. It was a pity that such a tragic question should be brought into the party game at all, but they were quite prepared to meet the Uoaservatines on their own ground. (Cheers). FREE TRADE \V AS TUE VERY FOUNDATION OF GOOD EMPLOYMENT in Lancashire, and far from being indifferent to the evil of unemployment the Government were absolutely determined to grapple with it and reduce it to the lowest possible point. (Cheers.) Moreover, they were going to do it in practical, honest and straightforward says. (Loud cheers). So far no fiscal system had been able to prevent trade fluctuations, but in future the State would enable the workman to insure against the haunting dread and anxiety of unemploy- ment. (Cheers.) "I am very thankful," continued Mr. Crosfield "that we no longer have to talk shout the necessity of the State providing for the very old. (Loud cheers). We have done a bit of good work, I think, in that respect—(cheers)—and besides the pro- vision against the course of unemployment to which I have referred, we are bent on carrying out in the immediate future, if you send us back to do it— (cheers)—further schemes to deal with the dark days when a man unluckily loses his health or, through some breakdown, canuot figure as the .breadwinner for the family. In thus relieving the anxiety which often saps a man's mind and energy we shall make him a better and happier citizen all round." (Cheers). Alluding to the Budget, Mr. Crosfleld said the financial needs of the country had never been faced in a more manly style, nor in a fairer way to every part of the com- munity, than Mr. Lloyd-George—(loud cheers)—had faced them. He (Mr. Cresfield) confessed that he was one of those who did not believe the rumours that u parcel of very ill-informed, very prejudiced and care- less men who never, under ordinary circumstances,took the trouble to come to the House of Lords would dare to vote away the supplies to the King which were needed to carry on the enormous machine of British Government. He did not believe them because he knew that many of the weightiest Concervatives in the House of Lords were simply furious at the idea of these reckless wild nen from the back woods— (laughter)—taking the law into their own hands. But although the action of the Lords was nothing short of

A PUBLIC SCANDAL he was not Sorry it had been done—(cheers and a voice: " Never agu in.") For men so fortunate in circumstances to try and shirk their share of taxation and throw it on to the poorer part of the nation was—(a voice: "Mean.") Yes, he called it absolutely mean and un-English too. (Cheers.) But the rejection of the Budget was not the whole case against the Lords. It had become nothing less than humiliating that the pick of England who were selected for the Cabinet, should in all their work have to consider how they could secure the favour of the Lords to prevent their measures being mauled, mutilated and emasculated. The Government had worked honestly in the interests of democracy—they never had a Parliament which had democratic needs more honestly at heart—but all the time they wore faced with a certain feeling of impotence through the domination of the Lords. "1 am not sot-4." concluded Mr. Crosfleld "that we are able to get at close quarters with them and put an end to this absolute and irresponsible veto, once and for all. (Cheers.) It will be a good day for democracy, for all the people of England, when we have completed that work and I hope you will give us a strong backing in doing it." (Loud and prolonged cheers). Mr. PETER PEACOCK in proposing a vote of thanks to the speakers, made a capital speech on the political situation. Tariff reform, he said, meant taking from the poor to give to the rich, but the Bridget was taking from the rich for thc common good. Ile hoped Warrington would plump for Mr. Crosfleld who had the courage of his convictions and openly supported the Budget in Parliament. (Cheers.) Mr. liPsoN in seconding asked if it was a right and

div.head: MEETING AT GREENING'S WORKS.
div.p: MEETING AT GREENING'S WORKS.
Mr. J. Dodds and the Lords' Record.

The campaign opened very promisingly on Monday evening with a meeting in the dining hall at Messrs. Greening's works, Bewsey-road. There was a large gathering, the spacious room being well filled, and great enthusiasm was manifested. Mr. J. A. J. Morton presided and was supported by Mr. Batnuel Gleave (Free Trade Union), Mr. James Dodds, Councillors Wilkinson, Hawthorn and Skelland, Messrs. T. Pemberton, E. Wynne Jones, P. Peacock, P. O'Brien and J. Howes, junr. The CHAIRNI AN said that at the last election the held the Free Trade flag high in Warrington—(cheers)— and secured a great triumph in what had hitherto been an old Tory constituency. The coming election was to be more important than the last because it would be complicated with the question of the House of Lords. He believed the meetings which were held during the summer months made it clear that WARRINGTON WAS ',REF. TRADE TO THE BACK BONE _

—(cheers)—and he was of opinion that if the country as a whole could be tested on the fiscal question alone it would be found as strong for Free Trade as it was at the last election. Judging from the alarm of the Con- servatives they appeared to be afraid that the House of Lords was doomed and be hoped that fear would be only too well realised when the election came. (Applause). Tf progressives would work unitedly and enthusiastically, having in view the far-reaching issues involved, they would secure another splendid victory. (Cheers). Mr. J. DoPps then addressed tbe meeting. He said he had been in Warrington some thirty-two years but this was the first election in which he had taken a prominent part, although he had been a Radical all his life. (Cheers.) On the present occasion, however, the issues were so tremendous and so vital that every man should come forward and take his side, otherwise he might fairly be called a coward or a slave. (Cheers.) The issue was whether the Lords or the people, through their represetitatives, were to rule. The Lords had raised it not because they loved the people but because they hated the taxes in the Budget. Alluding to THE RECORD OF THE LORDS during the past century, the speaker said that in 1807 a Bill was passed by the House of Commons to provide a school for the education of the people in every parish in the country. The Lords rejected it and thereby retarded the education of this country for generations. The fact that they did that was sufficient to condemn them for all time. (Cheers.) Then in regard to the great Reform Bill of 1832. the Lords opposed it until they were threatened with the creation of . a sufficient number of Peers to carry it and then they gave way. In that, course of action they showed themselves more sensible than their present day successors who bad given themselves away and fallen into the trap. (Laughter.) The Lords rejected a resolution for inquiry into the operation of the Corn Laws and it was only after a tremendous struggle, led by Cobden aud Bright and behind the scenes by Gladstone, that the grand revolution was brought about. Tariff Reformers would have us return to the days before the repeal of the Corn Laws, but he would remind them of the words of Sir Robert Peel, a great Tory who took a sane and common-sense view of his duties and who said "he was happy to think that when the people ate their bread and thought of him they would feel it was no longer leavened by a sense of injustice as it, had been tinder the Corn Laws." (Cheers.) Alluding to the Lords' attitude to the present Government, which was returned with full power to do all that it had done, Mr. Dodds said that in 1906 a splendid Educa- tion Bill was passed through the House of Commons and submitted to the House of Lords. That measure meant among other things that the teachers in rate- supported schools should not be subjected to any test, but the Lords destroyed it. In regard to the Licensing Bill of last year, he (Mr. Dodds) did not like to attack the Church but he would be glad to see the clergy in Warrington helping to fight the liquor traffic. (Hear. hear.) When tbe Bishop of Liverpool spoke at. the demonstration in support of the Licensing Bill not a single beneficed clergyman in Warrington came to support him. ("Shame.") But many of them went to the brewers' meeting and one of them made a speech there. With regard to education, it. was only of late that the cry about the rights of the parent had been raised. Before the present controversy they did not hear snything about the views of the parents being consulted in the villages where Nonconformists laboured under such disadvantages. Another recent act of the House of Lords was the rejection of the Licens- ing Bill—a mealure which would have done as much for the poorer people of the country as any Bill that bad been passed and which would have gone a long way towards getting rid of unemployment. We spent £160,000.000 per annum in drink—would he be wrong if he said £100,00.),000 more than we actually needed ? How far would that £100,000,000 go in improving the comfort of the people, in giving them better houses, furniture, clothing and food? It would create a greater demand for labour and the question of unemployment would be killed for generations. (Cheers.) Lest of all, the Lords had rejected the Budget, although Mr. Balfour had said that the

COMMONS HAD SOLE AND UNCONTROLLED POWER over finance. The Lords pretehded that they wanted to refer the measure to tbe people, but that was not their usual attitude. When- ever a Tory tiovernment was in power, all the measures they had passed, however reactionary and however much against the interests of the people, were approved by the Lords, but when a Liberal measure came along—a measure for which the great majority of the members of the House of Commons had been elected by the great majority of the people—they hung it up or killed it as they had been doing during the last four years. Did the electors of Warrington intend that to go on ? (Cries of "No.") If so, they were not the men he took them to be. He hoped they would all -unite in support of a Government which had a grand record. Mr. Winston Cnurchill—(cheers) —in his speech at Preston gave a magnificent statement of the case for the Lib‘tral party—its determination to deal with social reform, to improve old age pensons, to see that men out of employment were looked after, that the children Were fed and that by and by there should be general .emploYment, or at any rate no starvation, throughout the land. (Cheers.) They had to ensure the passing of the Budget to begin that grand process. If the people of England did not support the Government now it would be an eternal disgrace to them and England would deserve to go down unhonoured and unsung. If the Lords had done such a thing three hundred years ago they would have lost their heads. Our Constitution having stood for hundreds of years, with thatparticular rule that the Lords were,not to touch a money Bill, it was a people's matter and the Lords could have no right to deal with it. After having for so long pocketed the unelrned increment, through our improper laud laws, the Lords now declined to pay their fair share of taxation, although they could well afford it. Ho said • " Shame upon them." (Cheers.) With regard to tariff reform, he did not believe that any of the leaders who were supporting that policy really at heart believed that it would do what they said it would do, because if they thought for one moment they would see it was impossible. If the tax on £140,000,000 worth of manufactured goods failed to exclude them from our country how would it provide mow work for our people ? If, on the other hand, the tax kept them out, lv how would they oain the revenue for old age pen- sions, social reform and Dreadnoughts? Mr. Ure said truly that it would be impossible, when they con- sidered the expenses of collection and the time it would take to get the scheme in working order, to raise the money by tariff reform. While he (Mr. Dodds) did not say—and he did not think Mr. Ure ever meant to say—that the pensions would not be paid, which ever party was in power, he saidthe money would not be found in that way. Then again, if goods were made dearer by Protection and money would not go as far, there would be fewer things manufactured and consequently less work for the working- men. The Lords appeared to think the workers were like dumb-driven cattle. But Mr. Philip Snowden never said a truer word than when he told the Conserva- tives in the House of Commons "You must net treat the

div.head: ANTI-BUDGET BELLMAN.
div.p: THE ANTI-BUDGET BELLMAN.

In the Newton Division the bellman is engaged in peregrinating the streets and making this announcement: "God save the King and all loyal people! Those who are not loyal, let them go to a colony of their own and take the daft Lloyd George and the Budget with them."—" Daily News" December Bth, 1909.

reasonable thing that a small permanent committee of the Conservative party should always have the power to -destroy or to maim Liberal measures ? (Cries of "No ") Englishmen boasted of their freedom, but what as it worth? They sang " Britannia rules the waves " but they now found that Britannia wore a coronet. (Laughter.) They said a great deal about the British lion. but the British lion sat in the gilded Chamber, while the people were British sheep. (Laughter.) All classes were prepared to pay their fair share of taxation except the one class with its many mansions and countless acres. Those wealthy people nor only refused to pay their share but said sranebody else must pay it. The day of retribution was at hand. The great barrier which had held back the torrent of national indignation was giving way, and in the great leap of the mighty flood the House of Lords , would be overwhelmed tor ever. (Cheers.) Mr. DRURY, a veteran worker, having impressed upon the gathering the advantages of Free Trade, the vote was heartily carried. A similar compliment was passed to the Chairman on on the proposition of Mr. C. B. Parker, and the meet- ing closed with cheers for the Budget, Mr. Lloyd George and Mr. and Mrs.Crostield.

div.head: MEETING AT THEWLIS STREET.
div.p: MEETING AT THEWLIS STREET.
Mr. Crosfield on the Lords' Misdeeds.

Another crowded and highly enthusiastic meeting was held in Thewlis-street schools on Wednesday evening. Alderman Burton presided and was supported on the platform by Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., Mr. J. Dodds, Mr. R. Lewis (Manchester), Alderman Tinnion, Councillors Hawthorn and Locker, Rev. C. Harvey Cook, Messrs. P. Peacock, G. T. Rushton, T. Barton, J. Critchley, B. Farrar, E. Wynne-Jones, Joseph Owen, E. England and J. Howes jour. The Chairman said the Lords were trying to arrogite to themselves such powers as to make it impossible for any Liberal Government, no matter how capable and hard working, to continue in office long. He urged the workers not to barter away the political freedom which their forefathers had won for them. . It would be wicked in the extreme to tax bread, when so many people had such a hard struggle for existence. (Cheers.) Councillor HAWTHORN said he felt certain all present intended to vote for the Budget and return Mr. Crosfield to represent them again. (Cheers). The issues were very simple, but very great. They had to drive the Budget through and

SMASH THE VETO of the House of Lords. (Cheers). It was sheer humbug for the Lords to say they rejected the Budget in the interests of the middle classes and the working classes. They had shattered the Constitution under the pretence of preserving it; they had attacked the democratic system under the pretence of an appeal to the people. Having reviewed sonic of the misdeeds of the Lords, Councillor Hawthorn said their record in this and preceding Parliaments had confirmed the opinion of Mr. Gladstone when he said their policy was "mistrust of the people, qualified by fear." (Cheers). Mr. ROBERT LEWIS, in the course of a stirring and witty address, said the Lords were endeavouring to get hold of the purse strings, and the power of the purse had in the past and would he in the future the assurance of our liberties. In every struggle between Parliament and the Crown it was the power that Parliament held over the purse strings which assured to us the redressing of grievances and the securing of our liberties. (Cheers). The two policies before the electors were the maintenance of privilege and monopoly or the adoption of progress and reform. (Cheers). The Liberal Government were broadening the basis of taxation so as to include Dukes, Earls, Lords and Barons. The heaviest burden was to be laid on the shoulders best able to bear it. (Cheers). , Alderman TENSION said there were some pertinent questions which he would like the tariff reformers to answer : What was a manufactured article and what was a finished article? He could give a good many illustrations where the finished product of one manu- facturer became the raw material of another. What were they going to tax and how much duty would they impose? Were they going to levy such a small amount that it would be more a nuisance than anything else, or were they going to put on a large tax and entirely exclude the foreigner's goods ? MR. CROSFIELD'S SPEECH.

Mr. A. FL CROSFIELD, M.P., who was greeted with cheers and the singing of "For he's a jolly good (ellow," said he did not think they were likely to have to give their votes again on any political issue so far- reaching, so fraught with momentous consequences to the livelihood and welfare of the whole nation, as the great issue that was shortly to bo settled. (Cheers.) Whilst the Lords had brought things to a crisis by their audacious attack on the finances of the country, it was but the culmination of the policy which they bad pur- sued with regard to Liberal legislation. The first important task that was undertaken when the Liberal Government was returned to power, was an

EDUCATION BILL introduced by Mr. Birrell. That was a complicated measure and occupied a vast amount of time and debate in the House of Commons. All he would say with regard to the broad, general principles of that Bill was that it would have assisted in getting rid of the injustices under which so large a part of the population of England was labouring at the present time—injustices which unfortunately found a place in Mr. Balfour's Bill. At the same time the Government carried concession to the utmost limits and he voted for those concessions. The Roman Catholics were satisfied ; moderate, reasonable, liberal- minded Churchpeople were satisfied; the grievances of Nonconformists were dealt with. That Bill went up to the House of Lords and just because there was a cer- tain party of extreme men, ‘tho were not satiEfi 0
unless tbey could get a kind of ecclesiastical ascendancy, the Lords played up to that party and threw out the measure. The
PLURAL VOTING BILL

which embodied the simple proposition that the voting power of every British citizen should be equal (cheers)—shared a similar fate. In 1907 the House of Commons carried very important measures connected with small holdings and revaluation in Scotland, hut although that legislation bad the overwhelming support of the Scottish members of Parliament, the House of Lords rejected it. 11Ir. Crosfleld next touched upon the

LICENSING BILL, which he said was urgently needed and, while ensuring thmt after the lapse of twenty-one years the nation should resume control of the monopoly, it was u measure of red generosity to those interested in " the trade." After the representative Chamber had devoted a good part of a year's work to the Bill, the Lords stilettoed it in the dark before it came into the Upper Chamber. (" Shame.") Recently the Commons passed the

LONDON ELECTIONS BILL which provided that if a man changed his residence in London duriue the year he shoud not be deprived of his vote. (Cheers). A gteat many Conservatives recognized the reasonableness of that measure, but the Lords threw it out for purely electioneering purposes. The Bill only concerned London but it would have led to other measures affecting the whole country, for the Government were anxious to get rid of the anomaly wherever it existed and to make voting as simple and easy as they could. (Cheers). The Lords played an absolutely selfish party game, with no pretence at impartiatily, but sometimes they allowed a Bill which they considered bad to pass, rather than run the risk of incurring popular disfavour, A case in point was the TRADES DISPUTES BILL . _

—a measure calculated to—lin-l-cl—thrTs-c;tles of justice fairly between capital and labour, and which the Lords passed with execrations. The Old Age Pensions Bill which, in the words of Mr. Birrell, had done more to add to the sum of human happiness than anything that had been passed by the House of' Commons for genera- tions—(cheers)—was also passed by the Lords with criticism and obvious dislike and suspicion. Referring to the schemes that would be financed by the Budget. Mr. Crosfield said a very large charge upon it related to the defences of the country—a provision which we were bound toimake so long as the wretched, wasteful and wicked competitive game between nations went on. There was no disposition on the part of the Government to knuckle under to anyone. But in addition to that non-productive expenditure which bad to be faced, the Government had in view fruitful expenditure on social reform, and they were going ahead with that work when a body of untrained, biased and prejudiced men had the impertinence to try and usurp the right to bring the government of the country to a standstill and chuck out the Ministry. In dealing with the issue that now confronted them, the electors bad to remember all the beneficent and just measures which had been thwarted, as well as the present crown- ing act of the

div.head: REVOLUTIONARY RICH
div.p: REVOLUTIONARY RICH

who bad Fought to assume a position that would rob the people of a large portion of the birthright that belonged to every Briton. (Cheers.) Having thus brought things to an issue, he was thankful that, under the leadership of one of the coolest and ablest men who over held power in the State—(cheers)—the pro- gressive forces were no longer going to fence and skirmish with that assembly of privileged and selfish people. (Cheers). They were coming to close quarters, to deal finally and effectively, not by abolishing the Second Chamber, hut by curtailing its power, so that never again would the people be treated with such ignominy and contempt. (Loud cheers). Mr. JA.MES DODDS said the issue before them was vital and tremendous, and their whole future depended upon it. He supported Mr. Crosfleld with all his heart, because he kuew he was

A GENUINE RADICAL. / (Cheers.) He (Mr. Dodd) could not understand how any workingman could vote for the Peers as against the People. Tariff Reform would perhaps be to the advantage of a class which was already getting enough, but it would be taken out of the pockets of those who could ill afford it. (Cheers.) Mr. P. PEACOCK proposed a vote of thanks to the speakers. The Rev. C. HARVEY COOK, in seocnding, said the corning election did not merely involve the question of Mr. Lloyd-George's Budget or Free Trade v. Tariff Reform. The issue was:
WHO SHALL RULE?

'(Cheers.) "Are you going to rule ?" asked -Aft.. Cook. (Cries of" Yes.") "Are you sure ? ("Certain.") Yon are not going to be hoodwinked? ("No.") Either you are going to be under the thumb of the Lords or you are going to put the Lords under your thumb. Which are you going to do? ("Put them under," and a VOICE: "Clear them out.") No, we won't clear them out, that is too drastic. I like some old things to look at • they are interesting as antiquities.' (Laughter.) The speaker concluded by saying that he supported Mr. Crosfield because he stood for the great principle of the rule of the people, for the people, and by the people. The vote was enthusiastically passed and Mr. Crosfield returned thanks. He said that if the question before them was' Free Trade alone it would be a great and sacred cause to tight for and he would go into the con- test with a big heart. But the issue was greater still. It concerned the right of the nation to work out its salvation on progressive lines, and to get rid of anomalies and injustices and the extreme hardships that too many of our people had to face. In short it cm:teemed the character, the dignity, the sense of responsibility and the manhood of our people. (Cheers). A vote of tharks to the Chairman concluded the meeting.

div.head: HOME-MADE MUSIC STAND.
div.p: A HOME-MADE MUSIC STAND.

Besides looking really ornamental if well put together, the music-stand here described has the advantage of costing little, which is a consideration. To begin with, we shall want six strips of one-inch mahogany. Three of these are twelve inches long and of an inch wide, the other three are sixteen inches long and 1 3-16 inches wide. Plane and smooth these strips with fine glasspaper, and fasten thew together with small brass screws. Put two screws at. each join. The three nar- row strips are placed upright; one of the wider strips is fastened to these about three inches from the top, another is put at the

bottom, and the third is fastened at right angles to this. At the back of the middle 'upright you must now screw a piece of wood of an inch thick, shaped as in A. In this we shall insert the upright rod.
TO PREVENT THE WOOD WARPING.

For the base of stand cut two triangles of ;wood (deal will do) t of an inch thick, as in Glue or screw these together so that the grain of the wood goes in opposite directions. This will give additional strength and pre- vent the wood warping. At the three corners cut out a groove a of an inch deep and s 4 of an inch wide. Now cut three pieces of deal, a shade more than of an inch thick, and Si inches long, shaped like c. Take care that the grain of the wood goes lengthwise, or it ;will be liable to split. These can now he glued into the grooves of the triangular piece to form the base of the stand. Get a piece of brass tube, 2 feet 9 inches long, and 7-16 of an inch wide; bore a hole in the centre of the triangle and insert the tube. See that it fits tightly. We now want another piece of tube, 20 inches long, to slide easily within the first piece. Then take a third piece of tube, 3 inches long, to fit fairly tightly in the second piece. Bore a hole in the piece of wood at the back of the stand marked A, and insert the short piece of tube. It can be fastened with a little glue. Leave about 11 inches projecting; this will go in the second tube. You will now have a stand which can be ad- justed to various heights. To keep it at any height you must put a screw in the outer tube, near the top (see D). The top of the stand, if mahogany, merely requires rubbing with a little linseed oil ; the base, if made of deal, ean be painted and varnished according to fancy. The cost of the whole is under half-a-c;Dwn, and will not be at all difficult to make.
A USEFUL STAMP REGISTER.
Stamp collectors always like to keep ac- count of their stock, but this is not easy un- less the stamps be counted every few days, or

div.head: d-S
div.p: d-S

a careful record made of all purchases, sales or exchanges. To save trouble, an ingenious arrangement, on the basis of a perpetual calendar, has been devised, and it may. be pasted in the back of the album. You may have as many slips as you please; the names of the countries to be written over them. Alter the figures to tens, hundreds, etc., as required. The register is kept in the opening at the centre, the marker being drawn up or down. •

the best in the interests of the cause for which the party exists. Just the same policy applies to the election tactics of the Labour Party Accident at this election has made us the temporary allies of the Liberals in the sense that both they and ourselves are against the House of Lords, and I would not refuse the assistance of any ally who would help honestly to destroy the arrogant usurpation of the rights of the people by any non-elected body.

div.head: NEXT TURN.
div.p: THE NEXT TURN.

The probability is th9,t the next turn of the whirligig of politics may bring us into acute opposition to the Liberals. But, be that as it may, it is absolutely certain that the Labour Party will never surrender one jot of its power of independent action. It is free now—it will always be free—to take its own line of action, and in taking its own course, the Labour Party will always be moved by two considerstions : namely, how best to build up a great democratic party, pledged to use politics to deal with the root causes of poverty, and how, during the process of building up that party, it may influence the thought and actions of other parties so as to bring about reforms which will palliate the severity of present-day evils; always using its influence upon other parties in such a way as not to hinder but to help the first of these considerations.

div.head: CO-OPERAT/VE SOCIETY QUARTERLY MEETING.
div.p: CO-OPERAT/VE SOCIETY QUARTERLY MEETING.

The quarterly meeting of the members of tbd Warrington Equitable Industrial Co-operative Society was held on Monday evening in the new central premises. Mr. T. Wadsworth (president), presided over a good attendance including the members of the Committee and Mr. J. Jarman (secretary).
THE 'COMMITTEE'S REPORT.

The Committee reported that the sales for the seven weeks had reached the record tot 1 of £30,147 Bs. BLd. being an increase of £4,078 Os. 3.3. over the correspond- ing period last year. The membership is now 9,696, 213 new members having joined, and 63 lapsed or left the district ; a nett increase of 115 in seven weeks. The Educition Committee had commenced hook-keeping classes apin for the employees, and, also an adult class in the principles of co-operation. more were being well-attended. They wished especially to call attention to the children's CbriAmas entertainment and to ask members to obtain tickets early as a limited numheronly could be issued. A formal opening of the new central premises, would be held in the Parr Hall, on February 20th, and would take the form of a public meeting and concert. The Committee recommended that an inter:m dividend of 3s. 2d. in the £ ha paid on the sales as above, from September Bth to October 20th. The PRESIDENT said they were making great progress. The success they had met with since opening the new premises was beyond their anticipations. It would be news to some of them that they had secured a site in Gorsey-lane for new premises which would tend to alleviate the congestion of busine-s in branches in that part of the town They were in negotiation with regard to other premises in town.

div.head: Tlikl LATE MR. RATHBONE.
div.p: Tlikl LATE MR. RATHBONE.

The PRESIDENT referring to the late mantivr—Mr. Rathbone—spoke of his devotion to the work of the society and said there was no denying the fact that owing ta his efforts they were able to erect the new buildings. They were all very sorry that he did not live to see the premises opened. lie proposed that a letter of sympathy be suit to the relatives of Mr. Rathbone. This was unanimously agreed to.

Mr. T. Wadsworth nas again elected president of the society for the coming year.
OTHER ELECTIONS.
Nine cindidates for sea's on the committee were nominated for three vacancies and the" following were elected :—Messrs. Timperley 119 votes, Bibby 112, and Seed 76. _ _

It was decided that Mr. Jones be elected meinber's delegatb to vi&it and report on the C.W.S. quarterly meetings in the place of Mr. Lowe, who resigned the the position after holding the position after holding the position for two years. Mr. Lowe was thanked for his services and he suit- ably replied. Mr. J. Green Chappel was unanimously elected auditor for the ensuing year,

div.head: TiliC JUBILEE.
div.p: TiliC JUBILEE.

_ Mr. MAYBORY proposed "That a small sub-committee be appointed, consisting of four meinters of the com- mittee and four members from the quarterly meeting together with the Piesident and Secretary, to consider what steps shall be taken to celebrate the Society's Jubilee, and report to a further meeting." He said other societies celebrated their jubilees in one way or another and he thought they should celebrate their's in a way which would benefit the town and his fellow members. (Hear, hear.) The secretary said the committee would be very pleased if any member had any suggestions to make. 11 they would band them in, in writing the committee would give them consideration. The following four members were elected Messrs. Maybury, Lowe, Hill and George Leach. The four members representing the committee were elected privately.

div.head: TIIE ANNUAL TRIP.
div.p: TIIE ANNUAL TRIP.

AZ Mr. Farrar raid it was suggested by the Educational Committee that the annual excursion next par be to Scotland end that they visit Glasgow and Edinburgh. The excursion 'would start on Walking Day evening. Mr. EVANS said the trips should be within the reach of all. They should take into consideration all the members and not orly the select. The SECRETARY said that for the last trip they had they started taking contributions early arid people did not feel the loss. They would be prepared to do the sime this time and there would be more time than before. Continuing ho pointed out that both Glasgow and Edinburgh could not be visited and they would have to agree which place they were going to. Mr. ENGLAND said that from a historical point of view Edinburgh was cf more interest than Glasgow. Personally he would prefer to go to Edinburgh. It was propose'), seconded and carried that Scotland be visited and Edinburgh be the centre.

CHRISTMAS TREE AND TREAT. Mr. FARRAR intimated that the Annual Christmas Tree would be held on Monday and Tuesday of Christmas week. They would be ready to accommodate 600 on the Monday, and 650 on Tuesday. Concluding be said the little children would be well looked after on entering and leaving the buildings. (Applause).

Parent's Bronchitis & Children's Weak
Chests Cured.

A very important point to remember about Peps, the great breathe-able remedy for throat and chest ailments, is that they are a perfectly safe medicine for old and .young, robust and invalids. Hence the wise mother always keeps a box of these silver- wrapped tablets handy in the house when coughs, colds, and sore throats are rife.- Peps contain none of the opium or other harmful drugs to be found in cough mixtures ; and besides, Peps are exceptionally successful in cutting short worse chest ailments if used at once. Mrs. A. Gates, Seafield Cottage, Rushington, near Worthing, Sussex, writes :—" For a month at a time I had to stay in bed with bronchitis, suffering from severe coughing fits, sore throat, and pains across my chest. My breath came in gasps, and my voice often left me altogether. Six years of this miserable exist- ence without any benefit from doctors' treatment made me think there was no relief from bronchitis. But Peps made me change my opinion. "I was suffering from a particularly bad attack when I first heard of Peps two winters ago. I was waiting for someone to fetch the doctor when a friend came in with a few Peps. I took these and felt so relieved that when the messenger came I sent him not for the doctor but for a box of Peps. I marvelled at the relief Peps brought me, not only to my throat- and chest, but from 'the spasms of coughing as well. I rapidly picked up as I regularly took Peps. My husband and children were delighted to notice that I scarcely coughed at all. "Finding the little tablets so good for my severe case I gave a.dose to the children when they caught cold during a spell of bad weather. For them also Peps proved splendid. All six of us in our family now think very highly of Peps. I have certainly never heard of anything to equal Peps for bronchitis.'

With the passing of that sentence upon John Baxendale, and his disappearance from the world of men, something at least of the public excitement abated. The world is a busy place, and one sensation succeeds another so rapidly that a man and his crime are easily forgotten; there might perhaps be a revival, when it came to the dawn of that dreadful day when John Baxendale was to hang; but •for the moment the thing was ended. There were those, of course, for whom the thing could never end at all; those friends who stared into each other's faces,- and asked themselves, if not in actual words, whether this thing could be, and whether the John Baxendale they knew was to be swept out of life like this, without a hand being raised to save him. First among those 'was Evelyn Kaylor, who, as might be expected, had been absolutely prostrated from the day of the trial, and, indeed, for whose reason and very life some fears were at first entertained. She would see no one; she kept her room, and lay prostrate on her bed, sobbing as if her heart would break. John Baxendale was innocent.; the proof of that had been in the telling it to her; and yet John Baxendale was to die. Next was the lawyer, Felix Goode, Who went distractedly from one legal friend to another, puttting his case, and getting, if the truth be told, but small sympathy. He was referred to with shrugs by younger nil; being past his work, and being deceived clever scoundrel; and he pleaded ' and pro, tested in vain. As he had known from the first, he had not the smallest scrap of evidence to support anything he said; and, above all, de- spite the search that was made in every direc- tion, the other man, of whom he talked so persistently, could not be found. Rufus Cridge had disappeared utterly, and if he ever reappeared it would be only after John Baxendale was dead. So thought the old - man, bitterly enough, as he beat his hands against that blank wall he had himself helped to raise years before. There were but three days left to John Baxendale on earth;- and to the old man, alone in his rooms in the gloomy old house in Bloomsbury, the thought was horrible enough. He sat at the table where he had sat once be- fore, on a night when John Baxendale talked with him, and when all the world outside clamoured for John Baxendale. The windows were open, as they had been then, and the muffled noises of the street floated up to him. He sat with his. elbows leaning on the table, and his chin propped in his palms, staring out at the tree tops. His heart was aching for the man who was to die; for,. in his fashion, he had loved John Baxendale, as someone straight, and fine, and wholesome that he had seen grow up from boyhood. He chafed to- night at the thought of how utterly helpless he was; of how, with the secret knowledge in his mind of what the truth was, he was still powerless, and had arrayed against him all the weight of the law, which meant willy-nilly to have this man's life. Sober, quiet old crea- ture that he was, he was almost in a mood to rush out into the streets, and shout for some- one to help him—someone to go with him to beat down the walls of the prison, and drag out the man he knew to be innocent. He had not lighted his lamp, and the shadows were thick in the room. From gaz- ing out of the window he turned his listless . "eyes to a corner near the door, stared harder, and then started to his feet, overturning his chair. "Who's there?" he demanded. A. figure emerged from the shadows, and moved si- lently towards him. With his heart beating unpleasantly he took a step forward, and saw that it was a woman clad in black—Johanna Cridge. "How did you get in here?" he asked. "I've been watching the house for some hours," she said. "Your servant slipped out . to the pillar-box with a letter, leaving the door ajar; I came in." "What do you want?" he asked, paling a little at sight of her determined face, and glancing round towards the bell. "A little talk with you," she replied coolly. "You needn't be afraid of me; I'm not here to harm you," she added contemptuously. • The old lawyer saw in this visit some faint hope for the prisoner; felt that perhaps,, after all, this extraordinary woman had relented, and meant to save John Baxendale. He waved his hand towards a chair, in token that she should be seated. But she shook her head. "I'll stand, thank you," she said. "After all, I've very little to say, but it must be said . .

now. The venges,ce I- planned through so many years would not be complete without that; and, as you know, I don't do things by • half-measures. In the first place, I know where Rufus Cridge is." . The old man looked at her keenly; she was coming to the very crux of the matter at once. He had a curious feeling for a moment that he might—feeble old creature though he was —seize her, and wring from her what she had to tell; that now, most of all at this hour, strong and drastic measures were necessary. But he put that thought from him; he deter- mined that he would, if possible, win her con- fidence, and get her to tell him what she knew. "You know where he is? " he replied to her quietly. "And you are willing, I take it, to let me know where he can be found, so that a great injustice may be prevented from hap- pening. This is kind of you, Mrs. Cridge." "Don't be in too great a hurry," she said, stretching out a hand to stop his hurried, halt- ing thanks. "I told, you I knew where Rufus Cridge was to be found; I did not tell you I would let you find him." "But you will—you must," he exclaimed, hurriedly. "You cannot let this thing go on any longer; you will give me the chance to set John' Baxendale at liberty, and to put Rufus Cridge in his place. You will—you must !" "Look at me, Felix Goode," she said. "Am I the sort of woman to work for a quar- ter of a century with one object in my mind, and one only, and then to give it up? YOU who know nothing of women, may at least un- derstand that: that I would not turn aside now, when my vengeance is in my hands, if all the hosts of heaven barred my way. And, most of all, would I go straight to that ven- geance because you pleaded with me for this man's life." "But what have I to do with it; how have I hurt or offended you?" "I'll tell you; I'm here to tell you," she answered him. "Years and years ago, after the John Baxendale who is dead had wronged me, he sent you to me as his represeniative." "I remember." said the old man, with a sudden sinking of the heart. The woman continued her story: _ _
"You

came to me (it was your duty to dolt, and you I would be paid to perform that fluty) to offer me 'money—a certain income—if I would be quiet, and say nothing and do nothing. You remem- ber how I replied to you; you may, perhaps re- Member what my rage and my scorn were that such an offer should be made at all. Heaven help me! I had loved the man with all .my heart and soul • I had given myself gladly to him because I loved him. Do you think—you -man of law, who knows nothing of women— do you think that such a love as mine could •be bought, or sold, or paid for. I would have gone away; I would have died in some ob- scure corner rather than shafne -him; but when he shamed me through you, I deter- mined to do this thing. Shall I turn back now? I have nursed and fed and trained a monster; and that monster has brought the house of Baxendale to ruin and death—and I am satisfied." "But think—think for but a moment," pleaded the old man, earnestly. "You don't love this man, even though he has been as a son to you." "Love him?" Her scornful laugh rang through th- "1 ha+4 hint . „inet. as

"Call by all means," she retorted, with a shrug of the shoulders. "In the first place the man will tell you that you don.t know what you're talking about—because the murderer of Bella Ogden is safe in prison, and will be hanged three days from this time; and in the second place I should tell him, jor ainyone else, that, having been interested in John Baxendale (alias Rufus Cridge) I had come to ,see if there wits no possible chance of a reprieve for him, even at this eleventh hour. So you would fail again, Mr. Felix -Goode." " And an innocent man must hang," said Felix Goode, sadly. Chiefly because he has the misfortune tc Dear the name of John Baxendale," she re- torted. "And now, having said all that I came to say, I will go." "1 guppoBe I shall not -See you again? he said, with mechanical politeness. "If you should happen to be outside the prison three days from hence, when a black flag goes up, you might see .me in the crowd," she said.
"Will nothing soften you?" he answered, with a shudder. "What mercy do you ex- pect from your God?" "I have had none yet—from God or man," she said; and with that last word lcft him.

Now, strangely enough, although she bad said that Rufus Cridge would not be found anywhere near her, he was to be found that very night in Middleton's Rents. She did not know that; and Felix Goode, feeling that the word she had said about the 'matter was true, made no effort to follow her. So, as she turned into Middleton's Rats in the dankness, a figure lurched up to her • and spoke to her. "Mother, I must have a word with you."

She did not even turn to look at him. She felt something tighten in her throat, and wondered if by chance the lawyer had taken it into his head to carry out his threat and ve her watched. Without apparently .oticing the man, she turned about, as though she had forgotten something, and walked away, retracing her steps until she came to a quiet cul-de-sac, in which she was alone with the man; and there faced Rufus Cridge, with the momentary feeling that this might, after all, be John Baxendale, miraculously come out of prison. "Why couldn't you remain in quiet a little longer?" were her first words.

The man answered sullenly enough: "Be- effuse I'm sick and tired of this hiding and dodging, when it's no longer necessary. Bax- endale's under lock and key, and they're knocking together the scaffold for him. They've given up looking for me. Besides, it's another matter I want to talk to you about. The matter of that girl down at Deepington—the girl they call Evelyn." I "Let her alone; she's nothing to do with you," said the woman, sharply; for, to do her credit, she had that feeling of a woman for a woman that not all the bitterness of her nature had been able to suppress. "I Was John Baxendale once, for d day or two—and she belongs to John Baxendale," said the man, doggedly. "Consequently, as the other John Baxendale's gone, she belongs o me. Haven't I held her in my arnii? Haven't I tasted her lips?" "Apart from anything else, you'll run your sck into a halter if you go to her now, or if you're see!' in that neighbourhood," said Johanna Cridge. "Who's going to her, or who's going to be seen in that neighbourhood?" retorted the man. "All I want to do is to get hold of the girl; the game isn't complete until I do that. And I want you to help me." She hesitated for a moment, staring moodily at the -pavement on mhieli she stood. After all, it might be a better thing to com- plete her vengeance in this way—to bring disaster, not only upon John Baxendale, but upon the woman he loved. That would be a rounding off of the' matter she had not con- templated. Wliz not let this man icose to do his worst?
"How are you going to do it so as to keep yourself out of danger?" she asked, after a pause. „

"The easiest thing in the world," he said. "Suppose it were Dossible for John Baxen- dale to call to her to come to him; suppose she could be made to believe that John Bax- endale had broken prison, and was waiting in some place of biding, what then?" "I tell you it's rieky—and, apart frr:m everything else, a low game to play. and not worth the candle," said the woman. "You've lucky enough already over the matter. Why not leave it alone, and lie quiet until a'ohn Baxendale is got out of the way?" Not me!" he exclaimed, with a laugh. "I like risks; and I'd like to meet that dainty girl again who clung to me so readily when she believed me to be John Baxendale. Conte to that, I'm a better man than John Baxendale—and I'm sufficiently like him to take his ulace in this as in other things, If

you As on- t neip me— " No, I wop't !" she broke in, • "Then I'll get someone else to (lb it for me. Amos Voles might do it, or Saul Tuttle. It's only a matter of sending a message." "Be careful, Rufus, what you do," the woman warned him. "There is money flying about, to be taken by any man who can point out just now where you are. I know enough of Voles and the other man to know that they wouldn't hesitate to sell you if they could lay hands on you. Up to the present I'm the only one that knows where you're to .be found, and 1:m safe enough, but for heaven's sake don't put your life into the hands of another man." "I know what I'm doing," he retorted, ob- stinately. "Send Tuttle to the address you know. 'Warn him to keep his moutti 'shut. If he gives me- away—well, I shall know what to do with him." "Very well; the matter's in your hands," she said, with a sigh. "I will do as you ask.'' So they parted, Johanna Cridge to go back Middleton's Rents, and Rufus to drift sway into the shadows back to the obscure lodging he had taken. In due course, Johanna Cridge, reluctantly enough, sought out Saul Tuttle, and gave him the address and the, message. "You'd better be 'careful, Saul," she said. "He's not a man to be trifled with. He's got some scheme on hand, and he wants your help.; but don't tell a livifig soul where he's to be found." Mr. Said Tuttle swore by all the gods he knew that the secret- was safe with him, but before completing the business went off to his friend and crony, Mr. Amos Voles. For, if the truth be told, in this curious business of wheels within wheels, these two conspirators were a little disgusted with the turn of events. Vengeance was all very well in its way, but it seemed, up to the present, to have been most unprofitable, from a pecuniary point of View. Nothing had been got out of it worth the having, and the very place which they had been assured was to be sacked by them was now nothing but a blackened ruin. More than that, they knew already that heavy rewards had been offered for the cap- ture of that mysterious man known as Rufus Cridge, and the secret of his hiding-place had been well kept by Mother Cridge. Now, in a moment, that secret belonged to Saul Tuttle, and it was a marketable commodity. Being of a timid nature himself, however, he took Amos Voles into his confidence about the matter. "It's the charnoe of a lifetime," said Tuttle, impressively. "Besides, w'ere'e the 'arm? Wot 'ave we ever got out of it, from first to last? Wasn't there to be pickings? An' wasn't we promised this, that, an' the other over it. There's a 'undred pounds for the man that finds Rufus Cridge ; wot'e the matter wiv you an' me splittin' that 'undred between us?" "S'pose anythink 'appene, my friend, so that they don't get • Rufus," suggested Amos Voles, with a shake of the head. "I can see you an' me facing lin after that—very pritty interview, I don't think." "It's quite safe an' quite easy," said Saul Tuttle. It seems 'e's after this girl that I've got to take a message to. W'ile I'm takin' the message, you can see this lawyer fellow, an' git 'im to come to the address at the same time. If I know anythink of Rufus, 'e'll be there to meet the girl, then they can land 'im, as safe as 'wises. An' it's a 'un- derd quid to be divided between us." "I'll do it," said Mr. Voles, with much de- termination. "We 'aven't bin treated too well, you an' me, Saul. I don't see why we shouldn't git a bit out of it. You go an' see the young lady, after you've got your mes: sage from Rufus. I'll go an' see the lawyer, an give 'im the office-as to w'efe Rufus is. We may be doin' ourselves a lot of good over this. Saul," he added, "quite apart from the reward that's offered." So the worthies separated, it being ar- ranged that Saul should first see Rufre Cridge, and understand how the land lay in that direction, and should afterwards com- municate with Amos Voice, telling him ex- actly when the girl was supposed to keep the appointment; there could then be no mistake ,about finding Rufus Cridge in his hiding- place. Mr. Voles faithfully promised to eer. form his part of the contract, and in clue course to divide the reward with Tuttle. Behold Saul Tuttle, therefore, diving down

into certain mean streets near the rive'r, and so coming presently to a villainous den—a sort of underground kitchen, where Rufus Cridge lived in solitary state. See him pre- senting himself before his intended victim, smooth of tongue and anxious of manner au ever, even with treachery in his heart. "You're a deep 'un, Rufus. I should never 'are thought of lookin' for you 'ere," said Tuttle. "Or you'd have sold me long ago, eh?" re- torted Rufus. "Do you know that Mother Cridge has an idea that you might be dan- gerous, that it's not wise to trust you When there's money offered for me?" "That isn't kind of Mother Cridge at all," said Mr. Tuttle, almost - whimpering. "Should 1 be likely, Rufus, to give away a friend?" "Not if that friend intended to cut the heart out of you if you did," said Mr. Cridge, pleasantly. "Because that's what I'd do. you know, if I had to break gaol to get at you. You haven't such a thought in your mind, I hope?" "Now, 16 - it . likely?" asked Tuttle, trem- bling from head to foot, and beginning al- ready to repent of the bargain he had made. "I wouldn't do such a thing, I wouldn't in- deed." "You'd better not," said Rufus, fero- ciously. "Now, what I want you to do is this: I want you to take a message to a young lady who lives in London. You've seen her down at Deepington. Since this precious lover of, hers was sentenced she's come to, London, where she lives with an aunt in their town house. I've found out all 'about that, and I've founds out also that at certain hours of the day she walks in the garden of the square where the house is. You've got to get speech with her somehow, and you've got to give her the message that comes from John Baxendale. She's .not likely to read news- papers, and 60 she won't know anything about him, except such as she hears pri- vately. You've got to lead her to believe that John Baxendale has escaped, and is waiting for her. Can you do that?" "I can do anything—for a friend," said Mr. Tuttle, a little dubiously. "But suppose she makes inquiries, and finds -out—" "That John Baxendale's in prison? She won't do that. -She'll believe any silly mes- sage that may came•concerning the man she's fond of. Get hold of her; bring her here. Do you understand that?" "Yes—yes, I understand," said Tuttle. "What am I to say to her? I tell you, Rufus, I don't believe she'll swallow that about escaping from prison." "It's a bit steep, perhaps, and, after all, she may watch the newspapers, to see what they say about Baxendale," saiji Cridge, thoughtfully. "You're right, Saul, we Must try another game than that. Tell her that you can take her to a man—a friend of John Baxendale—who can prove his innocence. Tell her this friend knows the real murderer. But impress upon her that she must come' alone; that if she tells anyone, or attempts to bring anyone with her, nothing shall be said. Tell her that. Then, on your own ac- count, .see that she brings no one else. Girls are tricky enough, and artful enol.gh, and she may decide to give the game away to someone else. Be careful, for your own sake," he added, menacingly. Saul Tuttle went off, armed with the ad- dress of the house at. which Evelyn was liv- ing. He had seen her at Deepington, and he understood also that she was tall, and dressed completely in black. There could be small chance of his mistaking her. He haunted the square in which the house stood, contrived somehow to miss the girl on the first (lay, but on the second was more successful. He crept along outside the railings enclosing the gar- den, and, peering through, saw Evelyn pac- ing up and down tinder the trees. Watching his opportunity, he called to her in a -stage whisper: "Miss! Miss! Could 111 ve 'arf a word v.ith you?" She came slowly across the grass towards him, looking at him through the railings curiously. "What do you want?" she asked. Saul glanced. over his shoulder and lowered his..voice still wore. "It's about—about—Mr,

Daxennale,- no sino. He saw the effect of that name at once. The girl began to tremble violently. "Go round to the other side of the garden, and I'll let you in by the gate there, she whis- pered. 'And, oh !—be quick!" Saul hurried round, and found the girl at the gate waiting for him. She let him in, and together they paced up and down in the shelter of the trees, talking earnestly. Saul had difficulties to contend with at the outset. "But surely I may bring someone with me, someone who is a friend to him also, and would do anything to serve him?" she asked. "It won't do, miss, it won't do at all," said Saul, emphatically. "These was the words of the friend that can put you on the right track. 'She must come alone,' says the friend. You'll spoil everythink if you 'aven't got the pluck to do it yourself, an' without nobody interfering." "I've courage enough for anything if only it will help him," said the girl. "But I can't start now. I might be watched, per- haps followed. I can go to-night." To-night's the best time," said the man. " At nine o'clock I'll be 'ere, just outside this gate. Meet me then, an' I can take you straight to the place." She promised, and Saul Tuttle crept away. In due course he met that friend, Amos Voles, and told him what had happened, and what plans were afoot. "Go and find Mr. Goode, the lawyer, and bring 'im straight away to the place you know," said Saul Tuttle. "Mind you get yer money, in case of any accidents 'appenins afterwards. You can't be too careful in this world. An soon as the girl's there, I shall do a bunk, an' if I was you, Amos, I'd send the lawyer-man rather than take 'im." " I think so, too," said Amos, with a shiver. "I've no desire to meet Rufus Cridge, if he finds out wot we've done. In any case, 31r. Goode 'ad better take 'elp.9 At the time appointed Saul Tuttle was to *be seen lurking in the shadows of the square. He had not long to wait. The girl came well before her time, and motioned to him to lead the way. He glided out of the square, while she followed. Only when they came into narrower and less frequented places did she move up by his side. " Where are you taking me?" she asked. ".I can't tell yer the place. I ain't allowed to," said .Tuttle; raising his hand, and hailing .a four-wheeled cab that was passing. "If you'll get in, miss, I'll ride on the box an' direct the driver," he added. The girl got in, and the cab went on and on, through endless streets, as it seemed, and into quarters of London that grew more and more squalid as they we‘nt. At last the cab stopped, at the end of a street where Squalid- looking men and women were lounging at doorways and out of windows. Saul paid the cabman, and took the girl by the arm, and hurried her down the street, and so into a maze of courts and alleys; twisted suddenly into a dark entry, and began to descend some Steps. So at last he thrust open a door and bade her enter. "You'll find the friend in there," he said. She went in, and in a moment( the door was closed and fastened. As she turned in the dim light of the place, she saw a man stand- ing with his back against the door, looking at her. And it seemed to be John Baxendale. (To be continued.)
A BOY HERO.
TOM LEWIS.

Thomas William Lewis, the newsboy who behaved so gallantly during the rescue opera- tions that followed the Newport Dock disaster, was presented with the Albert Medal by the King. On hearing the story of his bravery Hs Majesty said " Well done !"

KING LEOPOLD'S I-IEIR:• PRINCE ALBERT. • Prince Albert of Belgium, King Leopold's nephew, is heir to the Belgian throne. He is a handsome, ftesh-complexioned, good- tempered young man. He is extremely popular, and has a penchant for engineering.

div.head: KING OF THE BELGIANS.
div.p: THE KING OF THE BELGIANS.

• King Leopold, the second of the Coburg Kings of the Belgians, was born on April 9, 1835. His father, Leopold 1., became king of this small state in 1830, when it freed itself from union with Holland. As a Prince he developed Imperialistic ambitions, and he pictured to the Belgian Chamber the glories -nd the advantages of Empire alike from a sentimental and commercial point of view. History has yet to pass jud2,ment on his dealings in the Congo. Many hold him primarily and solely responsible for the terrible tragedies of the Congo basin; horrors that have shocked the civilised world have Id; him unmoved; and he cannot hope to be left witliout blame for the murder and mutil Won of the unfortunates who could not collect their rubber tax.

div.head: ROYAL PALACE AT BRUSSELS.
div.p: THE ROYAL PALACE AT BRUSSELS.

The operation on the aged King of the Belgians was carried out in the Laeken Palace at Brussels. The capital of Belgium is rich in beautiful buildings, and the Palace with its quaint design is apt to escape the notice of sightseers. The Palace has been denuded of many of its priceless possessions to pay the debts of the aged monarch, but it is hoped that many of them will yet be restored to the walls of the Royal apartments.

div.head: BELLE FIELD AND ITS ECCENTRIC
div.p: BELLE FIELD AND ITS ECCENTRIC
BUILDER.

Who has not, after climbing Hill Cliff, admired the situation of the large old house known as Belle Field? The level plain of the Mersey stretching far to the right, the Appleton reservoir in the foreground, the Cheshire hills and more distant Welsh mountains to the left make a picture of rare and varied beauty, and we feel that the man who first planned a dwell- ing here made a choice that could hardly be surpassed. The house has been modernised and altered, and even the landscape has under- gone marked changes in the century and a half which have passed since AS first tenant looked out upon it; but a few connecting links remain to join us to one of the most attractive, and eccentric of men.

ADMIRAL HARE. We wrote last week of the tenant of Stockton Lodge, Captain Boyer. We are now to describe his friend and bosom companion Admiral Hoare, the builder of Belle Field. It may be worth while to recall in a sentence the sea fighting which brought these two men together. We were at war with our then restless rival, France. The French fleet had been carrying reinforcements to the French Canadians and Admiral Boscawen was sent to intercept it. He waited off Newfoundland, but the French Admiral passed him in a fog. In October, 1755, Admiral Byng attempted the same task and

div.head: BELLE FIELD, APPLETON.
div.p: BELLE FIELD, APPLETON.

also failed, and upon A second failure was shot by order of a Court Martial. The event greatly agitated the country, but the interest has now faded and we need not discuss it in detail. Our present interest lies in the fact that it brought into close friendship Captain Boyer and Admiral Hoare'

When Captain Boyer became Naval Superintendent of the Mheshire district, his friend the Admiral decided to settle as close to him as might be, and in surveying the district decided to build a house on the then lonely crest of the hill. He obtained a lease from Sir Peter Warburton, and none will deny that he chose his ground exceeding well.

In those days a rich woodland spread away to the south, the castle of Halton and the Helsby hills forming its background. T,o the west the Mersey glistened in its winding course to the sea, and there was no Widnes or Runcorn to blot the rich valley and darken the air.

till morning, when the parson being sent for, conjured the spirits into the lied Sea, and the house has been pretty quiet ever since. "True it is, Mr. Hatchway Makes mock of the whole affair; and told his Commander that the two goblins were no other than a couple of jackdaws which had fallen down the chimney and made a flapping with their wings up and down the apartment. But the Commodore ivho is very choleric, and does not like to be jeered at, fell into a main high passion, and stormed like a perfect hurricane, swearing that he knew a devil from a jackdaw as well as any man in the three kingdoms. He owned indeed that the birds were found, but ..denied that they were the occasion of the uproar. For my own part, master, I believe and much may be said on both sides of the queStion ; though to be sure, the devil is always going about as the saying is."

Hawser Trunnioh is an attractive figure as he lives in the pages of Smollett and the reader may make merry over the story of how he was " teased and tortured into the noose of wedlock" and of how the strangely- wooed Mrs. Trunnion introduced reforms into his curious household. It must not be assumed that the copy is a close one, for Smollett had a rare wit, and allowed it to run free, but the original of his Hawser Trunnion was most certainly the builder of Belle Field.
A. M.

div.head: ADMIRAL'S IDEAL.
div.p: THE ADMIRAL'S IDEAL.

The Admiral had ideas of his own on the subject of what an ideal house should be and doubtless inflicted sore trial upon those who carried out his plans. To the old salt there was only one kind of life worth living and that was the nautical. If he had to live on land it must be in a house that was shaped like a ship and that had all a ship's accoutre- ments. The house was long and its windows like port holes. His sleeping-room was fitted with a hammock and his servants were com- pelled to rest in the same kind of appliance. In front of thei house was a circular garden dignified by the name of quarter deck and here the Admiral took his exercise. A flag pole stood in the centre and the British flag floated proudly from it together with such other flags as were hoisted to signal to imaginary ships or real men.

div.head: SEA MANNERS.
div.p: SEA MANNERS.

Admiral Hoare had been a real Admiral aboard his flag ship and was resolved to be an Admiral as long as he lived. Hence all who approached him were required' to do so with doffed hat and every other mark of respect. Bells sounded the time of day just as aboard ship and he took his time by his sextant and the sun. In his log book he noted the points of the winds and all the occurences of the day and he dined,supped and went to bed just as though in mid-ocean. He was too old to learn a new language and,' continued to talk salt and water as though he lived in the midst of it. "He was a terrestro-nautico animal" says one who knew much of him "but with all his foibles not a warmer-hearted, kinder, or more hospitable creature ever lived." The harmeless old Man appears to have divided the' world into two uneven halves, those who belonged to water and those who lived on land and he seems to have con- cluded that the latter were a negligible tribe whose ways were not worth learning.

div.head: QUARTER DECK,
div.p: THE QUARTER DECK,

Though Belle Field has been improved out of all recognition we may still find traces of the Admiral. The quarter deck still remains. He formed his circular garden by the building of a stone wall ; outside of this a trench was dug so as to increase the height of the "deck" above the imaginary water and the proud Admiral as he paced it could look down on the supposed billows beneath. From the flag staff he gave his orders to his men, It must have been a sore task for potato diggers to learn the language of the sea. The announcement for " dinner " or "cease work" floated in the form of coloured flags and they must learn the signals or miss their meals. Such was the eccentric Admiral and as we survey his quarter deck we can hardly refrain from drawing a mind's-eye picture.

div.head: SMOLLETS "HAWSER TRUNNION."
div.p: SMOLLETS "HAWSER TRUNNION."

It will help us in our picture if we turn to the early chapters of Smollets novel " Peri- grine Pickle." Smollet knew the quaint lovable old Admiral and under the name Hawser Trunnion he drew his picture. This is how he is introduced: "The loquacious publican soon gave him sketches of all the characters in the county; and among others, described that of his next neighbour Commodore Trunnion, which was altogether singular and odd. 'The Commodore and your worship' gaid he 'will soon be band and glove: he has-a power of money and spends it like a prince— tkat-is in his own way--for to be sure lie is ti bit bumoursome, as the saying is, and

div.head: OUR MISCELLANY.
div.p: OUR MISCELLANY.

• In the last issue of the " Examiner" a correspondent calls attention to the similarity between our account of William Eyres and that written by Mr. Page in a" Sunrise brochure. Little is known of Eyres and his press, but the facts were placed together with great care by the late Fitchett Marsh in his Literary history of Warrington in the 18th century." It is from this source that the information given in our article and Mr. Page's book is drawn. The story is so slender as not to admit of any marked variety of treatment, but we are not conscious of borrowing phraseology. We plead guilty of having borrowed the same illustrations as Mr. Page and acknowledge the kindness of the " Sunrise " Press in granting the free use of them.

It may interest our readers to know that the " Sunrise " Press claims to be the lineal successor to the famous Eyres Press. William Eyres handed over his business to William Haddock from whom it has descended to Mr. Walter Crompton. Several relics are still preserved in the printing shop, notably some composing" sticks," or hand frames in which the type is placed. It is quite con- ceivable that the famous books of John Howard were set in these worn but still usable "sticks." We understand that some of the wood cuts which helped to adorn the Chap books are still in existence.

Before leaving the subject of the chap books we had better say that our inclusion of" Maria Marten of the Red Barn" was no error. The issue of the books did not end with the 18th century and continued long enough to include this first class mystery. We have handled a copy of" Maria" during •the past few days and at the risk of bad dreams have indulged in another perusal. A. M.
