div.head: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
By Philip Snowden, M.P.
THE LABOUR "ALLIANCE."

A certain section of the Press has been publishing sensational items about a Liberal- Labour alliance, and very definite statements have been made that the Labour Party had withdrawn some thirty prospective candi- dates under the terms of some compact with the Liberal Party. If there were any truth in such statements, the Labour Party must have surrendered not only its independence, but its very existence, for there has not been the announcement of one instance where the Liberals have withdrawn one of their candidates to allow a labour nominee a straight fight with a Tory. The newspaper story is one of a compact in which the Labour Party gives away everything and gains absolutely nothing in return.

div.head: REPEATED DENIALS.
div.p: REPEATED DENIALS.

These reports have been denied by respon- sible officials of the Labour Party, but the denials have not been accepted by those who invented the reports of withdrawals and alliances. Ido not suppose that if I add my denial to those of my colleagues on the Executive of the Labour Party that it will satisfy those who aro inventing such stories for Party purposes. But, notwithstanding, I do repeat that there is absolutely no truth whatever in the assertions of "understand- ings" or " arrangements " between the Labour Party and the Liberals. If anything of the sort has been done I know nothing whatever about it, and I ought to know. But I do know that the Executive of the Labour Party has never had any proposal from the Liberals in any shape or form, and that the Labour Party has never taken any action whatever to withdraw any candidate out of consideration for the interests of any other party.

div.head: NO WITHDRAWALS.
div.p: NO WITHDRAWALS.

The fact is that there has not been the withdrawal of a number of candidates. So far as I know only one candidate who had been endorsed by the Labour Party has withdrawn, and in that case the action was taken entirely by the local Labour organisa- tion. The list orconstituencies published in the Press from which Labour candidates are said to have been withdrawn is a list of places where no candidate has been in the field at all, but where there has been some talk of an irresponsible character about bringing forward a Labour candidate. Much harm is done to the Labour movement by the actions of well-intentioned and enthusiastic young men who have little or no idea of the seriousness of a Parliamentary contest, who bring forward motions in branch meetings in favour of adopting a Labour candidate. This gets ,into the Press, and is made to appear serious, whereas there is nothing at all substantial about the announcement. Nine-tenths of the places from which it is said Labour candidates have been withdrawn are of this character. In some cases the local people have never even applied to the head-quarters of the Party for the approval of a Labour candidature; in the remaining cases, with the one exception already mentioned, when the application_ came before
the national executive The candidature was squashed because of its obvious futility. A FURTHER FACT,
This is the true explanation of all this
alk about a Liberal-Labour compact. If

further proof of the want of foundation for such statements be required it will be found in the fact that not one in one instance has a Liberal candidate who is opposing a sitting Labour member been withdrawn. If the Labour Party did enter into a bargain it is pretty certain that they are not such fools as to give everything away for nothing.

div.head: IN LABOUR'S INTERESTS.
div.p: IN LABOUR'S INTERESTS.

The fact is, that the Labour Party, in its own interests, is not inclined at this election to multiply candidatures. Those who have followed me during the time I have been writing this column will know that personally I have always been opposed to reckless Labour candidatures. My influence in the councils of the party has always been used against approving any sug- gested candidature unless there was a reasonable prospect of winning the seat, or at least of polling a vote which would be a credit to the party. I don't believe, except under the rarest of circum stances,in what some of my friends call "propaganda fights." I have never seen anything but disaster come to the local movement as the result of premature contests. lam just enough of a Fabian to believe that the policy of Fabius is generally the best for the Labour and Socialist party to adopt in regard to Parliamentary Candi- datures, namely, to wait in readiness for the most favourable time and then. to strike hard and sure.
OBVIOUS FACTS.
It is no use shutting one's eyes to obvious

facts. In some quarters I know it is enough to make one a suspect if one ventures to suggest that it is wiser to wait than to rush headlong to ceitain destruction. This coming election is an exceptional One. It is not going to be fought on the relative merits of Liberal, Tory, or Labour. The average elector this time is going to know only two parties—the one the party of the Peers, and the other the party of the People. He is going to vote for the candidate who is most likely to win for the-side that he approves.

div.head: AN INJURIOUS POLICY.
div.p: AN INJURIOUS POLICY.

I could imagine nothing which would do more to injure the future of the Labour movement in this country than that the party should show itself indifferent to the supreme issue of this election. If it takes any action which shows that it is more con- cerned about political wrecking than about asserting the rights of the democracy it will alienate public sympathy to such an extent that for years to come the present ground occupied by the party will not be recovered. If on the other hand, the Labour Party shows by its actions that it can put principle before party, and the interests of a great democratic issue before its desire to spite other political parties, it will have won the admiration and gratitude of that portion of the electorate which is now sympathetic to the Labour Party, but not of the Labour Party, and that gratitude will develop into practical support. WHAT INDEPENDENCE IS.

There is no sacrifice of independe.nce in such a common sense policy as this. It is all dictated by a regard to the best interests of the Labour Party now and in the future. The independence of the Labour Party in Parliament is in no way compromised because it votes with the Tories or with Liberals on some particular question. The party is... free on the very next question which arises to select other allies. It is the great advantage of any independent party that it can also select at any time and in any circumstances the course which seems to it

div.head: OUR SERIAL STORY.
div.p: OUR SERIAL STORY.
[ALL RIGHTS RESERVED.]

learnt to hate his- father liatellinCior hio likeness to that father. I've been tempteci more than once, during all these years, to cut myself adrift from him, and to leave him to his own devices. But that would not have suited me; that would not Lave fitted in with my scheme. It isn't for love of him that I keep Rufus hiddtrii." "Very well, then," nd urged more eagerly yet; "then why not give him up to justice r why not tell the tat& about the matter, and let this other man go free? His home is in ruins; he has suffered all the degradation that a man may suffer; at least give him back his life. This other man, Rufus Cridge, deserves to die for his sordid crime. Don't send an in- nocent man to the gallows." "The innocent man, as • you call him, is John Baxendale—and lie shall hang," she re plied. "There's no sentiment about the mat- ter; but I suppose I shouldn't be the woman I am if I did not come here to-night to shew you what my power is, and what I can do. For the first time in all these years, during which I have waited and watched, and starved, and lived Miserably—for the first time I bold in my hands the balance between life and' death. That's a great thought; that's what I've worked for. A word from me can send Rufus Cridge_ into the place now held by John Ritxendale ; but that word shall never be spoken by me." He saw that she meant all she said; he saw also that argument was useless. He paced the room for a moment or two, and then came back to her. _

"Very well, then, there's no further need to talk; he said. "I will wish you good evening.' She laughed and shook her head at him. "Oh, wise man of law, and when I go out of this place you will have me followed, and so discover for yourself what I will not tell you, eh?"

He started a little at that strange reading of his thought •, made a deprecatory move- ment with his hand. "I had not thought of it, but still—" "Oh yes you had," she broke in. "And you thought, I suppose, that I should be fooi enough to lead anyone that followed me straight to him. I'm not so simple; Rufus Cridge is miles away. You may do what you will; you may have me arrested—but still I should not speak. I suppose you understand, by the way, fully what happens to the house of Baxendale? " she added.

"I don't understand you." He stared at her in some perplexity. "By the death of John Baxendale the house of Baxendale ends. It is already in —tins; but with his death its a convicted inur- ..erer his estates go to the Crown. I only tell you this—or remind you of it—inf older that you may see how completely I have done my work. John Baxendale dies a shameful death, and will be buried within the confines of a prison •, his home is in ashes; his estate will be confiscated. Could anything be more_ com- plete?" "Will nothing • move you?" asked the old man.

"Nothing," she replied calmly. " Suppoee I called from that window to that constable I see passing now, and told him to come up here; suppoce I gave you ifito his charge—telling him that you know where the real murderer of Bella Ogden was to be found ? " _ _

div.head: HIS FATHER'S SON.
div.p: HIS FATHER'S SON.
BY TOM GALLON
Author of " Tatterley," "Dicky Monteith," "Kiddy," "A Rogue in Love," "Fate's Beg' gar Maid," " Tho Charity Ghost," &a.
CHAPTER XI.

div.head: CHRISTMAS AND NEW YEAR HOLIDAYS
div.p: CHRISTMAS AND NEW YEAR HOLIDAYS
1. & N.-W. Arrangements.

With the near approach of Christmas and the New Year, many enquiries will be made as to what facilities will be offered by the Railway Companies. The London and North-Western Railway Company, as is their usual custom, are always to the fore, and they have made elaborate and far-reaching arrangements for cheap and comfortable conveyance of the public to all parts of England and Scotland. Quite a welcome feature in this Company's arrange- ments are their excursions to London, and as the service is a very expedient and comfortable one, it is antici- pated that a large number of people will t Ike advantage of the Christmas Eve trains. This is a facility which has not hitherto been offered. Excursion tickets will be issued from Lime-street and Edge Hill on the 24th December available, for 3,4, 5,7, or 8 days, and on the 26th inst. for 1,2, 3 and 6 days, and on the 31st inst. for 2,3, and 4 days. Th& usual Saturday to Monday tickets will be issued as usual on Saturday (Christmas Da3), so that there does not seem to be anything wanting with regards to the London arrangements, in addition to these trips the North-Western have arranged excursions on the 24th December to South Wales, York, Darlington, Bridlington, and other North-Entern Stations, Carlisle, Edinboro', Glasgow, and all parts of Scotland, Oxford, Peterboro, Leamington, Birmingham, Wolverhampton, and many other places, and the tickets are made available so that if necessary the traveller may stay until after the New Year festivities are over. We would commend our relders to apply for hand- bills at the Town Offices and Stations, and see for themselves what arrangements have been made for their comfort.

div.head: CEIRISTNIAS PARCELS.
div.p: CEIRISTNIAS PARCELS.

The London and North-Western Railway Company have made complete arrangements for the collection, quick transit, and prompt delivery of Christmls p trcels in all the principal towns on their system, and all parts of Wales, Scotland, and Ireland. Special "Parcel " trains will be run, and through vans will also be attached to the principal passenger trains for the accommodation of the traffic, and additional delivery and collection services by parcel vans and carts between the Receiving Offices and the Railway Stations will be in operation during Christmas and the nrecading we ek. Senders are advised that as an extra precaution, a duplicate address label should be enclosed in each parcel so that the name of the consignee may be ascer- tained in the event of the outside address becoming detached or defaced.

div.head: GREAT 'CENTRAL RAILWAY.
div.p: GREAT 'CENTRAL RAILWAY.

Excursions are being run by the Great Central to London, Nottingham, Leicester, Rugby, Stratford-on- Avon, Sheffield, Lincoln, Hull, Newcastle-on-Tyne, Filey, Scarboro' and other North-East Coast Resort!. A new departure this year is excursions to London on Fridiy, December 24th, by afternoon and night trains. Seeing that in the past it has not been possible to reach the Metropolis prior to Bank Holiday, without payment of the full ordinary fare, it is hoped that the additional facilities will bo appreciated and taken advantage of.

div.head: STRANGE QUARREL AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: STRANGE QUARREL AT ST. HELENS.

Maria Middleburst, a married woman, of Water- street was summoned at St. Helens on Monday by Elizabeth Conley, midwife, for assault and wilful damage to her cloak and umbrella. Complainant said that she lived at Westfield-streer, and on Friday night about 7.30 when she was going down Brook-street, she saw Mrs. Middlehurst on the footpath talking to a neighbour. She stood near them, and defendant said, "Are you come for that money that I owe you ?" Witness replied that she was, Si hen defendant told her with an oath that she would not get it. She bad been told this many times during the last eighteen months that the fee had been owing. The Mayor.—What is the fee for ? Witness.—Attending her at a confinement. Defendant rushed at her and broke her umbr(lla and tore her cloak.
Defendant said that Mrs. Conley wenu into her house and beat her.

A witness supported plaintiff's story as to the assaul and the damage which amounted to 30s. Mrs. Middlehurst was bound over for six months, and ordered to pay £1 for the damage, the total. amount to pay being a le.

The Lib rariiis and bbjectionabie Novels.—The great majority of people will no doubt approve the action of the leading London libraries in refusing to circnlate books "which are regarded as transgressing the dictates of good taste in subject of the treatment." although the proposal does not appear to meet with the support of the leading novelists. The London daily press could have settled this question if it had pleased by refusing to review the works published by firms who were lax in such matters, but the London Press has not availed itself of the opportunity, and the evil might have been continued for a long time to come, if it had not been for the libraries, which have gradually attained a very powerful position in the book world, and have been moved to exercise their power by com- plaints from subscribers. It, has been suggested that where new novels are thus boycotted, the result will be to advertise them, but that objection is raised to every attempt fo suppress disagreeable literary pro- ductions, and it is obvious that if it were accepted there would never be any reform. Besides the chief object isnot to prevent the circulution of objectionable books among the peolde to whose taste they are adapted ; it is rather to prevent them from being foisted upon unsuspecting people who strongly object to that class of literature and to protect the minds of the young from pollution. It is a choice of evils, and the lesser evil is to leave such novels to those who hunger for them, there being some reason to anticipate that it that course is adopted the matter will in the course of time adjust itself to the satisfaction of right-minded people. Surnames.—What's in a name? Sir Raert E. Matheson thinks there is a greal deal, and he has pro- duced a special wort on the surnames in the United Kingdom. From this it wears that the live most common names are in their order.

ENGLAND. SCOTLAND. IRELAND. Smith, Smith, Murphy, Jones, • McDonald, Kell v Williams, Brown, Sullivan, Taylor Robertson, Smith. The most Taylor, fact is the great preponderance of the Smiths, who even in Wales outnumber the Jones. Many surnames have a connection with the early employments or customs of the people, hence the Bakers, Coopers' Fishers, Turners, Wrights, Smiths, and so on. In romance the heroes have more aristocratic names, whilst the villain, the adventuress, and other characters, have each more or less Christian names of a certain class. "Frank " is seldom a misanthrope, "John" seldom a villian, "Jack," "Tom," and " Harry "are usually good fellows, but " Dick " and "Charles" whilst having good hearts, are more likely to have a past and" George" is more often than not a heavy person. The. Destruction of Plumage and Song Birds.—Mr. James Buckland's lecture this week on the destruction of plumage birds brings once again before the public a subject on which the Press has spoken with one voice, although scarcely anything has been done to prevent this distruction either in this country or on the con- tinent. The Wild Bird Protection Nuts are in many parts of the country absolutely a dead litter; in some cases the County Councils have taken no action, and even where they have issued schedules it is nobody's. business to see that the law is enforced. Meanwhile the cause would be helped if women generally would refuse to wear osprey plumes, and similar ornaments. This is of conrse an entirely voluntary matter, and it is unfortunate that on the occasion of a Royal function some years ago, a few people who felt strongly on the matter' should have adopted rather a dictorial attitude towards Royal Princesses on the subject. That India- eretion does not however, detract from the importan2e of the question, or the soundness of the plea, and if the King and Queen would kindly forget that incident— which they can very well afford to do—and make their influence felt on the side of the birds, they would help the matter immensely. About Mourning.—Queen Alexandra's exceedingly deep mourning for her sister-in-law Princess Welder- man, brings before us the fact that as the years go on, we show less and less disposition to follow in Royal footsteps, aud plunge ourselves into" deep black." Crape is now little seen, indeed monrning generally is of the slightest and worn but a brief time. Dull cashmere, or soft cloth, are usually chosen for day wear, while for evening the materials preferred are

Another old Warringtonian passed away last week in the person of Mr. William Bate, who lived with his granddaughter at 14, Clifton-street. Mr. Bate, who was eighty-nine years of age, was born in Church-street. At an early age he was apprenticed to wiredrawing at Minn. Rylandc Bros. works.

The concern was then in its infancy, only two jodrney- men and three apprentices being employed. Mr. Bate remained with the concern during the *hole of his working life, retiring about twelve years ago. He had been connected with the Ancient Order of Foresters for seventy-one years and he was also a. member of the Ancient. Order of Shephers from its formation, the Widows and Orphans' Fund and, Burial! Society Board. Mr. Bate was a strong belieVer bit trade union principles and identified himself with thee Wiredrawers' Society. In politics he was a Liberal! but took no active part in public affairs, lit his younger days he attended the Parish Church. His wife predeceased hint sixteen years ago and he leaves; three sons.

LORD NEWTON ON REFORMING THE LORDS Lord Newton, speaking on Tuesday night at the Old Kent-road Baths, London said :—" lam satisfied with the House of Lords so far as it goes, but I would prefer to see changes in it. Ido not mind admitting that, there is a good deal to be said against the House of Lords. It is far too large; there are too many people in it of the same class, and- who consequently think too much in the same way, It contains some men of first- class ability, and a good many of second-class ability-, but quite equal to the ordinary member of Parliament. It contains a certain number of people who have got no special qualification for politics, and, to be quite frank, I would be content to do without them."

Death of the Queen' Sister-in-Law.—The Danish Royal Family have suffered a great loss by the death of Princess Waldemar, sister-in-law of Queen Alexandra. She was the daughter of tbe Due de Chantres, and, owing to the exile of her parents front France, was born .on January 13th, 1865, in this country. She married Prince Waldemar, the youngest brother of Queen Alexandra in 1885, and leaves a family of four song and a daughter. Princess Marie was a highly gifted woman, as a Painter, sculptor, author. and a brilliant conversationalist. She was universally popular and beloved in Denmark, and the circumstances of her early death were rendered the more sad by the absence of Prince Waldemar and three of his sons, on a Far Eastern tour, and who have only just left Ceylon on their unhappy, hastened return home. Malks of toe Gentlewoman.—Very thoughtful and interesting is the little volunie entitled "The art of Living." Containing a series of addresses by Mrs. Creighton' the widow of the late Bishop of London, and published by Longmans, Green and Co., at Is. 6d. The self-sufficient girl of the present day, is perhaps inclined to resent advice. her main ambition is to attract attention, and naturally Mrs. Creighton has many candid criticisms to make, of her clothes and manners. She refers to the over-dretsed woman one sees in the streets, wearing a style of dress which is suitable for people who ride in carriages, but ridiculous fur those who have to climb in and out of crowded omnibuses— or trudge the muddy pavements. Then again it is true in the case of a great number of girls, that they are not so amiable as they might be. They use their liberties to amuse themselves, and regard all social intercourse from this point of view, deeming it a bole to have to talk to some dull old gentleman, or middle-aged woman, and making no secret of their preference fer some more attractive entertainment when this offers itself. All this is no doubt part and parcel of the modern craze," to have a good time," but it is the every day little evidences of refinement of mind that stamp the gentlewoman. In Mrs. Creighton's little book, the reader will find many useful hints and sugges- tions with regard to these " gentle " attainments and usages of good society, which alone still give one the air and bearing of a gentlewoman. . .

crepe de Chine and chiffon. The flowing veil is still worn by fashionable women the fabrics employed for this always becoming acce!sory being light black ninon chiffon, or lace, the border of the latter being traced in chenille or fine cord. By a considerable majority of women and girls, white and grey are taking the place of black as mourning part. Hair ornaments. Net cap; of pearls or diamonds aro having a great rogue among girls in the evening, the new caps being Imager than those of Jubet fame, leaving only the front part of the hair above the ears free, Another favourite hair ornament at the moment is the single ostrich Vp, arranged at rather a rakish angle. At several evening assemblies not only has such a plume appeared in the hair, but a cluster to match has found a place on the left side of the deoulletate. Old World Materials.—Bracaded velvets are leading for smart afternoon wear, and brocaded satins hold a similar position at n'ght. And these fabrics are donned successfnlly by quite young girls. The debutante how- ever usually introduces embroidered gauze or crepe de chine, when a brocaded fawn is under consideration, very yonthful and lovely effects being thus obtained. For dressy afternoon wear the long coat is already a mode of the past the Russian jacket and the Russian blouse having taken its place in our affections. Either style lends itself well to the favored brocaded velvets. ' MADGE.

LIBERAL MEETING.—A well attended meeting was held in toe Council School on Thursday evening. Mr. C. Roylance pr,sided and there were present Mr. King M.P.. Mrs. King and Mr. W. Canning (Manchester). Mr. King spoke just over an hour and in that time he touched on every detail of the Government's pro- gramme. He explained why the Government had been forced to peek the opinion of the country in that pretent crisis. Be appealed to the electors of Hatton on the ground that he stood for more freedon and wider liberty ; for the Commons against the Peers'; for Free Trade against Protection and also for the Budget, because he believed it was the people's Budget. After the speech, questions at the Invitation of Mr. King were put. These were very ably answered and seemed to give entire satisfaction. Mr, King had to leave early for Grappenhall, where he Ulm addressing another meeting, but before doing so Mr. Roylance moved a vote of thanks to him for the work he had done in Parliament as their representotive. He. (Mr.. Roylance) said that Mr. King was a good, honest and most useful member. Mr. King briefly replied and asked the electors of Hatton to calmly study the questions for themselves and then act in acoordance to their own convictions by voting for the candidate who in their opinion was pledged to carry out what they considered best for themselves and the co,antry. A very useful and instructive meeting was thus brought to a close.

Mrs. Simpson of Warrington also addressed the meeting and said that .they were now dealing with the greatest evil that exists and as a member of the Warrington Board of Guardians she learned from experience that poverty and the neglect of children by their parents, were largely due to drink. , Mrs. bimpson's address was greatly appreciated and gave a great stimulous to the workers. A MIDNIGHT SCENE.—Percy Hill, Booth-bill, Lymm, who appeared with a large plhster On his right cheek, summoned &mites Moslon,_ Tbe Poplars, Lymm, and Ernest Moston, Tannery Cottages, Lymm, for assault on the 10th December at Lymm. Mr. Keogh, Altrin- chum, appeared for the complainant and NI r..A. Browne, Warrington, for the defendants.—Mrs. Keogh said that cumplainant was a draper carrying on business at Booth-hill, and attended various markets in the district. The defendants were brothers-in-law. The facts were , that this cowardly and brutal assault was committed when complainant was returning from the Northwich market. As he was passing West Legh llouse at 11.45 he saw a man standing in a recess in the wall. It was Ernest Moston. Moston said "Hello," and com- plainant replied. Moston then struck him a violent blow on his face. Complainant did his best to defend himself, but the other defendant (James) came up and gave him a blow on the face with a stick. Complainant ran away and the two defendants followed him, striking right and left. Complainant eventually got to the Police Station and was taken froth there to Dr. Burrows, who put four stitches in his face. The following morning as the defendants were passing com- plainant's house they again threatened what they would do to him. The assault was most premeditated as the men waited on the road to way-lay the man.— James Blair, said be saw the assault committed, and Dr. Burrows described the injuries inflicted on the complainant, which consisted of ,a long contused wound over the right cheek-hone which had evidently been caused by a fairly heavy blow.—Mr. Browne for the defence said he pleaded, "Not guilty" technically. Defendants had a very serious grievance against corn- plainant'; or they would never have done, ' what they were alleged to have done. Defendants were brothers- in-law to the complainant. Mr. and Mrs. Hill, had been married for about 12 year?. They had been on most comfortable terms until sometime ago, when in consequence of his always staying at week-ends, his wife got hold of a letter at Northwich post office addressed to him and signed "Your loving sweetheart:'. Her father saw the letter and kept it. Complainant afterwards asked for it back and his wife got it from her father and gave it to him. Later she saw him burning a letter on the hearth one of them being signed "Loving sweetheart.' Last week she was getting his breakfast ready when he threw, a cup at her and broke her nose. She had been trying to screen him for some time, but her parents felt. there was something wrong and she showed them her nose. Ernest Moston only visited Lymiu occasionally and he got there on Thurs- day night, and heard about the provocation, and went to his father's house. The two defendants afterwards went down to the station but missed their train, and as they were walking down they saw the complainant, who evidently shouted to them. So defendan,s in the heat of the moment struck at him, reinetre)er lug what he had done to their sister. It was well known that com- plainant was a very good boxer and was well able to ' defend himself. James who was across the road did not strike complaintant with his stick, although he bad lone at the time. They were most extenuating circum- stances, and both defendants were of good charactet.— Complainant's wife who had been called to give evidence against her husband was not allowed to do so. the action being considered illegl by the clerk.—The Chairman said that defendants might have had grievances, they were not allowed to take the law into their own hands.—They would be fined 58. and costs each.—Mr. Keogh applied for advocate's fee, the sum of one guinea qach being granted which made the total costs £2 1 ls. 6d. each. Grappenhall. GRAPPENHALL TENNIS CLUB.—The annual meeting of the members of the above Club was held in the schoolroom, "Ferndale," ,Grappenhall, on Thursday evening. There was a good attendance. Cooksey, Mr. Pharaoh (hon. treasurer), and Mr. Crogg (bon. secretary). Several votes of thanks having been passed to retiring officials; the meeting terminated. LIVELY PARISH COUNCIL MEETING.

A meeting of the Parish Council was held on Tues- day in the school. Present Mr. F. Wareing (chairman) Messrs. L. Greening, Jenkins, Lister-Kaye, Lomas, G. Ashton, Bacon, Bolton, Collins, and Cuarles H. Houk (clerk). SEWAGE SCHEME.. %. _

A letter was 'read from the Cleric to the Urban Dis- trict Council of Runcorn Mr. G. F. Ashton in reference to the Sewage Scheme contract. He pointed out that before any work was commenced the. Parish Council would be notified. Along and lively discussion followed. The Chairman pointed out that the intentions and arguments of the Council had been mis-reported ; at the Same time he bad to admit that the Parish Council were powerless after the discision of the District Council had been arrived at. Mr. Jenkins then read the act relating to such cases and argued that before any scheme was introduced the Pariah Council ought to be notified. , The Chairman: You are only wasting time Mr. Jenkins by going over the ground again. Mr. Jenkins: But what does the act say? The Chairman: I don't trouble what the Act says. Mr. Jenkins: Oh! don't you? Tbe Chairman • No, I don't. Will you sit, down and, Mind Yeur own business,' Mr. Jenkins then attempted to press another refer- ence to the Act when the Chairman interjected by telling Mr. Jenkins again to sit down. Mr. Jeukins : It is no use you Mr. Chairman trying to throw dust in our eyes. The Chairman : You are nothing but an obstruc- tionist! Nothing but an infernal humbug. Mr. Bolton (District Councillor) : Such a contract is now being entered into and I shall only he too pleased to answer any question in relation thereto. The Clerk pointed out something in reference to the Act in an undertone to the Chairman. Mr. Jenkins: Will the clerk speak audibly when he has anything to say? The Chairman: Will you mind your own business and sit down. Sit down! Mr. Lister Kaye : When this sewage scheme starts Mr. Chairman it will mean a contract which in time will run into the thousands, and we ought to thrash it out thoroughly. The Clerk read an extract from the Act which states that the Parish Council could only recommend to the Urban Council. Mr. Jenkins pointed out that already £7O had been spent. , The Chairman: That was for preliminary expenses I presume. Mr. Bolton: Yes, that is so, and I might say that such expenditure has been spread over a , number of years. The matter then dropned. LIGHTING PETITION. The Clerk rehd a petition signed by 14 residents of Albert-road asking for the erection of a lamp at the end of the road.' Mr. Kaye questioned whether they 'had power to erect a lamp. The Clerk: We can only recommend to the District Council. The Parish:Connell has authority to.light. Mr. Ashton stated that the District Council had recently elected a committee of four as a Lighting Committee of which Mr. Bolton was one. Previous to that the Parish Council had powers. ' Mr. Bolton t More mis-staterrents Mr. Chairman.

The Chairman : The Rural Disttict Council erected four lamps in Victoria-ma and no one knew anything about th,m until they were there. In the face of that it doe ti seem that they are really the Lighting Authorities. -Mr. Greening: We want lamps at onto. In some parts it is very dangerous. A long discussion ensued and the following resolutioa was moved by Mr. Jenkins and seanded by Mr. Ashton: —" That we write to the Local Government Board ',forming them that the Rural District Council of Runcorn are lighting streets and generally incurring unlimited expenses and the Parish Council has not been

advised or consulted in any particular. Will you say if this is right ?" The Clerk: It, is not advisable, Mr. Chairman, to pass such a resolution in face of the Act and I just mention this in, justice to myself. Mr. Jenkins: Why should - Tbe Chairman: Just close your clap-trap for Heaven's sake. Mr. Kaye moved an amendment to the resolution:and the amendment was carried. Mr. Collins then mosed the following resolution: "That this council regrets that the lighting of Victoria-road was undertaken without the Parish Council being consulted on the matter, but trusts that in the future on such matters the Parish Council will be consulted, also that the parish Council considers that two lamps are sufficient in the Victoria-road and recommends that two of them be removed and erected where most needed." This resolution was carried by five votes to three. 2 MR. JENKINS AGAIN. Mr. Jenkins then read a letter from the cleik in answer to a request to inspect certain books. The Clerk . stated that the books Mr. Jenkins required were often out of his possession and it was most inconvenient to suit everybody. The Chairman : What does Mr. Jenkins object to. Mr. Jenkins : The Clerk points out that th is is a precedent but at the same time I may inspect the bo4,lcs.
—.....,. r. Kaye : While I was an overseer I ny, ratepayer gould inspect the books and they were always available. Moore.

THEFT FRO.Ai MOORE HALL.—At the Daresbury Petty Sessions held at Stockton Heath on Tuesday, Albert Pover and Reuben Grice. of Frodsham Bridge, ple.tded guilty to stealing a pair of wooden hoist blocks, valued at loe., the property of the exois.,of the late Mr. John White, of Moore Hall, and also to stealing two sauce- pans, valued at 55., the property of George Hicks, coachman at Moore Hall. Prisoners went to Moore Hall for a Toad of hay and whilst there they took the articles mentioned. They parted with the saucepans to an Irishman for a couple of drinks and sold the blocks for is. 3d. to -a Mr. Rigby at Frodsham Bridge. On hearing that a pair of blocks had been stolen Rigby informed the police.--Prisoners were arrested by 11.0 Preston. They were sentenced to fourteen days' imprisonment.

TAXI-CAB A CCIDENT.—Mr. James MCBTOPTI, who resides at 21,Blaine-street, was cycling along Fairfield- road on Tuesday morning and on turning into London- road was knocked off his machine by a taxi-cab which was coming from the -direction of Warrington and which contained several people. The conveyance passed over the man who was dragged along the ground. After being attended to in Mr. Franklin Bennett's shop he was conveyed to the Infirmary. He had sustained scars on the face from the machinery under the taxi and was badly shaken. Fortunately no bones were broken.

Percival said Mr. Clarke gave him permission to catch rabbits and he had heard nothing ito the contrary. He handed a letter to the Bench. The case was dismissed.

BEECH HOUSE SCHOOL.—Tbe pupils of this school gave their annual concert on Friday evening in the Halt Cafe Assembly Room before an appreciative audience of parents and friends invited by the Principals. the Misses Westbrook. The Vicar (the Rev. James Collins) presided. The chief attraction was the play "Cinderella," the characters being taken as follows :—" Fairy God- mother," Mabel Priesiner; "Fairy Violet," Dora Wallace; "Fairy Bluebell," May Dash; "Cinderella." Freda Weaver: "Prince Truelove," fertie Berrey; "Baroness Tumble Down Dreary," Marion Rigby; "Baron," Master V. Stubbs;." Lady Clotilda and Lady Angelina" (drughters), Clara Hall and Gladys Strange; "Alberto" (Herald and Page), Master S. Berrey ; "Lady- in-waiting," Dora Wallace. All the pupils acquitted themselves well and tbe delight of the audience was expressed in very frequent applause. The programme also included pianoforte and violin selections by the Misses Westbrook. The Misses Marion Rigby, Dora Wallace, and Freda Weaver executed a beautiful "Butterflies Dance," which, at the request of the audience, was repeated. Some effective tableaux also called forth round upon round of applause.

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
KILLED BY A WAGGON.

George Rhodes, aged twenty six, of Cr tb-strPet, St. Helens, was killed about one o'clock on Monday after- noon at the St. Helens Colliery. It appears that Rhodes wa3 in one of the haulage roads, when he was knocked down by a waggon and so seriously injured that he died almost immediately.

div.head: SHOCKING COLLIERY ACCIDENT.
div.p: SHOCKING COLLIERY ACCIDENT.

George Banks, aged thirty-three, a colliery rlaywage- man, of 22, Vernon-street, St. Helens, was killed late on Saturday night at the Ashton's Green Colliery. Banks, who was married, had for nine years worked at this colliery, and on Saturday night he went with William Pennington and James Critchley to carry out some alterations and repairs in the main haulage brow. While they were at work filling fallen roof into boxes to be taken away a stone fell out of the roof and struck the signal wire, which caused the man in charge of the engine to start the motion. Then trouble began for deceased was caught between the box he had been filling and the roof, and more roof came down. He wis badly crushed, and when got out, after being pinned w enty minutes, he was unconscious and dying.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON.
MR. J. A. SEDDON, M.P.. AND AGRICULTURAL INTERESTS,

Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.P. for the Newton-le-Wilhws Division of Lancashire, attended a meeting of the Liverpool and District Farmers' Club, held on Saturday afternoon in the rooms, Houghton Arms Hotel, Great Nelson-street, under the chairmanship of Mr. John Pimbley (Maghull), for the purposes of discussing with the members questions affecting their industry. Mr. Seddon, replying to a question as tdthe possible effect Tariff Reform in England upon the agricultural industry, said he had made personal inquiries in Germany as to the effect there, and he found that the German farmer was not the prosperous man they would expect to find according to the statements made as to the benefits of Tariff Reform, in f:A. ct , he was the most miserable creature on God's earth. He had to work seven days to the week, and even then only eked out a miserable existence. Judging the farmer in Germany by outward appearance he came to the conclusion that the Englishlarmer had the stability and prosperity than ho saw anywhere in the Northern provinces of *Germany. In America the conditions were not much better. That being so, he felt convinced that Tariff Reform would not help the British farmer. Replying to the point as to Retaliation and the exporting of form produce. Mr. Seddon said he always understood that the great , market for that was the home' market, and that it was only the surplus that ever found its way into the foreign markets. What I was wanted was that the purchasing power of the large consuming bedy in the country should be raised higher and that. could not be done if they were going to mpose burdens which could only have the effect of r eventing the spending classes from being increased.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
WIDNES TOWN COUNCIL. FAVOURABLE RATABLE COMPARISON.
A suggestion which met with considerable approval was made at the monthly meeting of the Widnes Town Council on Tuesday,. . . .

Alderman H. S. Timmis asked the Chairman of the Education Committee if, in view of the tact that parks and open spaces were provided directly or indirectly out of the rates for the ' uie of children during the summer months, the committee would consider the advisability of opening a room in each of the schools during the winter months in which the children could play, and thus 'keep them out of the streets, for the benefit of their hesith and morals. (Hear, hear.) The suggestion was very nyapatbeticallv received by the deplay-chairman (Councillor F. Neill), who expressed the opinion that it would receive the cordial considera- tion of the committee.

Councillor D. Wilding (deputy-chairman of the Firance Committee), in presenting a comparative state- ment of the rates in some cf the larsost towns, said that whilst during the past ten years Widnes rates had increased by twopence the average increase for the country was is. 3d.. and th.tt despite the feet that greater demands were being made by the turgesses for motor 'buses and improved roads. (Hear, hear.)

div.head: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.
div.p: PALACE AND HIPPODROME.

Believers in that old adage "Laugh and grow fat " should pay a visit to the Palace and Hippodrome this week,' as hutnour bolds full sway. Fred Karno's Company of comedians are great laughter-makers and present two exceedingly comical turns," Casuals" and the " Mumming Biros." The Casuals" is a great novelty, and the first scene shows a small crowd waiting for the "casual door" to open. An amusing incident occurs here, as a travelling musician mistakes the iVorkhouse for a theatre and plays a well-known ditty and afterwards takes round his hat. On being told it is the entrance to the Workhouse he walks off in disgust. The interior of the " house" is next shown where all the casuals are being searched. The broken down golfer who, While " tip-y " also mistaliqs the Workhouse for the theatre, makes himself well at home. At the finish a warder enters and says that the Chairman of the Board of Guardians is about to pay a. visit. On entering, this gentleman asks if there are any . complaints to. make. The polfer rushes in attired in his dressing gown and,complains that there is a scarcity of billiard chalk in the billiard room, also that the tooth brushes are moulting and so on. Another .inmate asks for a fire in his room' and the Chaitman tells the wat der to order a ton of coals, and in a whisper instructs the man to give the inmate a bucket full, and send the rest round to his house. Humour abounds throughout the sketch. The " Mumming Birds" is is an up-to-date travesty on. the modern music hall, and is in simple words a stage upon a stage. The audience are kept in roars of laughter by the antics of an obstreperous school boy who 'makes frequent use of his pea-shooter, and a member of society much the worse for drink. The rest of the programme is well varied. Dan Whitley proves a popular comedian, and 'makes a great hit with his song " It's for your sake that I'm singing here to-night." Quick changing artistes are seen to advantage in a scena entitled "Fun on the Midland," by Thomas and Taylor. C. J. Sheldon, the comedian in-a white evening' suit, the Sisters Henderson in their refined musical speciality act, Fritz Kornau, "the human flute," and Victor and Louis, in "'f he Golfer and the Caddie," complete an excellent programme. The Palace Perfection Pictures . illustrate interesting scenes on the Canadian Pacific Railway, and a humorous series entitled the "Boxing Fever." The orchestra, under the baton of Mr. Ernest Widdop, contributes attractive musical items.

div.head: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME,
div.p: NEXT WEEK'S PROGRAMME,

A.novel attraction next week will be an "Amateur Carnival for ladies and gentlemen" in which £lO prizes are to be competed for. It is open to all kinds of entertainers and local amateurs are requested to give their names in at once. The other items on the programme will be:—Wilr Van Allen, a Tramp Comedian; lan Colquhoun. the Great baritone, who will introduce a new patriotic song "Mighty Mother England" ; the Brothers Ford in a concurrent singing . and dancing act ; Ben Richards, vocalist; Barrington in his unique and interesting musical specialty ; Ellis and Campbell comedians and dancers ; Rose Everett commedienne ; and the Palace Perfection Pictures.

div.head: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.
div.p: CROSS COUNTRY RUNNING.

Warrington Athletic Club journeyed to Clock Face on Saturday last, for the inter club fixture with their old friends Sutton Harriers. Trail was laid over about 7i miles of very heavy country by five members of Sutton and 1 of Ravenhead ; the latter joining in the three cornered race added to the interest of the run and had out their best team of the season.

Unfortunately several Warringtonians, including the Captain, EL R. Jepson, turned up just too late for the start, which took pjace from the Clock Face Hotel, and a count of five a side Was agreed on for the run through which resulted as follows ; Sutton H.C. and A.C. : S. Welding; 1; C. Straw, 2; J. Smart, 6 ; .1. R. Smith,?; F. J. Whittle, 9 ; total, 25. Warrington : F. Antrobus' 3; J. Parsonage, 4 ; J. Twiss,s • W. Antrobits 11 • H. HolLrook, 15 ; total, 38. Ravenead : H. Wilcock, 8; J. hill, 18; H. Naylor, 19 ; H. Lee, 20; J. Craine, 26 ; total, 91. .1. Parton:lga set a strong pace and when two miles had been covered was leading by 50 yards. but lack of knowledge of the locality lost him and a clubmate their positions. Owing to failing light the trail layers bad wisely decided to avoid a barbed wire patch, as much as possible, but in doing so got on the road about 500 yards from the finishing point, making the run in much shorter than usual in such races.

There was very little between the first half-dozen to finish. These included L. Drinkwater of St. Helens Recs., who, as a second claim member of Sutton was having a try for the gold modal offered by the landlord for the first man home and he only just missed it by inches.

F. Antrobus and .T. Twiss ran finely, finishing closely and strongly. These two are coming on. J. Parsonage fell heavily at the last jump and all things considered put up a good performance. There was a good gap behind these and when last season's top sawyers have regained their form the locals should be capable of holding their own in the best company. At all events Sutton's visit on January Bth will be particularly interesting. A well served hot-pot and tocial evening put all on good terms with themselves and everybody else. Each group seemed proud of their trophies gained in the Liverpool Senior, Northern Junior and Liverpool Junior Ohampionship respectfully end each are hoping to exchange them for higher honours in the near future.

Most clubs will be running off their Christmas handicaps to-day but following their custom of recent seasons Warrington A.C. will contest theirs on Christmas Day morning. To-dav's flxfure is an ordius.ry run and Novice Race from Bridge Inn at three o'clock prompt. We are requested to ask ticket sellers for the "meet" to return unsold tickets and cash early as posiible.

div.head: Smallpox Hospital.
div.p: Smallpox Hospital.

Dr. Petronell Manby, an inspector of the Local Government Board, held an inquiry at the Town Hall on Tuesday morning respecting the application of the Town Council to burrow £3OO for the completion of the Smallpox Hospital at Great Sankey. There were present :—Councillor Hirtles, the Deputy Town Clerk (Mr. Hallway), the Assistant Town Clerk (Mr. T. H. *lairs), the 13orongh Treasurer (Mr. John Fairhurst), the Assistant Borough Treasurer (Mr. W. H. Woodcock), the Borough Surveyor (Mr. Longdin), the Medical Officer 'of Health (Dr. Ilibbert), the Chief Inspector of Nuisances (Mr. Flood), the Building Inspector (Mr. ugars), and Mr.Houghton (chief clerk) borough treasurer's iffice. Mr. Hallway said that the original loan of £10,129 was sanctioned in 1901, and since that time they had either expended or set aside a sum amounting to £9,432 2s. Pd, leaving a balance of 5:696 17s. 3d., available for the erection of the administrative block. That sum was not con- sidered adeqriate for the erection block as was contem- plated in 1901. There had b4n.repeated communica- tions between the Local G-oveinment Board and the Health Committee, as to the nature of the building, and it was found that ..-E693 17s. 3d. was not sufficient; hence the application. The bnilding would be so des;gned that additional rooms could be rapidly added in the event of an epidemic, some in a few hours and others in a few days. Mr. Longdin and Mr. Hibhert gave evidence, and Mr. Hallway informed the Inspector that the plans would be submitted to the Rural District Council. e

div.head: Budget Proposals for Increased
div.p: The Budget Proposals for Increased
Licence Duties.

Sir,— Some few weeks ego my Committee were able by the Lindness of Mr. Joseph Rowutree to offer a copy of the abridged edition of " The Taxation of the Liquor Trade„" the authoritative work of tererence upon all questions of liquor and licence taxation, to Sny works engaged in advoeating the Budget proposals for increased licence duties, etc. That offer elicited a very wide response. It may be, however, that there are still some workers who do not possess the book, but would value a copy in view of the forthcoming General Election. when that portion of the Budget relating to Licensing will doubtless be much discussed. Application for the book shou'd be made to the Temperance League, Parliament Mansions, Victoria- street, London, S.W., accompanied bv threepence in stamps to defray cost of postage.—Yours etc.. A. F. HARVEY, Secretary.

div.head: Miss Brooke-Hunt Replies to Mrs. Crosfield.
div.p: Miss Brooke-Hunt Replies to Mrs. Crosfield.

Sir,—l have no quarrel with Mrs. Crosfield's answer to my statements in a speech at Warrington when she says it stands to reason that the cheaper food and clothing are, the more the people can buy of them ; therefore manufacturers produce more, and thus MORE HANDS ARE EMPLOYED.' Precisely. But in the case of sweated goods and free imports, which are the cheapest goods in our market it iSTOREIGN HANDS THAT HATE BEEN SO YULT,iTUDINOUSLY EMPLOYED. Does Mrs. Crosfield approve of that? And would the thrifty housekeepers of Warringt In, when once they have grasped THE COST OF THEIR CHEAP GOODS, consider they had really driven a satisfactory bargain for themselves? I have too high an opinion of their intelligence not to douht it. With regard to Trades Unionists, their objects and methods, I would ask Mrs. Croefield if her sense of logic permits her to hold the view that it is good tactics to protect the conditions of their labour with- out also protecting the fruits thereof. Believe me, faithfully yours V. BROOKE-HUNT. , 19, Hanover Square, London W.

div.head: Tariff Reform. Taxing the Capital.
div.p: Tariff Reform. Taxing the Capital.

Sir,—Tariff Reform does rot necessarily imply the taxing of foodstuff-3. A Protectionist legislator may or may not put an import duty on the neeessaries of life. "It is a quite open point. It is well-known, -however, that the Unionists of this country intend to try the experiment, they do not intend to allow food to come in duty free. In this and other lotto's I intend to deal solely with the Tariff Reform movement as it threatens to develop in our own country, and therefore I am going to take it for granted that there is to be a tax on such necessaries as bread. .

• -DeS-pite a most remarkable and unwarranted state- ment of Mr. Wyndharn's a few days ago, it is absolutely clear to even Tariff Reformers themselves, that a tax upon corn must inevitably raise the Trice a bread. _

Now, I cannot conceive how Tariff Reform can raise the rate of wages or remedy unemployment to any substantial extent, and I shall try to show in letters at future dates, that such thoughts are mere fallacies and delusions. -
If you are not going to materially benefit the poor man either with an increase of waßes or employment, instead of being a benefit, Tariff Reform must surely be a burden to him. . _ - -

There is another aspect in which one must look at this taxing of necessities, it is in the light of the Political Economist. A great cry has recently been raised by the Unionist party that the Budget is going -to tax capital, because they argue that land is capital. I would like to remind tho-e gentlemen that their own pet financial scheme would be a still more direct attack upon capital, and upon some of the most important species of capital too. Food, clothing, and all the accessories that are consumed or used produc- tively by workers constitute capital. All that,goes stimulate and sustain labour is capital. The wealth of a nation is measured by its prosperity, and pros- perity naturally depends on the amount of capital, provided that it is fairly well distributed, that a nation possesses. This is at once obvioua from the fact that in a prosperous country labour and wages must be good, and from wages spring capital. It therefore appears that the more capital, in the real sense of the word, there is in a country, the better. But, as I have tried to explain, food stuffs are capital : it therefore appears that the-mote food- stuffs and other articles for the sustenance of labour the better for the country. That is to say, that the cheaper food is the greater will be the prosperity of the nation. The taxing of eatables, which are not luxuries, is therefore opposed to all the ethics of political economy, for it is nothing better than the taxation of capital. It seems to me that half the Unionists of to.day do not thoroughly understand the ttue meaning and functions of capital. Take for instance another of their favourite war-cries, " Sending capital abroad." If the Liberals are driving capital cut of this country it can only be said that the Conservatives are pro- posing to do so on a much larger scale. By the taxa- tioh of necessities coming into this country, they are keeping much capital out of it, because as I have already asserted, these necessities represent capital, and, if there is no great revolution in wages, the -demand for the same will be without doubt decreased. Certain forms of capital should never be taxed., and more espec'ally that portion of capital that stimu- lates and sustains labour. If this part of capital is manacled then the whole labour market is fettered.

The present promising condition of some of oni industries has been mainly brought about by the cheapness of food. If food rises in pi ice, and if your system holds good, so should labour, because the worker has to pay more for his upkeep. If labour rises in price, that is, if wages gl up, then it will cost the manufacturer more to produce the goods in the making of which he is engaged. In some of our trades this would have it bad effect, as they are only able to compete in foreign markets on accoun) of the cheapness of labour over here. The only effect that the taxing of food stuffs, or Capital, will have on England seems to be that it will make it much harder for the poorer classes to live.

Protectionists seem to think that we are to starve ourselves that our Co'onies may reap, as they think, a benefit. They talk about a Colonial Preference, and forget all about the poor of their own native land, the poor on whom the brunt of the food taxes would fall. Surely the preference that ought to be given is a \ preference to the labourers of Britain, apd let that preference take the form of untaxed capital—of free food.—Yours etc., Burtonwood, Dec. 16th, 1909:
H.M.
