div.head: FREE TRADE CAMPAIGN. Councillor Roberts Replies to Miss Brooke-Hunt.
div.p: FREE TRADE CAMPAIGN. Councillor Roberts Replies to Miss Brooke-Hunt.

The Free Trade League, which played so prominent a part in the last elseition, is again the field. The first meeting was held on IA ednesday evening in Greening's Dining Hall, where a large number of people assembled under the presidency of Councillot H. Roberts. He was supported by Messrs. H. J. Leech (Manchester), P. O'Brien, W. Webster, J. A. Morton. K. Henshall, A. Rathbone, S. Rigby Armitage, and H. G. Roberts. The CHAIRMAN said that they were met there that night on the eve of a dissolution of Parlia tient, and while it was not his intention to enter into party politics he thought they were entitled to consider how it waft that this somewhat unexpected dissolution had been brought shout. They were all aware that there was a need of £16,000,000 of taxes which was caused by two facts : first, the sum necessary to provide old age pensions—(hear, hear)—in regard to which, he thought, there was no man in the room who would raise ths slightest objection, and he doubted whether there was one outside the room Who wou!d dare to lay the slightest objection to that very needed reform. The other factor was the provision, of an enormonsly strong navy caused by the addition of so many new Dreadnoughts. If th'ey remembered a short time ago the gentlemen who were now kicking up such a shiouy about paying the bill were the loudest in their demands for the groat addition to the fiiihtin,, forces of the navy. (Hear, hear). Their demand had been met, but the bill remained to be paid. Certain pro- positions in the shape of it. Budget were submitted to the Howe of Commons as the means to raise this money and the striking characteristic of the Budget was that it went to those wbo could best afford to pay. The Bill was KICKED OUT BY AN IRRESPONSIBLE, NON- REPRESENTATIVE BODY OF MEN and those who made the greatest fuss about paying the bill, which they themselves had largely helped to create. The average inctome of the Dukes was .£BO,OOO per annum. The bulk or the men were getting £1,500 a week end rather more and they were the men who were the loudest in their opposition to pay the 13111. The alternative was TaryT Reform. There was a meeting in Warrington a short time ago at which Miss Rrooke- Hunt made a very able speech from her point of view. In dealing with a lady in politics one had to be extremely careful, because one never knew what might happen. (Laughter.) All he had to say in regard to tnat speech was, that when she tried to persuade the ladies that it would be a good thing to put a little tax on Imported wheat especially when an equivalent of that tax was going to be taken off tea, sugar, and articles of that kind—they had only got to look at the fact. that she was described as Miss Brooke-Hunt to see the illogical position of that statement. (Laughter.) If she had been the wife of a working man who had to keep house upon ,C 1 ss. or Li 108. a week she would not have said that. When he thbught of how women kept their houses clean and sent their children to school in a respectable manner, he felt inclined to raise his hat to them for their ability and thrift. (Applause).

div.head: MISS BROOKE-HUNT
div.p: MISS BROOKE-HUNT

said that they would take the tax off tea if they would allow them to put a tax on bread. If she had thought about it for five minutes she would have known that the quantity of tea, which bore a tax of sd. a pound was infinitesimal compared with bread. There could not be a greater fallacy than the statement of Miss Brooke- Hunt—even to suggest that workingmen and women were such arrant fools to allow the tax on tea to be taken off so that a tax could be put on bread. (Hear, hear). During the last 50 yews a Free Trade Govern- ment had not put a single penny on food taxes, but during the last ten years of office of the Tory Govern- ment they put on 81million pounas on tea and sugar alone and yet they were being asked to trust ,a Tariff Reform Government. Their history proved • that instead of taking taxes off food they put taxes on food. We had had a programme from Birming- ham which, as it came from Highoury,was authoritative In that programme the taxes on tea and sugar were to be retained and taxes were to be put on wheat, butter and bacon. He was a Free Trader, absolute and corn- plete—(applause)—and he put his principles in regard to Free Trade before everything else for the reason that it was no use going in for social reform if the country became commercially Lankrupt. (Applause.) He was convinced that there was no other policy by which the supremacy of this country as a manufacturing nation could be mOntakned but the policy of Free Trade and he absolutely opposed any tinkering with it in any shape or form whatsoever. But more than everything be did most emphatically protest against the

div.head: ATTEMPT TO SHUFFLE TIIE RESPONSIBILITY
div.p: ATTEMPT TO SHUFFLE TIIE RESPONSIBILITY

of raising the extra money from the shoulders of those who could best afford to pay and take it out of the women and children of this country. (Applause.) Mr. W. WEBSTER moved the following resolu- tion : "That this meeting affirms its unshaken belief in the principles ot Free Trade adopted nearly 60 years ago and expresses its conviction that Free Trade is now more than ever necessary for the well-being of the community." He said that if the manufacturers would bring themselves more up-to-date there would be no necessity for Protection. Some years ago Mr. Chamberlain said that wire was going from the country and Warrington" in particular. At the time he made that statement we in Warrington made as much wire as they did in the whole of Germany 31r. Chamberlain said that practically the whole of the wire trade was in Germany, which was not true. In 1901, the exports of British , manufactured wire amounted to £950,000. In 19C6 they amounted to £2,000,000 so that the wire trade was going and going very well. (Applause). He said that the reason the leather trade was not as it should be was because of the shortage of hides and not because of the importa- tion of American leather. He maintained that xve could not possibly thrive under Protection. (Applause). Motrros in seconding the resolution said that if , they wefe Free Traders and yet did not believe in the Budget it was neeessary that they should vote for Free Trade. If the late Lord Salisbury could have retained the position of Premier longer than be did the question of Tariff Reform would not have arisen. (Hear, hear.) Many of the Conservatives -who were supporting the Tariff Reform movement were not doing so honestly. He believed that they attached more importance to their party than to the real truth of the matter. The Free Trade question was the greatest movement that was before the people. A 2s. duty on corn would not stimulate the home grown wheat. It would need at least a 10s. tax to do that. (Applause.) Mr. LEECH in the course of a lengthy speech said that Free Trade was a necessity to the country. It was so because we could not feed half the people of the country. In the dap of Protection we could not feed the people and since then we had had 22 millions added to the population. There was only one way of paying for anything which we bought from abroad and that was by artiBles which we manufactured. Therefore, when we received imports we paid for them by exports which stimulated trade. (Hear, hear). The resolution was carried unanimously.
On the proposition of Mr. R. llENsitAr.r., seconded by Mr. P. O'BRIRN a vote of thanks was accorded to the chairman and the speakers.

div.head: Meeting at Brick-street. Speech by Mr. Rigby Armitage.
div.p: Meeting at Brick-street. Speech by Mr. Rigby Armitage.

A well-attended Meeting was hold in the firick-street Mission Room on Thursday evening. Mr. S. R. Armitage presided and there were also present on the platform :—Messrs. E. Wynne-Jones, S. Wright, S. W. Jeffery, H. Taylor (Bolton) and others. The CHAIRMAN said that they on the platform were not present because of their association with either

div.head: AND MRS. CROSFIELD'S HOME TILL AFTER THE ELECTION.
div.p: AND MRS. CROSFIELD'S HOME TILL AFTER THE ELECTION.

;er upon the occupancy of the above pretty country house at Penketh—which ection campaign. Penketh Grange belongs to Mr. B. Parsonage, and was Mr. Thomas Tunstall. It stands in the hollow on the right side of the road joins the Garden Suburb estate.

political party. Their only plea for being before them was Free Trade arid because they believed that it had a lot to do with the prosperity of the working men of the country. (Hear, bear.) They would before tint fight was over hear a great (iutcry about the pledges given by the Government with regard to a subject which the larger portion of the English population fought very strenuously for—getting rid of Chinese labour in South Africa. (Applause.) Before going out of office the Tory Government passed an indenture for 16,000 fresh Chinamen ,to be imported into South Africa in tree )Care. Now, owing to the Liberal Government, most of the Chinese had left South Africa and they were told that on the first of next month the last would have left. (Applause.) He had a very interesting document in his hand which he thought a good many of those present would have received. It was a document arranged by the Tariff Reform League and handed to the workmen at a certain wireworks at dinner time that day. It read "Please come ten minutes earlier to-day and hear a workingman address you on Tariff Reform, at the entrance of your works. Tariff Reform will reduce the cost of living and find more work." What would Tariff Reform mean eventu- ally ? Why a greater cost of living. What did- Mr. Joseph Chamberlain say when he introduced Tariff Reform? He said •` You mutt bear this like men for the Empire's sake." He (the speaker) thought that all Free Traders would sty "For the Empire's sake we will not do it." (flear, hear). They were all working people. They had all work to do. They followed their leaders very conscientiously and rightly who advised them as to conditions of labour, and as to whether they were getting fairly paid; as to whether the reduction of wages was right or not, and instructed them as to the advisability of demanding higher waees, and be hoped they would not be so foolish as to listen to the tales of the Tariff Reformers. A certain well-known person belonging to a Trade Union went to America to investigate the conditions of Labour under Tariff Reform and on returning said that £2O in England would purchase more than 2.30 in America. He mentioned that to show that the wages given in that country and other countries under tariffs were inadequate to maintain the normal standpoint of life. (Applau.e.) That gentleman's statements per- fectly bristled with very strong arguments relating to the cenditions of the working man in America under the high tariff as compared with England. He thought some of them present were wire workers engaged in the iron trade. At the present moment he asked them to Iliok at the difference in price between German and English rods. German rods were from 55.. to 10s. less than the English rods. Billets were from 15s. to 20s. Per ton less than English. They would be surprised to hear that Warrington manufacturers were the largest buyers of German rods, which were converted into•wire and structure work and employed a vast number of • men in our town. In conclusion he asked all present to consider their wives and children and vote for Free Trade. (Applause.) Mr. S. W. JEFFERY in proposing the resolution in support of Free Trade said he had great pleasure in doing so as he recognized the great crisis that was before them and he would strive to do all he possibly could to help the cause of liberty and right. (Applause). He referred to the increase of food taxes there would be if Tariff Reform were accepted. Employers knew that they held the cotton market by the smallest margins and if the cost of production was increased by the imposition of tariffs the result would be disastrous to Lancashire. Mr. S. WRIGHT in seconding the propooition said there were a good number of railway workers living about that neighbourhood. That was a question which affected them considerably. '['hey all knew that the rail way workers owed their living to the transit of goods from one place to another. What would be the consequence to the railway workers of this town if there were fewer goods to be removed, owing to the restriction of trade by tariffs ? Engineers would be thrown out of work besides the men working on the stations, etc. They would require fewer waggons and the waggon workers would be thrown out of employ- ment. The speaker quoted the prices of foodstuffs in Austria under Protection as compared with England showing how mueh cheaper goods were here. ~ Mr. E,WY.NINE-JONES supported and said Tariff Reform could not alleviate unemployment. In his opinion it would make it far worse and they would be greatly mistaken to exchange Free Trade for the policy of Protection. He pointed out that it was absolutely impossible to tax the foreigner. Even if they could, would it be right to ask the Germans to pay for our Old Age Pensions or for our Army and Navy? Concluding he said Free Trade would do much to break down the international barriers, international bitterness and international hostility. Let them stick to Free Trade. (Applause.) Mr. TAYLOR, gave an excellent speech dealing mostly with the unemployment question. The resolution was put to the meeting and carried unanimously. The speakers were then thanked by their services.

div.head: INFIRMARY.
div.p: THE INFIRMARY.
Centenary Million Penny Fund.

The Committee of this fond are evidently deter- mined to leave no stone unturned in their effort to bring the scheme to a successful issue. •On Christmas Day an envelope, with a printed appeal on the face, will be left at every house in War- rington and district and the public are asked to remember at this festive season their less fortunate brethren who are compelled to seek the aid of this Institution

The envelopes will be collected on Boxing Day and it is hoped that the Fund will benefit considerably, The work of distributing and collecting the envelopes has been undertaken by the members of the Church Lads Brigade and the Boy Scouts, who will wear an Official Badge.

div.head: Warrington and District Teachers' Association.
div.p: Warrington and District Teachers' Associa- tion.

Mr. J. Arm Wong presided over a general meeting of the above association held on Saturday morning, in the Wycliffe Memorial Building.—The Secretary (Mr. F. Longshaw) announced that the resolution relative to an increased subscription by members,and passed by Conference last Easter, would come into force next year. as from the Ist January. It was decided to support the candidature of Miss Cleghorn (Sheffield) for the vice-presidency of the NJ...T.. and as members of the Executive representing Lancashire, Messrs. Pearson, Kay (Liverpool), Sharpies (Manchester), and Aldrott (Blackburn). The next conference of the National Union of Teachers will be held at Plymouth during Easter week, and Messrs. John Upson, F. Longshaw, G. Newburn, J. Cann, W. H. Stansfield and Mrs. Siansfield were elected as delegates repre- senting the local association.—On the motion of Mr. Newburn it was decided to present Mr. J. Cann with an illuminated address as a token of esteem on behalf of the members, and for the valuable work he has dooe on behalf of the Benevolent and Orphan Fund of the N.U.T. Mr. Cann recently resigned the position of local secretary to the fund, and it is interesting to note, that last year, by special effmt, £lOO was raised by 191 local teachers. The presentation will probably take place at the next meeting in March. Several new tnembers were adraitted.

div.head: LIBERAL MEETING AT GRAPPENHALL
div.p: LIBERAL MEETING AT GRAPPENHALL
Speeches by Mr. A. J. Ring, M P., and Sir W. Crossley, M.P.

Mr. A. J. King, M.P., has arranged to hold two meet- ings a night in his constitueucy until the election, and after sneaking at Hatt9n he addressed a second meeting at Grappeahall on Ttursday evening. There was a good attendance, presided over by Mr. J. KenwOrtity, who wcs supported by Sir Wm. J. Crossley, Parr,M.P., Councillor C. Jackson Holcues,and Mr. A. H. Rathbone.

The CHAIRMAN said there was no doubt that we had arrived at a crisis in matters of this country. Those who bad read the htstory of the country for 100 years would see that the House of Lords had rejected or mutilated almost every bill sent to them by a Liberal Government. In these days we found that when there was a meeting in a certain house in London and a decision was arrived at their orders were obeyed as in the ease of the Licens- ing Bill. It was about time that the power of the Lords should be crippled. (Applause). Mr. Balfour in a speech soon after nis defeat in Manchester said that although they were in a minority in the House of Commons the Unionists would govern the country. They now knew that the Unionists were governing the country by way of the House of Lords. That veto ought th be taken away. (Applause). Sir William Crossley, Bart., who was received ,with loud applause, said that they in the House of Commens considered Mr. King to be one of the honesteist, truest, and straightest men in the House. Of course Mr. liing was a peace man—all Quakers 'were peace men— and he honoured them for it.(Hear,hear).He did not know whether it was a practical policy. They were not taking any notice of that as far as the Navy was concerned, for we must have a strong Navy. Alluding to the Budget, he said it provided £3,000,000 for education. if the Germans were gaining on us it was because of their better technical education and we were going to push that forward. The Budget would find all the money that we wanted this year and at the same time it would greatly grow and we should get a little more every year out of the new taxes. We knew definitely from headquarters that the Tariff Reformers meant to tax food. The Budget did not tax food. When we got tariffs trusts were formed. They would say: "We are protdcted from foreign com- petition ; let us take a bit 'more profit." They made a ring and put up the price and of course the working- man was the sufferer. Under Tariff Reform, clothing and food would be increased and as far as be could see house rent would be increased. The latter because a great amount of foreign doors and windows were used in the erecting of houses. If houses were dearer to build, then not so many houses would be built and it would affect ,the builder. If houses were dearer to build then the rents would go up. He contended that Free Trade was best for us all. Sir William dealt at some length with other proposals in the Budget and his remarks were received with enthusiasm.

Mr. King, whose appearance was a signal for loud applause, said that the Literal Government ought to have been in power at least 2 years more. But they were not frightened now that they were to have an election. They were not ashamed of their record,nor of their programme before them.(applause).The prerogative of dissolving Parliament rested with the Crown in the case of our present Constitutional Govern- ment. The Crown was advised to dissolve on the advice of the Prime Minister. That had been the state of things for many hundreds of years. Mr. King said that this election was necessitated by the extreme action of the House of Lords. The House of Lords under the constitution was supposed to be impartial, judicial, and to strengthen the weaker portions of Bills and improve them. They knew that the Lords had long lost any claim to inipartiality. (Hear, hear). The House of Lords was now a promin- ent wing of the Tory opianisation. The result was that when the Conservatives were in power we lived under a single chamber, for everything that the House of Commons did was agreed to. When the Liberals came into office the Upper Ifouse always looked to see if there were anything that effected their own interests. That was not the worst of it. They had been so encouraged by the immunity which bad attended them when they bad mutilated measures that they had been emboldened to claim the right to interfere with the undoubted privilege of the House of Commons over finance. It was for the electors to say whether they would allow the laws and the taxes to be made by those whom they sent or by irresponsible peers. (Applause). Let them look into the character of the two Houses. What about the House of Commons. Ire bad been constantly struck with the fact that in the House of Commons there had not been a matter in question in which some of the members had not been experts—in connection with agriculture, mining and other questions. If they turned to the Education question they had men in the House of Commons of all denominations. Really, the House of Commons was the concentrated essence of all things. What had they in the House of Lords ?—the land-own- ing class, the brewers and the wealthiest men of the land. They had very few men who knew anything about the ordinary business of life. In the House of Commpns they had a rule which was scrupulously obser4d, that if any matter came before the House in which a member of the House was directly interested lie stood aside and did not take part in the debate or vote. In the Upper House they only took part and voted on questions which affected their direct interest. What was the position or the Unionist candidate at, the at next election ? Mr. Sykes was a very good follow, but he was going to ask them to send him to the House of Commons in order that he might sign away and vote away the privileges which their forefathers won for them. (Applause). It had been said that the people loved the peers, but it would be a very bold man who would say that the peers loved the people. (Applause). He maintained that the pension could not be paid solely on Tariff Reform. They would have to adopt most of Mr. Lloyd-George's taxes in order to find the money. He looked forward to the day—and he did not think it was so far distant as some thousht —when the workingpeople of all nations would realise the enormous waste of armaments, and would demand that quarrels should he settled by arbitration. (Applause). In conclusion, Mr. King said that if they voted Unionist, they would confirm the action of the House of Lords, and then the making of laws would have passed out of their hands. He stood by Free Trade because it was best for the country. He believed in the Budget because it would promote the welfare of the community. (Loud applause.) Mr. Holmes moved :—" That this meeting heartily approves of the action of the Knutsford Liberal Association in again adopting Mr. King as our candidate, and also thanks Sir William Crossley for his address." Mr. Rowland seconded, and it was. carried unani- mously

div.head: _LETTER FROM MR. LONG.
div.p: _LETTER FROM MR. LONG.

Mr. King, in his reply, mentioned that he had received a letter from Mr. W. Long, in the course of which he said "Oh for 20 years of one's milestones for such times as these, with the capacity for knocking about or taking one's share of work. However, I know you have a grand lot of good workers, and I hope the result will be satisfactory." He moved a vote of thanks to the Charman, which was heartily accorded.

div.head: LIBERAL WARD MEETINGS.
div.p: LIBERAL WARD MEETINGS.
(Continued from Page 8). Meeting at Church-street.
MR.CROSFIELD ON "THE GAMBLE WITH THE
PEOPLE'S LIBERTIES."

On Thursday evening a meeting was held i the National Schools, Church-street, when there was another very large and enthusiastic gathering. Mr. George Walker presided, and was supported on the platform by Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., Councillor Middleton (Oldham), Councillor Locker, Councillor Wilkinson, Messrs. C. E. Parker, J. Dodds, P. Peacock, E. Wynne-Jones, J. Jarman, G. Wallington, IV. Clegg, and J. Howes, junr. The CHAIRMAN said the dissolution had not teen brought about because the Government had lost the confidence of its supporters in the House of Commons or in the country. It was certainly one of the finest and most democratic Governments we had ever had, and its legislation would rank with the best that had ever been passed in the history of the country. If the Conservatives were so greatly in favour of old age pensions as the professed to be, how was it that only , 12 voted for the third reading? The l3udget was a splendid measure, for it taxed wealth and rot poverty, and insisted that men who for sadly too long had lived on the energies of the democracy, should gmke a sacrifice more commensurate with their rewards. (Cheers). Mr. E. WYNNE-JONES said he noticed that •

SIR GILBERT GREENALL HAD BEEN COMPLAINING that from the Liberal side they got nothing hut abuse. He (Mr. Wynne Jones) thought the other side could give them a great deal in that, respect. Sir Gilbert might have referred to the words of --Lord Rosebery, who said that ia that House of nearly 600 Peers there were only 150 who were fitted, either by ability, ,experienue or anything else, to pronounce a judgment, ranch less give a vote upon a sgbject like the Finance Bill. (Cheers.) The House of Lords was the one barrier that stood in the way of all progressive reform and the issue they had to face was the extinction of the veto of the House of Lords or the extinction of Liberalism. Under Tariff Reform the price of food would be increased by lat least 10 per cent, so that the ss. pension which had brought so much joy, peace and harmony into many a home would be worth only 4s. 6d. Councillor MIDDLE'ros than delivered an interesting and racy speech. He said the electors would have to make the choice between " supper ra " and a "super tax " which were the outcome of Tariff Reform and Free Trade Finance respectively. The Dukes who objected to pay their fair share of taxation had behaved in a mean, shabby and contemptible spirit. (Cheers.) It was for the people to make sure that the Lords had said the "lest word" on finance for the last time. (Cheers) Mr. A. H. CROSFIELD, M.P., who had a magnificent reception, said that at the coming election they would not only haveagain to defend the Free Trade citadel, captured sixii years ago, but they would also have to defend what was won for them by their ancestors a great deal further back—the right of representative government. (Cheers.) Amongst the able men in the Conservative party who had refused to have anything to do with the preposterous and disgraceful attempt to go tack to the evil system of Protection was the late Lord Goschen who summed up the controversy very effectively when he told his fellow-countrymen that it was nothing less than a gamble with the food of the people. To-day they were face to face with the same gamble, but with another tacked on to it—a GAMBLE WTH THE PRIMARY LIBERTIES Or THE

• BRITISH CITIZEN. (Cheers.) The Protectionists had over-shot their mark and no part of the country knew that better than Lancashire. (Cheers.) When they met to celebrate the coming victory—(cheers)—which would be fraught with such great consequences for the country, they would not forget the good work that Mr. Winston Caurchill— (cheers)—one of the very advanced and progressive members of their party, had put in. (Cheers.) So far aa his (Mi. Crosfield's) politicil recollections extended —and he took a keen interest in politics a long way back into his teens—he could assure them that he could not remember a time when the different ranks of the great progressive army were so splendidly united as they were to-day. (Cheers.) As Sir Edward Grey said the other day, they were

div.head: ABSOLUTRLY UNITED
div.p: ABSOLUTRLY UNITED

and they would go into the battle on the question of finance and the pernicious irresponsible veto of the Lords, with their whole strength. (Cheers). He sub- mitted that looking at the matter with the full responsibility of free British citizens, they must come to the conclusion that the time had now arrived for them to make a good job of this business. (Cheers). The continual rejection or rnutiliation of Liberal measures by the House of Lords was not only an indignity to the Ministers of the Crown but, through them, to the whole democracy of Britain. (Cheers). He had bad four years of Parliamentary life aril year after year it had been borne in upon hies that the present condition of thines, apart from the question of money Bills, was absolutely impossible. When he heari people who were supposed to be responsible people talking about "DAMNING THE CONSEQUENCES" , he knew what they meant. They wanted to "dam" the stream of progress—probably in more senses than one and he was sorry to see that in some cases they had found opinion so awkward in the country that they had started to " damn " their audiences. (Laughter.) He did not regret that the House of Lords had now made the biggest mistake of their, lives. They had done it; the people had to deal with them, and the fight was coming very soon. (Cheers.) Mr. Crosfield dealt with the Free Trade issue, pointing out that the simple. solid foundation of Britain's marvellous commercial success was low cost of production, and in his opinion it was nothing short of sheer idiocy, it was even suicidal to ask us deliberately to throw away that advantage. (Cheers). He hoped the people would give such an answer to the great questions now b.fore them as would settle them once and for all. (Cheers). The Government were bent on social reform. They had got their heel on sweating, and they meant to stop it. (Cheers). They had tackled it, partially by trade hoards and they had perhaps a bigger question to face in dealing with shop hours because, to his mind, many of the HOURS WORKED IN SHOPS were simply criminal. (Cheers). The Government had been kicsed out not because the King had decided in consultation with his Ministers to dissolve Parliament, hut because those men who had been trying, step by step, to encroach on the liberties of the people had thought that with the aid of their plutocratic Press and all the arts and dodges of machine-made politics they would be able to gull the people. (Cheers). After discussing the objects for whim the Budget sought to provide funds, Mr. Crosfield replied to a member of the audience who raised a question with regard to the out-relief disquali- fication for the old age pension. He said he was glad the point had been riised,'because if the Budget passed one of the very first things Mr. Lloyd- Georee looked forward to accomplishing was the removal of that pauper her. (Loud cheers.) In con- clusion, Mr. Crosfield said there was plenty of good work ahead of them. When they had put an end to the poser of the reactionaries, they would go on with steady, orderly and useful democratic reform for the good of the old country and of the whole of our people (Loud and prolonged cheers.) Mr. Dodds Raid he knew from his experience of the people of Warrington that, whatever their politics might be, when they, clearly understood a great moral issue they were willing to support the cause in which they put their faith. (Cheers.) If the electors were persuaded to go in for tariff reform, whoever else got the advantage it would be at

TILE COST OF THE COMMON PEOPLE. (Hear, bear). The Lords had never taken a single fetter off liberty in this country and not in any instance had they freely supported the development of freedom. The electors had "got them '' this time and they would take good c tre to draw their teeth, so that never again would they he able to ston the progress of the people's cause. (Cheers.) Mr. Dodds asked his hearers to beware of the attempts that were being nude to raise a

div.head: SCARE .AGAINST GERMANY.
div.p: SCARE .AGAINST GERMANY.

From his experience he knew that the Germans did not want war but were as anxious as we were to live at peace, at any rate for a long time to come. He wanted the country to have plenty of naval strength to defend her coasts but he hoped to see the time when, in the development of God's moral laws, people would forget about differences of nationality and creed and unite on the principles—which were the principles of the Free Trade movement—that God made man of one flesh, and it xvas His will that we should exchange our various products the world over, to the mutual advantage of all. (Cheers.) Mr. C. E, PARKER, Mr. P. PRACOCK and others also spoke and a vote of thanks to the chairman and speakers was enthusiastically accorded.

div.head: LAST NIGHT'S MEETING.
div.p: LAST NIGHT'S MEETING.

• Another Crowded and enthusiastic meeting was held last evening in St. James' schools, Latchford. Mr. E. Wynne Jones presided and was supported on the platform by Captain Crestleld, Mr. and Mrs. C. E. Parker, Mr. J. Dodds, Councillor Locker, INTeisrs. R. Posrett (Runcorn), I'. Pemberton, J. C. Holland, P. O'Brien, J. Jarman and P. Peacock.

Mr. C. E. PARKER pt.inted out that we imporeed a great deal of our foodstuffs from the United States and yet in New York, the capital of that great wheat- growing area, the people paid almost double the amount for their bread to what was charged in this country. That was owing to the great trusts and combines which grew under Protection. (Applause). Captain CROSPIELD said he believed he was right at this juncture in throwing in his lot with the Liberal party because be was of opinion that their maintenance of Free Trade and their sympathetic attitude towards the masses were likely to promote peace and to stimu- late patriotism. (Applause). The other speakers included Mr.% H. Posnett, Mr. J. Upson, Mr. J. Jarman end Mr. P. Peacock.

div.head: EMPIRE RINK.
div.p: EMPIRE RINK.

The increasingly popular and well managed Empire Rink in Museum-street, announces special attractions. for Xmas week. A n.uinber of coloured lamps have been added to the already elaborate illuminations, and the new " cinemato " is soon to be in operation. Announcements of all kinds will be thrown on the screen, and some uncommon flash-lights will be thrown on the skaters. A waltzing competition open to, everybody is announced for 'I hursday evening next, and some valuable prizes will be awarded. Expert skaters from Manchester, Liverpool and other towns are expected to compete. On Christmas Eve there. will be a mistletoe session, a complete novelty to• rinkers. We haye not got particulars of the pro- gramme for this occasion, but we imagine it should be attractive and amusing, as well as seasonable. The great event of this past week has been the grand Kelly night on. Thursday. There were 350' skaters present and 200 spectators. Little Hugo, the- marvellous trick skater from Karno's troupe at the Hippodrome, appeared as Kelly in a wonderful costume, and did some side-splitting things on the rollers. Four members of the Hockey team as burlesque postmen, delivered envelopes to the ladies. present, from the contents of which they had to find Kelly. The winners were Miss Bibby and Miss, Minards, and their respective prizes were a handsqme- silver belt, and a crocodile leather and silver purse.

div.head: PRIORY SCHOOL.
div.p: THE PRIORY SCHOOL.

There was a urge attendance on Wednesday last, at the Assembly Hall, Winmarleigh-street, on the occasion of the Priory School concert and prize distribution, The first part of the programme c msisted of pianoforte solos and a fancy dance, also two action songs given by the younger pupils. After the report had been read by the head-mistress (Miss Dring) Councillor Fulton- Smith gave a short address and then distributed the. and certificates. The proceedings closed with a capital performance of the operetta "Santa Clause in Japan." The singing and pretty dresses of the children, were much appreciated by the audience, and reflected great credit on those who had trained them. Royal Court Theatre. At the Royal Conn Theatre this week Mr. and Mrs. F. G. Kimberley's company present " Her Secret Lover " which is described as Mrs. Kimberley's. masterpiece. It is certainly a story of enthralling interest, and a capable company does justice to the many powerful and exciting scenes. Miss Lillian Herries, as Ivy Seymour, takes chief honours by her sympathetic portrayal.—Next week the theatre will be closed, re-opening on Monday, the 27th inst., with. Mr. T. E. Ward's new production " His Real Wife."

WARRINGTON BLUE COAT CHARITY SCHOOL. —NOTICE IS HEREBY GIVEN, that the TRUSTEES of the above SCHOOL will, at their neAt Quarterly Meeting, on the 17th day of January next, proceed to elect three children (3 Boys) to Vacancies now existing in the Institution. No Candidate will be eligible unless an application on his or her behalf (forms of which may be obtained from the Clerk, at his Office, 3, Winwick street), shall have been, made to the Clerk to the Trustees, at least four- teen days previous to the day of Meeting. In electing Children, the Trustees make Orphans their first choice. Those deprived of one parent come next in consideration, and after them the children of parents who have the deatest number and the slenderest means. Dated this 16th day of December, 1909. HENRY GR EENALL, Clerk to the Trustees.

The Committee invite application from fully-qualified Medical Practitioners for the appointment of MEDICAL OFFICER to the Workmen, Membership about 2,000 to 2,500. Remuneration at the rate of 38. 6d. per annum for each member. The doctor provides all necessary medicines, oils, bandages, Sze. Private practice is (allowed, but no other works club, friendly society, or public appointments are to be taken. Candidates to-state age and qualifications, and to be prepared to begin the duties on the Ist February next. The doctor must reside in the immediate vicinity of the works. Any further information may be obtained from the undersigned, to whom applications should be addressed not later than 31st December, 1909. P. C. PRICE, Secretary. Bewsey Offices, Warrington.
